reviews: Seems I missed the "removable" part in the name, because I got these thinking they'd be just super-sticky, and I was disappointed that they weren't.  But, now knowing what they're supposed to be - basically, super Post-its that are all adhesive and no loose paper - I can review them in that light.My first note on this product was that they didn't stick at all well to the plastic kitchen garbage cans that I use as recycle bins - they basically peeled themselves off within a day or two.  I later found some very fine print on the packaging stating that they might not adhere well to certain textured plastics, and I had to concede that the bins do have a very slight texture on the exterior.  I stuck another one on an untextured part of the interior of the bin, and it appears to be sticking fine.Everything else that I've stuck the labels to so far has been good - smooth plastic storage bins, painted metal panels, and paper.  Unsticking and re-placing the stickers has also gone well on all of those surfaces, though you do need a fingernail or other thin object to get the first corner of the sticker up.Although my package is labeled for laser printer use, I had no problem printing a sheet in my inkjet (even twice on the same sheet, one of them backwards from the recommended feed direction).  The standard Microsoft Word Avery template called out on the sheets works, but I did have to adjust the upper margin to get it to print right; although the sheet has uniform 1/2" top and bottom margins, the printer moved everything down 1/8".The only real complaint I had with these, other than not sticking to the textured plastic, is that they include 4 each of the yellow, green, and pink sticker sheets, but only 3 blues, and the blue is, IMHO, the best color.  The yellow is a very bright yellow without crossing into fluorescent.  The green is likewise a bright lime that's not quite fluorescent, and the pink is about halfway between fluorescent and hot pink.  The blue is kind of a deep aqua color.

The Epson WorkForce WR-3620 has been a dream of a printer for setup and use. We have been using it regularly for the last month without any complaints.First, setup: Plug in, install ink, and connect to wifi...done. There are very easy pictorial instructions that outline what to do. I would recommend that from the beginning you set the printer up for Epson Connect and Google Print. Setup is pretty easy for both of these, all told from opening the box to printing from a mac, iPhone, and windows PC remotely via Google Print took about 15 minutes.Epson Connect lets me print easily from my iPhone and iPad. Google Print lets me print (even remotely) from Google Chrome on any computer connected to the internet even remotely (without installing drivers). This flexibility in printing from multiple sources in a flexible variety of ways is a nice benefit of this and other Epson printers that I have used.Printing performance is very good as well. Printing, particularly black pages of text, is incredibly quick (reported at 19 ppm). The quality is very high; I agree with the advertising that it is a laser replacement. The ink is not as water resistant as laser, but it is definitely much more water resistant than previous experiences I have had with ink jet ink which runs on contact with water. This just has some slight smudging when soaked in water. Touching the dry printed page with wet fingers does not smudge the ink at all. As a Realtor, I used to use a laser printer for the purpose of not having printed contracts ruined by pages getting slightly wet. I now have no need for a laser printer.The scanner auto feeder works well but not perfectly, jamming up more often than I would like especially if there are any creases in the page, but for flat pages, we can run through stacks of 30 pages without any jamming or multiple-page-at-a-time problems.I am incredibly happy with this printer. You may want to consider getting the WF-3640 however, due to the larger paper tray (500 instead of 250).After a month of regular use we have not yet had to replace ink, so I cannot speak to how quickly the ink runs out.

I do not believe many reviewers have thoroughly tested this product. We tried them in a variety of printers, in a variety of environments (hot/cold/humid/etc), and on a variety of media (paper, cardboard, glossy cardstock, plastic). Our results were nearly identical to other Post-It label products.In summary, a fantastic product, but with a near fatal flaw for many people - paper jamming. Here are our results:* Colors: A subdued neon - 3-4 sheets of each color: green, yellow, blue, and pink. The colors are great for reading black text. (Other brands we've tried are too bright, and distract from the text.)* Adhesion: Seriously exceptional. They stick great to a variety of surfaces: file folders, file folders, cardboard boxes, regular copy paper, books, plastic (i.e., shrink wrapped items & blister packs). They even stick well to textured surfaces, like the side or back of a VHS tape. Same results each time - great adhesion. I'd even feel ok using these as shipping labels.* Temperature: We tried these in warm (80F) and cold (20F). They do exceptionally well in the cold - even standard packing tape has problems in 20, but these adhere pretty well. They do not fall off easily.* Moisture: They even hold up well when slightly damp, or exposed to slight humidity. Unfortunately there is no way to report any "long term" testing at this time (i.e., if your records storage is not climate controlled - but I have no reason to suspect any problems).* Removability: Yes! They peel clean & easy.* Re-usable: Yes! If using on cardboard, they can peel & re-use 3 or 4 times. If using on file folders, or a smoother surface (blister packs, glossy book covers, etc), even more. Adhesion is great.* Printer Jams: OOPS! ... design flaw may affect some people. Tested in 5 machines - jammed at least once in every machine. It jams in our laser printer & laser copier nearly 25% of the time. It jammed in our ink jet printer once or twice.The problem is that these are slightly thicker than some cardstocks, and slightly wider than 8.5" (actually about 8.55"). They don't feed in our plain paper copier/fax machine AT ALL - the paper width cannot be adjusted, and it simply wont grab the sheet.WHEN PRINTING: Make sure the paper width in your printer can adjust slightly, and make sure not to mix them with other types of paper - take out your copy paper when printing with these labels. Also, it tends to feed better through "straight feed" printers (like our ink jet) as opposed to laser printers which feed paper through an S-shaped drum. And, if your printer has had problems with thick papers, such as cardstock, expect problems with these too.* Re-feeding through printer: Here's another potential problem. They work best in only one direction. It's not designed to print 10 labels, turn it over, and print 10 different labels at some point in the future. That will waste labels for some people, who don't need to print 30 labels at a time. Also, if you try to feed it through a laser printer more than once, the edges will start peeling (due to the heat I suppose, which is not an issue with ink jet printers).* Laser vs Ink Jet: When they did feed properly, the resolution was great on both types of printer. This is also an impressive accomplishment - be advised when most label companies say *both* laser and ink jet, they really mean it's been designed for ink jet, and your laser toner may or may not flake off.* Cross-comparison: We compared these to 3M, HP, Avery, Office Depot Brand, and Office Max brand removable labels. They rank BEST for adhesion, temperature, removability, and re-usability...but *WORST* for printer jamming.* Conclusion: They are excellent in every way except for occasional paper jams.

2nd UPdate - I'm pleased to say that despite having to have this repaired relatively quickly, Epson customer service was superb. We boxed up the scanner and sent it to a repair shop. Communication was excellent throughout the entire process. It was repaired and returned quickly. Epson followed up during the repair and after to make sure everyone was taken care of properly and in a timely fashion. Very pleased with how the repair was handled and machine is working just fine to date.----------Original update followsOriginally I gave this a five star review because it works exactly as advertised, was easy to hook-up, performed perfectly with all software including adaptive software for the visually impared and provided terrific results. Unfortunately, it only took a month before breaking down so long term reliability may be questionable. Contacting Epson customer support has yielded moderate results - they are domestic based which is nice but require user to have repaired at their authorized repair center (the nearest to use is over 100 miles away so we will be packing and shipping at our expense). Wait time is 4-6 weeks once received. Fortunately we have another and use this for personal use but would be a serious inconvenience for small business/home office users.After reading other review it appears this is not an isolated problem and far from rare - what are the chances of the same problem cropping up? Feeder is indeed the issue for this as well followed by scanning mechanism. Epson would not send replacement but rather wants to have repaired instead.Bottom line - appears to be of dubious quality and prone to scanner/feeder problems.----original review follows----Any scanner that names itself "perfection" is really asking for trouble but fortunately, this Epson actually lives up to the name and the claim! To be frank, I didn't have much of an expectation for this color scanner in part because it is an Epson...years ago I used to purchase only Epson products but was so disappointed and frusted by the last few that I switched to Brother.About a year ago I purchased a small color scanner from Canon which had received good reviews but it was so totally lacking that I sent it back. Needless to say, I didn't have high expectations for this but since I have literally thousands of old photos, negatives, documents (documents, documents) a scanner is essential. For documents, I've been enjoying the Epson Workforce Pro GT S50 which is blazing fast, has a small footprint and performs like a true workhorse (again, Epson is living up to their name!)and earns every bit of it's reputation...it's amazing but it's built for documents. However, the current Epson Perfection v500 is very similar to the photo scanner with the addition of a feed for documents which makes it especially well suited for a do-everything scanner. I was especially interested in how it would perform with photographs. I'm thrilled to say it was far superior to the canon which was utterly dismal despite the reviews...the was faster and resulted in far more clear results. Hands down there simply waas not a comparision.Hook-up and installation was extremely simple - no compatibility issues. I've just purchased a new computer and will be installing Windows 7 on it so I'll try to report back to see how it peforms with that. However, it worked equally well with vista and xp without major drama. The energy efficient status is very nice, it's a quite machine and although a bit larger than the other, still compact enough that it doesn't use up a lot of space. Additionally, the Mercury Free LED and other "green" features are great ideas (about time!).A special consideration of supreme importance in this household is the ability to work with accessibility software including ZoomText for those with low vision and/or other disability. I am very glad to report both Epson scanners have worked flawlessly. Superb product for those running accessibility software and in need of a compatible scanner without a huge price tag.

We were hoping that this printer could replace our aging HP Laserjet 2100 and help us move to a paperless home office for all our Macs. Bottom line: no go. (For comparison, the LaserJet 2100 is decade+ old technology, but extremely reliable, and needs new toner only every couple of years or so.)Installation:- I have the latest version of Mac OS X, 10.8.3 and the latest driver download from Epson crashes when running it: can't install. I was able to instal the software over the network from another computer which has a DVD drive.Controls and Display:- The controls are easy to use and well labeled, but the display is incredibly low contrast. Direct light from in front of the printer is needed to read the LCD. It's not usable in the place we'd prepared for it in our home office. The most mysterious light on the front display is labeled "ADF", but it's not described on p. 1, "Using the Control Panel".Scanning:- Scanning over the network (tested with wired ethernet) works, but the software crashes frequently.- Scanning by initiating from the printer, doesn't work for us: the printer gets hung up in some kind of "processing" state; "Busy, try again later". Rebooting the printer doesn't help. "Test Settings" button causes the app to crash.OCR (Optical Character Recognition):This is a very cool feature to have in a scanner. In theory, what you get isn't just an image of your document, but instead an actual word doc with text you can search.- It isn't part of the printer: rather, it's separately included software and an extra step must be performed if wanted. Unfortunately, the software doesn't hook directly into the scanning software: it will only "Get Images From:" a file. And worse, the Mac version does not convert into "searchable PDF", just a PDF with a big image in it instead of text. So it's pretty much useless.Printing:- Printing in draft mode is fast, and pPrinting in the highest quality mode is half the speed of our old HP LJ 2100.- The printed output is low quality: characters aren't as smooth as the Laserjet.- Also, fonts aren't correct, to my eyes: Helvetica 10/12 is much too heavy.- The printer makes a high pitched squeal after every print job.Economy:A big selling point is that the printer is cheaper to run than a Laser. It would take months to compare, but we can look at the performance claimed by the manufacturers:- Epson WF-M1560* 223XL Black* $47.99 at epson.com.* 2400 pages* Cost per 1 ream (500 pages): $10.00.- HP Laserjet 2100* Our decade+ old, but very reliable laser printer which needs new toner every couple of years.* HP 96A toner cartridge* $128.99 at hp.com.* 5000 pages* Cost per 1 ream (500 pages): $12.90.Bottom Line:- It's no good for replacing an old HP Laserjet nor to make a Mac-based home office paperless, because OCR doesn't work properly.- Scanning is a pain: only works reliably by initiating the scan from the computer.- Printing quality is too low quality and too incorrect to use for professional documents.

This printer is suitable for a small home office. It has a simple setup, fast text printing,  and good network support with some nifty scanning options, but will take up a lot of space on the desktop and may have some issues with Windows XP machines. The printer comes with two standard size ink cartridges (XL versions are available for re-order), a USB cable, a phone cord, and a sample box of small photo paper.  Because I already have a fax printer, I did not look at the fax features.Pro:It has good specifications for this price point. It prints around 8.5 on the new printer scale in black, and about 4 when printing black.  It doesn't take a long time to print like some HP inkjets I have owned - the print starts and completes very rapidly. The document feeder will hold about 15 pages or so.The paper path is straight through, meaning that it is fairly simple to print on photo paper and Avery labels due to the a smooth paper path. The printer is designed such that the input and output trays are at very steep angles, so they don't take up as much room.The printer has a nice feature where one can press a single button and scan to a selected PC connected to the home network. The file then goes into a directory on the computer for later use. This feature works with the document feeder or the flatbed scanner, so one could easily scan in several pages. It is a great time saver because you don't have to "scan in" the document; it is "pushed" to the computer you select while you stay at the printer. Note here that for maximum scanning resolutions, the manual recommends using the flatbed rather than the feeder.The wireless setup was as described in the manual, and although it wasn't particularly detailed, the steps did work. But there wasn't a lot of explanation for the less experienced person, and the printer does not support the newer easy network setup options. I found it a lot easier to install on the Windows 7 machine, where one can simply add a printer via the built it menus; on XP one has to install the CD, which also downloads software at some points in the process. The network setup requires a USB connection to a computer; there are no setup menus to manually enter the network keys. But at least they include a cable.The device has the capability to scan to a thumb drive (or an external hard drive, I suppose), and the same USB port is used for PictBridge printing directly from a camera. The printer can connect to Bluetooth devices - but needs an optional Bluetooth module, so I could not test it.The printer does not use a power "brick", so the power cabling around the printer is clean.Con:There is no backlight for the LCD display, and I found it hard to read without shining some additional  light. I did not expect the same display quality as an LED screen, for example, but the device needs some kind of backlight. Plan to keep a small flashlight handy, or be sure the area near the printer is well lit.There is only one color cartridge, rather than separate cartridges for each color. That means if one runs out of (for example) cyan, the entire cartridge has to be replaced. This kind of system is more expensive to keep in ink. I'm a bit surprised, because my last Canon MX offered support for individual cartridges. Therefore if you print a lot of color, this device may be more expensive than a machine that supports individual cartridges.This printer is very large compared to other printers I have owned, including another Canon MX series multifunction device. It is designed so that it is not too tall (maybe a foot or so high), but is about 30% deeper and a bit wider than other multifunction printers. Basically, it is designed wide, deep and flat, whereas many printers today are more vertical. Additionally, the only path for the paper is via the input tray - on the back of the machine, taking up another several inches of depth.  Maybe this form factor is needed for some people; but in any case be aware and check the dimensions to be sure it suits your purposes.The scanner is a little bit slow, but acceptable for light use.There is only one input tray, and it holds only 30 pages. That isn't a lot of paper, and I would not recommend this printer for other than light home use unless one likes feeding paper to the machine.On my XP machine, I was unable to scan directly into Word 2000; the scan would preview but not actually scan. On my Windows 7 machine with the exact same version of software, I was able to scan directly.There is no SD or other card slot; one has to have a USB drive to print directly without a computer connection. Most printers have some kind of support for a memory card.Not really a true drawback, but several places in the owner's manual there are procedures for cleaning up the area around the print heads and interior. This is the first time I've seen such instructions, and it leads me to believe that the printer design may put some ink residue around the output area that may need to be cleaned up periodically.Summary: This is a decent printer at a decent price. For relatively light home office use it is acceptable; it prints fine and can scan directly to a remote computer from the printer itself, which will save time if a lot of stuff has to be scanned. If one prints a lot of black it will not be too expensive to keep in ink. Recommend for the smaller office or personal use.

I was given this product in exchange for an honest review, so here you go:I took it out of it's box (unlike some reviewers mine was simply just in the box, no zip ties) and spent the next 2 minutes figuring out how to put the staples in it. That's kind of annoying.However, that said, I then proceeded to staple all sorts of stuff around my apartment, including stapling a decorative border around the box from Amazon, and then staple sewing it to two other boxes.  So yeah, it goes through 3 layers of cardboard with no problems.  I also tested it on various thicknesses of paper and over other staples (I'm not the only one who staples something five times, right?)  Then on fabric and on that plastic packaging that every damn craftsman tool I bought from sears has been coming in lately.  (You know the type - it's also what you have to pry things like USB sticks and SD cards out of.)Based on that:WOW!  Didn't jam once.  That is...impressive to say the least.  I'm usually very good at jamming staplers.  I had to actually put a bent staple in it to jam it.  I see several other reviewers complaining about jams...so I don't know if they fixed it or if I just got a really good one.It also didn't put out any double staples or fail to feed.It also staples more than 25 pages though ultimately the real limit is when it can't fold the staple over any more.  It'll still drive it gamely in though....it just won't stay for obvious reasons.It's also really fast and smooth.  I sewed those boxes together quick in one smooth row.Design is easy to press down - would reduce fatigue if for some reason you actually use a stapler more than 30 sec a day.That said, I can't give it 5 stars because1) the sticking up flap annoys me and it's easy to get caught on things.  (At first, I thought it would also make certain tight areas harder to get to, but you can always put the bottom part in and staple that way, so it's good.)  Also, even though it's reasonably stable, because the top part sticks up it's easy to knock over.2) It also doesn't have the depth of my other much older Swingline...so if you're stapling in the middle of something you won't get as far.3) The far bigger flaw is that you cant open it up (so that the top and bottom swing 180 degrees apart and the stapler part can be pushed against things like upholstery or walls or whatever).  To me this is a big deal...there's a lot of times that's super handy.  The loss of this feature is the #1 reason I can't give it 5 stars.  I looked it up - Swingline calls this feature "tacking" To be honest, I didn't realize it wasn't a standard feature...most have it.

The first thing I noticed, as I lifted this out of its box, was how heavy it was...For accuracy and because I want to be thorough in these reviews I weight it and it's 2.25 lbs.)  By way (weigh ?) of comparison, myX-ACTO SharpX Portable Battery Pencil Sharpeneris 0.75 lbs.  My sense is much of the 1.5 pound difference went into  additional "motor" and rugged sharpening blades.The second thing I noticed was how well it sharpened a pencil...A comparison of the two sharpening mechanisms it interesting.  The heart of my portable sharpener is one of those simple, single blade, hand held sharpeners, for example one of these:School Smart Hand Held Plastic Pencil Sharpenerstuck to the end of a motor.  This sharpener has two steel shafts that are covered with spiral cutting edges which come to a point.  That difference may account for the second thing I noticed.  This large, heavy duty sharpener is quieter, much quieter in fact, than the smaller portable unit.  It also may explain why the Westcott Axis constantly creates a smooth point, both along the wood and graphite, while the portable and admittedly less expensive unit creates gashes, gouges, and all too often results in broken points.The third thing I noticed was how easily it sharpened a pencil...Between its weight and rubber feet, this sharpener sits solidly on my desk. I've always been a fan of writing with pencils; perhaps its ability to easily erase mistakes or maybe it's just the nostalgia.  In any case, if you're a regular pencil pusher then you know all too well the struggles with finding a good pencil sharpener.  Some never sharpen to a point and just eat your pencil.  Some sharpen uneven and lopsided which is annoying.  Some just continuously break the pencil tip no matter how carefully you try to sharpen them.  When I saw the "Westcott iPoint Curve Axis Electric Heavy Duty Pencil Sharpener" I knew I wanted to give it a go.  Here are my thoughts;Pros+ Sharpens pencils quickly and generally to a decent point.+ Easy to empty shavings bin (unless it's extremely full, then it can be a bit of a pain).+ Emptying the shavings bin is simple and is clear to see when it's full.+ Safety sharpening feature stops the unit from unnecessarily eating your pencils.+ Small and sleek design.+ 5 year warranty.Cons- You really should use two hands when sharpening. Also, changing the container when it's full of shavings can be messy and bothersome.  It works just fine for both casual and moderate use.  However, if you're a very active user of pencils I'd suggest investing in a more heavy duty electric powered sharpener.  The "Westcott iPoint Curve Axis Electric Heavy Duty Pencil Sharpener" is perfect for our home office and computer room.

Let's face it - there aren't a lot of differences in mailing labels, so they're hard to evaluate on their own.  I compared these side by side with the same size Avery Eco-Friendly labels (48160)to provide a little contrast, but I'll try to restrict my comments here to just the merits and failings of these particular labels.The included illustrated instruction sheet is quite useful, but it's only in English.  There are feed direction instructions on the top of each label sheet in English.  The stickiness of these labels is quite good; they're relatively easy to peel off the backer (3/5), peel with some difficulty (but cleanly) off regular cardboard with and without packing tape and shipping labels (4/5) and restick fairly well, stick fine to glossy cardboard (3/5) and restick almost as well, and are moderately difficult to peel off paper and take some of the paper with them (3/5), though suprisingly they still restick OK the first time.  The popup edge to help peel the labels off the sheet is OK, and not as well executed as Avery's.  If you tear off a column from the sheet of three, however, it leaves the popup edges exposed so they'll try to stick to whatever you set the tearoff down on and/or lose their stickiness on that edge by getting dusty. There are two popup perforations in the spaces between each column (and none on the outer edges of the sheet): one for the column to the right, one for the column to the left.I used the recommended built-in Avery 5160 template in MS Word 2003 to test these labels.  There was a little horizontal offset so that the left edge of the table cell fell off the cut label.  There was some vertical offset all the way down the page, so that the lower edge of the upper labels printed on the top of the label above (tested with a table row filled with color next to a blank row).  The lower margin is outside the printable range of my HP OfficeJet 6480 printer (and probably many inkjets), so unless the label contents stay well above the bottom edge of the table cell, the last row of labels gets truncated printing.  The labels have a fairly rounded corner, so while it's a more attractive shape than the smaller-radius corners on the Avery labels, more of the corner material in the table cells falls off these labels.  The ink dried fast.

Many years ago, when I was in school and dinosaurs roamed the Earth, single subject notebooks were all the same: 70 pages, a coil that reached out and scratched, and that weird perforation that left little dangling things from ripped out pages.My how things have changed.  My daughter always asked for "five star" when I was buying her school supplies, and I never understood why, even as I bought the premium school notebooks.  Today I sat down with these notebooks and found out why she liked them so much.Great covers:  instead of coated cardboard, the cover on these notebooks is a textured plastic. Lasts longer than cardboard and looks better.Back over with new binder feature: the back cover has a clever way of attaching it to your three ring binder. Pretty slick, even if I did need the kid to show me how it worked.Pockets.  Inside the notebook, the five star people have put in a couple of pockets so your handouts can stay with the notes.Tucked in binding wire.  Instead of getting attacked with binder wire, causing lasting scratches and destroyed sweater sets, this notebook has the binding wire tucked in.  It can't scratch you.Nice Paper.  The paper is of good quality, with little show through and tiny micro-perforations that keep you from having weird little dangling things hanging off your report.Is this notebook worth a premium price? Papermate's InkJoy is yet another low-viscosity, oil-based ballpoint.  It is similar to Parker's QuinkFlow, Schmidt's EasyFlow, Monteverde's SoftRoll, and some Japanese pens of brands I cannot recall at the moment.  There are slight differences (Paper Mate's version is a tiny bit smoother), but they are mostly similar.The ink flows a little smoother than normal ballpoint ink, but does not heap onto the paper like a gel or water-based ink.  This makes it smoother than a standard ballpoint, but the ink does not get used up as fast as a gel (though most gels have a wider reservoir).  It also allows for a smoother pen without a wide point.The drawback is a tendency for the ink to go on too thin, and it does not write as dark as other types of pens even though the ink, in the same quantity, may be just as dark or even darker than cheaper pens.  Medium-quality paper is OK, but extra smooth writing paper shows more pale spots as it writes.I am going to use these for my press-through style checkbook.  The fine-yet-smooth tip is great for that.  But for daily notes, I prefer something else.  If you want to stay cheap, Papermate's own Profile series is better for general purpose writing with darker saturation.If you tend to write small, this finer point is better than the thick lines produced by gel pens.

Self sealing envelopes are not a new idea.  Where I grew up, that's all we've had available to us for all of my lifetime, so I was surprised to come to live in the US and find that people were still licking envelopes to close them.  When I saw this item, my first thought was "oh, thank goodness - at last!"  The self-seal aspect of the envelope works very well.  The glue seems to seal the envelope well and keep it sealed.  The only issue I have had with them is that the glue seems to want to hold the flap down prior to use and I had to ease it up in order to fold it in and seal it.  My concern would be that with time, the flaps might actually seal open and thus be unusable.These envelopes also have a security feature to allow you to mail checks without risk that the contents of the envelope can be read.  I can't remember the last time I needed to mail a check so I will not need to use them for this purpose.  Nevertheless, being able to send correspondence with full assurance that the envelope cannot be held up to the light and the contents read through the paper, provides a degree of confidence in the product.Last, I wanted to add that the paper from which the envelopes are made is high quality, thick paper.  The envelopes do not feel flimsy at all.  I suspect this makes them less likely to be torn while going through the postal machines, and in fact less likely to get in or cause a jam of the USPS equipment.

I don't prepare very many written reports (I use electronic media) but I do like to write mini-diaries of trips with some photos of the highlights, and share them with family and friends. Before trying this paper, I had been using a similar, but lighter weight Georgia Pacific 20 pound paper -GP Copy & Print Paper, 8.5 x 11 Inches Letter Size, 92 Bright White, 20 Lb, 5 Reams/Carton (2500 Sheets) (998068C)The heavier weight of this 24 pound paper also gives it greater thickness.  I measured the height of a ream of this 24 pound paper at 2.25" vs. 2.0" for a ream of the 20 pound paper.The print quality using my laser printer appeared to be the same with both the 24 pound and 20 pound paper.  I also used an inkjet printer to print a recipe which had both black and red text and a small color photograph of the fully prepared food.  Both papers handled the text well, but this 24 pound paper seemed to reproduce the photograph with slightly brighter colors.This thicker paper should also be better for two sided printing since there is less chance of ink bleeding through or print being visible from the reverse side of the paper.  Also, the thicker paper has a better "feel" to it - the thicker sheet is less flimsy than the lighter paper.  Unlike some other reviewers, I did not observe any vertical or other ridges on the surface of the paper.  They may have received a bad batch.This 24 pound paper, however, costs substantially more than its lighter weight cousin and I intend to continue to use the lighter weight paper for everyday printing.  But when I need to print a document that requires two sided printing or is designed to impress, this 24 pound paper will definitely be my choice.

Ok, this is a sharp printer with some very cool features (wireless printing, print from phone, 3D printing - use with 3D glasses, etc).But after testing several printers (Canon, Epson, Lexmark, HP, Dell, etc), this one comes pretty close to last place. We did not experience all the problems other users are reporting, but frequent jams were a problem, and lower ink cost just isn't a concern any more (read on....).Beginning in late 2011, there are literally hundreds of generic & alternative ink options for just about every brand of printer...except for this one. For example, on our Canon MP600 all-in-one, we just recently bought 3 extra capacity black ink cartridges for $3.50 with free shipping (seehere). The Kodak charges about 15x that.Incidentally, the Canon is our recommendation for most home/home-office printing needs. We have an older model (MP600) but a newer modelCanon PIXMA MG5320is available for under $90, and does everything the average user would ever need. Simple to use, simple set-up. It does brilliant color, great photos, does color or B/W one-touch copies, beautiful quick scanner, and never jams or malfunctions. Plus, as I've said, the ink cost is roughly $1 per cartridge.If you have more specific needs, then you might need to look at other brands. For example, the Epson R-series will print directly onto a printable CD-Rom or DVD, which is a super cool feature if you ever need something like that. Epson also offers waterproof & archival ink, which is great for professional photographers printing up proofs.If have a larger printing need (say, over 5,000 pages per month), then you should look into laser printers - we recommend Brother for black & white, or Dell & Konica Minolta for color laser. But be prepared to spend a minimum of $500 on a quality color laser (or if you're a frugal shopper, check craigslist - we bought a like-new Konica Minolta for just $20!).So my bottom line is, the Kodak isn't really worth the headache or risk. If you're wanting a reliable, quality all-in-one inkjet for home or small office, check out the Canon Pixma. This is an unbiased opinion from someone who's had lots of experience with a variety of printers. Good luck!

These Avery tickets are designed for small runs where you want a customized raffle ticket for an event, perhaps a school or religious function.  Sure you could buy non-custom tickets at the office supply store, but how cool would it be for each person to hold an "official" raffle ticket from your event instead of a generic little red ticket?  These pages are exactly what you'd expect - 10 tickets per page, each with a perforated tab that can be removed.  The tickets themselves tear apart easily, and I found I could quickly free the tickets without accidentally tearing the stub.A few things would have improved the overall product.  First, 65 lb is a little light, and I would have preferred these to be 110 lb card stock to have a real quality feel.  Second, the online design software is cool, but not perfect.  You go to the Avery website and it allows you to create your own tickets.  The online designer has the ability to create sequentially numbered tickets, add custom images or photos, and even has the ability to embed QR codes right on the ticket (I used it to put a link to a contest website).  The software is not entirely intuitive - for instance, the number on the stub does not automatically match the number on the ticket unless you manually set both to the same starting ticket number.  There's a lot of capability in the custom number field, however, such as adding a prefix, suffix, or leading zeroes to the number.  The software is really quite powerful, and I had fun changing around the tickets.The other issue I had was that using my Canon MX882, I found the top of the tickets was cut-off since it was outside my printable margin.  If I shrank the page to fit, then the tickets weren't really centered correctly.  The software has the ability to adjust alignment by moving the whole design up, down, left, right, but if I adjust it down, then the bottom tickets fall between the perforations.This a nice product that definitely gets 4 stars, but I'd like to see an update to the software to make alignment a bit more user friendly, and a version that includes a heavier card stock.

My daughter is a very young first grader.  This workbook is perfect for her.  I think I would have thought it was simplistic before this year, but I have been watching my daughter learn to write and it has already taught me a lot.  Children begin by learning their letters, progress on to words, then partial sentences, and then complete sentences.  The classical model of schooling begins with a rote way of learning writing and that is what my daughter has been learning from.  In classical education, children repeat complete sentences and learn to write in complete thoughts from the beginning.  This book compliments that well, though because it allows young children to write words first (which is much easier to do as they are still practicing writing their letters), then parts of sentences, and then full sentences.  I've been teaching my daughter using both the traditional way of learning how to write that I mentioned earlier and the classical method.  I think they compliment each other well.I do want to mention though that this book is a little expensive to me at almost $6, but there is a set of 3 books that I think is a better value.Mead Early Learning - Stage 3, Set of Three Stage 3 Workbooks (52515)This set has 3 letter workbooks and this workbook is one of the set.I think this book would be good for use with a kindergartener/first grader after school or during the summer as enrichment. This is my first laminator and I have wanted one for a long, long time! I don't have children who's works of art I want to hold onto forever, but instead I participate in exhibitions for miniatures in which reference material is an absolute must in most cases!Presentation is of the utmost importance in my case and keeping my reference documents in pristine condition makes my organization-crazy self happy!When you flip the power switch on the laminator immediately indicates that it is cold and still warming up. The Canon PIXMA MP980 Wireless Photo All- In- One Printer is a very nice printer that eliminates cords and helps keep work spaces neater and cleaner. This printer utilizes wireless technology and this means you have greater flexibility as to the location of the printer in your home. No cords means no tripping and no stretching your cords/cables to the limits.I have used other Canon printers and they usually have their controls behind the front panel. In contrast, this printer places its controls underneath the LCD preview screen. Flip open this LCD screen and you will see controls for color, number of copies, navigation arrows, etc. The LCD screen is nice because it serves not only as a preview for what you are about to print, but also as a viewable menu for the printers commands. As you press the buttons, the command will appear on the LCD screen, to confirm what you are about to do.Extra features like LCD screens are nice, but what matters most with any printer is the print quality. Looking at printouts from this printer reveals well- defined colors that match very well with the actual colors of the items. This is even true when printing a page from a web site- the colors look very nice compared to the printouts produced by other printers I have used. Most important of all is the quality when printing photos and this printer earns high praise in this area. Pictures are very good without a color out of place. Comparing these printouts to those I sometimes get from a local store, there is virtually no way to tell them apart. Perhaps a seasoned photography expert can see a difference but I certainly can't. Even if you accidentally touch the photos right after they print, they are not likely to smudge.Looking for something to criticize with this printer, one that comes to mind is speed. This printer is acceptable in the speed department, but a little slower than with other photo printers I have used and it doesn't measure up to the claims by the manufacturer. However, for quality photos I am more than happy to wait the additional few minutes for the printing to complete. I would rather wait and have a great photo as my reward for patience.  I also haven't noticed any problems with paper jams. The slower speed might be part of the reason.Other problems with this printer are mostly minor, but they could create big problems for some users. One is the wireless setup. When you install this printer, it will ask you to select either wireless or wired for the network. The problem is that there is no selection for both. Most people who purchase this do so for the wireless option and probably only have a single device anyway, so the lack of a dual option won't matter. But for others, this could prove to be an annoyance. Also, this printer doesn't offer fax. This isn't a major issue for me since I rarely fax anything when I'm at home, but it could be a disappointment to those who see the words "all in one" and assume a fax machine is part of the package.So, in summary, the Canon PIXMA MP980 Wireless Photo All- In- One Printer is a printer with a few minor problems, but solid overall. The wireless technology is a great feature but what matters most is the quality of the photo prints and this Canon model receives high marks in this area. The network setup and connection could be improved and the LCD would be better if it offered touch functionality. But all things considered, this is a very good photo printer and it earns an easy recommendation.

Set-up was easy; all features (including fax) were tested and worked; the controls (touch screen) were easy to learn and use. Printing quality is excellent, but when Epson recommends using Epson paper for photo printing you better believe them (hard earned experience using generic Kodak photo paper which smeared all over); per page costs (ink only) about 10 cents at current rates (Epson T273520 Epson Claria Premium 273 Standard-capacity Color Multi-packcartridges good for 500 pages - check current prices and do the math); premium paper extra as for all photo printing.Among the things I look at in a printer are those things a unit does that other units don't. For this Epson XP-800 printer that would be these features:* duplex scanning with automatic document feeder (ADF)* duplex printing* dual paper cassettes* attached memory card (or USB device which isn't made clear that you can do that)Breaking down these features pros and cons:The duplex scanning with the ADF works, but at a rate of speed useful probably for only home use. Scanning a 10 page, two sided document directly to an attached USB device (PNY Attache 32 GB USB 2.0 Flash Drive) took 7.5 minutes. If you're going to use the ADF's rated capacity to scan 30 sheets of two sides it'll take 20-25 minutes. For me, that's fine for home use, but I can't see this in any heavy duty office capacity.Also, I did have several paper jam problems with the ADF. Though easy to clear, it was obvious that the ADF was at its best with very smooth, unwrinkled sheets of paper (I know, "duh"). NOTE: YOU CANNOT USE THE ADF TO DO TWO SIDED SCANNING WITH LEGAL SIZE PAPER!!! (buried deep in documentation).The duplex printing worked without a problem. However, this too might be too slow for some tastes. Scanning and printing (copying) 10 double sided pages took about 3.5 minutes (about 20 seconds/page). Heavy office use will still require a pricier laser printer.Dual paper cassettes: great idea, but you don't have two identical cassettes. The top one can ONLY hold the smaller format photo papers, and the lower one is designed for sheets of standard sized paper up to legal size. This is still a great feature as the paper is stored inside the printer and doesn't jut out. The bottom cassette can hold about 100 sheets of plain paper (less for premium thicker paper of course).Finally, attaching and using memory cards (and USB devices). One of the REALLY nice features. I'm actually more interested in scanning TO these attached memory devices, rather than printing FROM them. Almost any memory card works (though some, like micro-SD cards, require adapters). You can scan to an inserted memory card which makes this useful as a stand-alone scanning workstation (again, not industrial strength in my opinion). Attaching my 32 GB flash drive also worked perfectly. But, when I tried mySeagate Backup Plus 1 TB USB 3.0 Portable External Hard DriveI got "device not recognized."I really like this unit and it has tons of other features and uses, but I hope my covering these specific capabilities help you decide whether or not to purchase this. If the ADF isn't important, Epson makes an almost identical, less expensiveEpson Expression XP-600 Wireless Small-in-One Color Inkjet Printer, Copier, Scanner, 2-Sided Duplex. Prints from Tablet/Smartphone. AirPrint Compatible (C11CC47201).

We don't use hi-lighters often enough at work, so it always seems like when we do need them, every single one in the drawer is dried up and useless. That's why I jumped at the chance to try these new Sharpie Gel pens, as one of their claims to fame was that they won't dry out even if left uncapped.My boss and I broke open the package and each grabbed a marker, making swipes on newsprint and on an inkjet printout. We both looked at each other strangely and said in unison "wow, that's weird". Using this gel highlighter feels like a smooth crayon. If you've ever used oil pastels, these will feel very familiar.Of course, the next thing I tried was to see if the highlight would smear. This was our second surprise, even with very aggressive rubbing, the "gel" stayed where it was originally placed on a piece of regular paper. Well, it says it works on glossy paper, so I highlighted something in a magazine and immediately folded the paper over and rubbed aggressively on the highlighted area, and it stayed put! My boss used it on an inkjet printout just off the printer, and the ink didn't smear or fuzz. The bottom twists to advance the gel, and it says it lasts as long as a regular ink highlighter.It doesn't dry out, it doesn't smudge, it works on a wider variety of surfaces, it's just as easy to use, this is definitely a huge upgrade to an everyday office item.

I have small hands but large handwriting so, when I received these tabs, my first thought was "How am I going to write on these tabs?"  The tabs are attractive, unobtrusive, have a small adhesive footprint (esp. when compared to the Avery 3X3 1/2" tabs), adhere well to paper, remove easily and neatly and would make fine dividers or tabs if you were just marking pages (like tabbing recipes you want to try in a cookbook) without adding any identification to the tab.  However, if you plan to write anything more than a few letters or numbers on these tabs to identify what they're marking, you're going to have a problem unless you write very small and, in my opinion, that lowers the usefulness of the tab.In my 3 decades of experience using reference books for my job, it wasn't enough just to tab a page in a reference book--I needed to identify it for quick reference so that, if I was on the phone and someone needed an answer, I could flip immediately to the correct page of a reference book to find it.  The writing on the tab has to be large enough for me to identify the right page quickly...if the writing is miniscule, I'd spend more time squinting to read it or hunting for my reading glasses than answering the question.In summary, I liked everything about these tabs except for the size of the writing surface, which is why they're getting 4 stars vs. 5.  While the Avery 3X3 1/2" tabs have more writing surface, they also have quadruple the adhesive footprint of these 2/x1 1/5" tabs, so I actually would prefer these smaller ones for some applications.

But this is something most all gel pens deal with, and for the price this one is definitely one of the better ones I've used.

First, let me just say that I really do strongly recommend an item like this for anyone who does a lot of typing (particularly touch typing where multiples of your fingers are reaching and stretching as it really does help support your wrist and prevent fatigue as all those tendons are moving around.As for this particular wrist rest, on the whole I like it...I'm now using it at home and have used it for a typing session of ~4 hours successfully enough to say that it definitely does it's job.  That said, I have used Gel versions at work (this one is the one I have right now:Staples Gel Keyboard Wrist Rest, Black) and prefer them better because they are more firm and contoured - which is why although this one is perfectly fine, I'm going to give it 4 stars instead of 5.  There is, however, an interesting warming aspect to the foam that I think some people may prefer even though I don't (more below) and the anti-slip feature is really niceGeneral comments:1) Height: This one is "plumper" than my gel one, meaning it holds my wrists up higher.  As my home keyboard is a taller keyboard, this is actually fortunate, and I very much like it.2) Support: This is where I like the gel one better - it is firmer and although I don't know the exact reason, I feel it reduces fatigue better for me personally.  I can "feel" it working better...this one is certainly better than typing without, but even now after sitting at my computer for just an hour of typing, I feel more strain than I normally do at work with the gel version.3) Contours: although it has a wave shape to it, it does not have the contours to the actual top surface that the gel one has.  I think it may be more that I'm more used to the other, but I like it better for that.  On this one the foam is all the same height, and I find my right wrist trying to press in deeper to compensate.4) Heat: this one heats up (body heat) as you use it like a foam pillow on your head would as you sleep.  The heat is kind of nice on sore wrists actually.  Though I personally don't like it because it makes me sweat and that makes me itch and makes the rest a little...damp.  Meaning that I have to lift up my wrists and wipe them on my pants to "dry" them.  But if you're not a sweater and have naturally colder hands (or sorer wrists) I can see where this might actually be a benefit to you.5) Smell: When the gel one is new, it smells awful...took about two weeks to fade.  This one has a chemical scent to it, but it's not bad and I can only smell it when putting it right to my face.  So that's a plus for this one.6) Cleanliness: Okay, I will be using this one less in general than my work one, but I'll share some thoughts here.  This has a similar fabric cover - my other one gets gross and has to be replaced every 12-18 months (thank you, company I work for, for giving me a new one every time I ask...).  It is not cleanable as it's actually dead skin cells sloughing off and getting into the fabric...you can wash it with soap and water, but it gets stained and does not really solve the issue.  I will update this review if I notice anything different about this one, but I would suppose it would be similar (save that sweating more may make it worse).  To that end though, I DEFINITELY like the black ones better.  On some other colors, like grey, you don't notice it as much until it starts to smell (gross, I know, but it's one of those things you don't think about...) or release dust clouds when you whack it.  On black you start to notice when it gets bad...it gets "dusty" looking where it's collecting ick from you. It's a great reminder to replace it.  If I get to where I try to clean this one, I will update this review and let you know how that compares.7) Non-slip backing:  To me that is something about this one that is awesome.  My other ones have all had a rubberized, texturized backing, but it still migrates around the desk on it's own somehow.  (I never notice it moving...just eventually my keyboard is way over or something.)  This one has a much smoother backing that almost feels sticky (not actually...there is no residue) and it adheres to the desk well.  So far I have not noticed any movement in it...it stays right where I put it while I type.So yeah. Matter of opinion.  I'm glad I finally have one for home and it was nice to try a different type.  I'll keep using this one until it inevitably gets gross enough to toss out.  But, if I go to buy a replacement for it, I suspect I'll end up with a gel one for home too.

It's a great pen with a very fine point.Testing with the pen writing upside down and at angles, it works great. Before buying this I ordered a similar "defender-usa" system and returned it.  This system is similar, two cameras and a 7" monitor which accepts a 32gb SD card.  Set up was easy, just a matter of mounting the cameras and plugging them in to an electrical outlet. The camera's automatically sync'd to the monitor. I placed the monitor about 35' from the cameras and through 2 walls and reception is fine.  The defender system had problems with the monitor 15' away from the cameras.There are a few different modes that you can use with the system and I will try to describe them:1)Continuous recording.  This is what I wanted to do and I was disappointed to find out that while you can continuously record both cameras in 'quad view' there is no time stamp or audio on the recording. I called their support line (one hour wait) and the guy didn't seem to know how it was supposed to work, so I was transferred to someone else and waited another 15 minutes. I finally got confirmation that there is no time stamp and no audio if you record both cameras in continuous mode.  We are currently recording one camera in continuous mode and it works great- it breaks the video up into 10 minute segments on the SD card.2) Motion - I was nearly as disappointed with motion recording with this system as I was with the defender system. Both have settings to record 5, 15, or 30 seconds after motion is detected. I can't comprehend WHY anyone would design a system that does not offer a way to record motion until the motion stops!  Detecting motion is faster in this system than the defender, but neither system catches motion as soon as it occurs, this one starts recording a second or two after it starts, the defender system didn't record until 5 or 6 seconds after motion starts.3) Scan - scan mode, which moves from one camera to another can't be recorded in continuous mode, only motion. These systems seem to get confused when motion moves from the field of view of one camera to another, there is a delay in switching to the camera detecting motion unless it happens to be the one on the screen at the moment.Video is good, if my dogs are running the video is a little choppy but you can definitely make them out. Night video is black and white and is clear enough to make out anything that is in view of the camera.Audio is superb, I can hear people talking 100 feet away. The mic is cheap and some sounds are distorted but you can definitely make out words. It has two way audio capability which was nice when my husband was adjusting the cameras because I could guide him remotely while watching the monitor.Support is abysmal. I emailed the company with a question yesterday morning and never heard back so decided to call them, before you call make sure you have registered the product on their website or you will have to hang up and go register it before they will talk to you.  I was on hold for an hour to speak to an off-shore based support tech who had no idea how the system even worked, it was only after being transferred that I could get a half way decent answer.  Lorex really needs to step up their game with regards to support on a scale of 1-10 their support deserves a 0.I'm not sure I would have purchased it if I had realized how limited dual camera recording was, but that probably would not be an issue for most people and unless they have unique needs (I need 24/7 audio/video to prove that my dogs are not barking when my lovely neighbor calls animal control and claims they are) the system would probably be more than satisfactory.

When wrapping a boatload of gifts, during the holiday season, one of my biggest aggravations is trying to hold the paper in place while fumbling with the tape dispenser.  That is why the Scotch PopUp Tape Handband Dispenser seems like such a great idea.  It's small, convenient, and makes wrapping gifts much easier.  At least that is the case some of the time.At 2 inches in length, these little tape strips aren't always long enough to do the job.  This can be somewhat resolved by using more than one strip but I then found that I was burning through the meager 75 strips in no time.  The dispenser came with one pad, which was gone in a flash.  So I set out to purchase some refills.  I have found the price to be all over the board for these refills.  Buying multi-packs online will many times provide a more cost effective solution, especially on Amazon if you get it with free shipping.  Many people have complained about the price of these refills and at first I agreed.  However, when compared to the average roll of Scotch 3/4 tape, which usually contains 300 or 400 inches, you find that a 75 strip popup pack provides 150 inches.  Well I bought a 12 pack of these refills for a decent price, with free shipping, which provided 1,800 feet of tape.  When I did the math I found that these strips were really not that much more than buying multiple rolls of tape; roughly 4 to 6 rolls depending on the 300 to 400 inch capacity they usually have.  So if you enjoy the convenience of the handband dispenser (and it is quite handy!) and you don't mind shopping around online to find the best bargain for buying refills, then this little gadget may be the answer you are looking for.Now let's go back to the issue of these strips being only 2 inches in length.  I found that when wrapping large gifts this 2 inch length is just not enough.  In some cases not nearly long enough.  So while handy, I feel that this nifty tape dispenser should not be considered a total replacement for the good old roll of Scotch tape, with the built-in cutter.  I'll admit that 2 inches is long enough for many gifts, of small to moderate size.  But for those times when you need a piece of tape that is greater in length, then you will want to have that normal roll of tape within arm's reach.  So I guess you could say that the Scotch PopUp Tape Handband Dispenser is a nice to have but not really a need to have.  Since I am a man of convenience, I find this product and the refills are worth the money.  So next Christmas I will have plenty of popup refills and will also have a roll or two of tape.  But I can assure you that I will be using the handy popup tape strips for the majority of my wrapping duties.

I have the best luck with canon vs epson. I usually get 4 or more years from my canons. I like that the paper is front loaded because I can put it on a shelf and push it up against the wall unlike others that the paper feed tray sticks out of the back. Getting the printer setup for wireless was really easy too. The lcd and touch panel made it fast and easy to configure and enter the wifi password. You can also get a combo pack of one color and one black xl version. They range in price from $25, $30 and $50 for the combo pack. I find that the canon inks last longer than the epsons but if I have any issues with the 3 in one color ink, i'll be sure to post an update here.Another cool feature is that depending on what function you are in the button display will change. For example if your faxing, then the panel to the right of the lcd screen shows numbers for dialing the fax number. There's also a print a screen shot from your HD movie from your camera, which I haven't tried but for some may like this. I know I've had people ask me how do they make a picture from a movie and this function eliminates that and does it directly.There's a double sided printing function which is really cool, it prints the first page and sucks the paper back in and somehow gets it to print on the other side. I don't know how it does it but its kinda cool AND you use less paper!! The overall print speed is quick, its not overly noisy and  prints pretty fast from being in idle mode. Scanning is fast and sharp. I don't use the supplied canon program but use my built in mac program and the results were great.Overall for the price you can't go wrong with this all-in-one. Its easy to use and configure and does a nice job. Its not for high volume but more of a small home office.Pros:Compact all-in-oneFeatureseasy connectivitywifi up to NMobile/ipad printingPriceCons:Slightly heavy in weightNo separate color ink tanks (have to get the next model up the 882)No USB cord supplied for wired printing (but most people want wifi anyway)
