See the customer uploaded images for a comparison of the photographic output from this Epson Artisan 710 and theHP Photosmart Premium All-in-One Printer (CD055A#ABA)!Quick summary:  If I were the GEICO caveman, I would not like trying to install this Epson all-in-one printer/scanner inside my cave.  Only after I spent considerable time puzzling over Epson's install process and unintuitive control panel interface would I be happy, as the photographic output coming from this Epson printer was just fabulous.I haven't used this all-in-one very long (about 1+ week) now, but here's what I can tell you.  This is my first Epson printer since I bought a laser printer maybe 15 years ago.  And I've never owned an all-in-one device until getting this one.  So what follows is my experience with the Epson Artisan 710, from the lens of a GEICO caveman (you know, "So easy, even a caveman can do it.").  If you're not tech-savvy, pay attention as you might face the same challenges as this caveman did.INSTALLATION NOTES:The caveman liked what he saw upon opening the box.  Inside the big box, at the top, was a smaller box emblazoned with, "Open Me First" -- that had the cables, driver CD, and user guide inside.  However, the caveman is running Windows 7 now, and the packing materials only offered a slip of paper pointing me to the Epson website to download the Windows 7 print drivers.  That's not a big deal, but the Epson website could be clearer on what, exactly, the caveman needed to download, as there are more than one choice for Windows 7 users.  He had to figure out which download would both install the necessary drivers and enable networking capability.The caveman liked that Epson packed an extra black ink cartridge, but he was dismayed to learn that Epson gave a very miserly 3 or 4 sheets of 4x6 photo paper on which to print (so, you may as well order 100 sheets of 4x6 photo paper, too, if you buy the Artisan 710).  Shame on Epson for not including a package of 100 4x6 sheets!Removing all the packing tape went well for the caveman; Epson folds over one edge of each strip of tape so it's easy to grasp and pull off the printer/scanner.  The caveman liked that installing each ink cartridge met with a satisfying "click" sound, so he knew he installed the ink correctly.The caveman didn't like the paper tray at all, however.  It removes completely from the printer, but it's a baffling, sliding mess of chintzy plastic.  The caveman worried whether he might tug too hard here, shove to hard there, and the chintzy plastic would break -- then what would he do?  The caveman struggled to know how, exactly, to install the printer paper, and it took the Artisan 710 more than a few attempts to correctly load paper from the paper tray.  At one point, the caveman nearly pitched the whole mess out of his cave!The caveman also didn't like aspects of the wireless networking.  The Artisan 710 has an LCD screen, but it's not a touch screen.  Instead, several buttons on the Artisan 710's control panel are used to give the printer/scanner instructions.  It's a painful mess trying to enter a network security key through this interface; the caveman was mystified and had to actually read the manual to figure how to get his printer connected to his network.  One nice thing:  Epson configures the Windows Firewall automatically once the passkey is correctly entered into the printer.The caveman hated the arrogance of Epson, as the install process began littering his Windows Desktop with extra icons (without asking permission firstly), and setting the Epson printer/scanner as the Windows default printer (again, without asking).What *really* upset the GEICO caveman, however, was the the setup under Windows 7 enabled the printer function, but the scanner function somehow completed but failed to install correctly.  It took a few, aborted attempts at scanning for the caveman to realize something was not at all right.  The caveman had to do things like go into his router to figure out the IP address of his new Epson Artisan 710, so he could manually force the IP address into the scanner setup -- and even running the scanner setup was not at obvious for the caveman.  Happily the caveman's other, Vista-running computers didn't incur the same troubles installing the printer and scanner drivers, so maybe this was just a Windows 7 issue alone.  And once the WiFi was enabled, the Artisan 710 didn't give this caveman any troubles, so the installation troubles are a one-time experience to endure.Finally, when the caveman tried to pair his Bluetooth cell phone with this printer to print wirelessly and directly from his cell phone, he couldn't do it.  Yeah, there was a Bluetooth setting on the menu screen, but there was no way to enable Bluetooth or make it discoverable.  He kept getting "Invalid Operation" messages every time he tried to scroll down on the Bluetooth menu.  Come to find out, THERE IS NO BLUETOOTH on this printer!  You have to buy a separate, USB Bluetooth adapter, plug it in to the USB port on the front, THEN you can use Bluetooth.  The manuals don't say this, and even Epson's website obscures this important tidbit.  Very frustrating!!In short, if you are like a GEICO caveman when it comes to technology matters -- and you're running Windows 7 -- it  may be a challenge for you.  It was for this caveman.* * *USABILITY NOTES:Okay, back out of the cave now, how did the Epson perform?  Well, first off, lets just say that the photographic output was spectacular.  The colors are very rich, vibrant, and well-saturated.  Keep in mind that I purposely avoided making any tweaks or customizations of anything before writing this review, so what follows is an out-of-box experience using this Epson printer/scanner.  Your results can most likely be improved by spending more time customizing settings for this device.To test the scanner, I took a photo I had just printed and placed it on the scanner flatbed, then tried copying it.  Ideally, the copied photo would be identical and indistinguishable from the original, right?  But that wasn't the case.  The copied photo had decidedly less intense colors, less vibrancy than the original.  That's not to say that the copy was bad, it just literally pales in comparison to the original.I also tried comparing a scan from this Epson with a new HP all-in-one (the C309).  The Epson scans were less vibrant in color, somewhat blurred, and the white background of my daughter's drawing came out grayish on the scan.  On the upside, the scan picked up details on my daughter's drawing that the HP struggled to pick-up.  Again, this is using default settings for the Epson Artisan 710; your results could undoubtedly be improved by customizing settings for how to scan images.I dislike how the Artisan 710 chose to use a control panel with multi-purpose keys.  The "home" key switches between printer, scanner, copier functions, and I keep confusing the "OK" button with the "Start" button.  You use the "OK" button a lot to enter settings, but the Artisan 710 won't do anything until you press a separate "Start" button.  I suppose once you get used to this interface, it wouldn't be hard to use or get comfortable with.  I'm just saying that for a new user, it's not nearly as intuitive as, say, the HP C309 is.I haven't used this Epson long enough to talk about its ink usage, or whether it needs printhead cleaning too much.  As I continue to use this new device, I'll re-edit my review to share the experience I've had.* * *In summary, then, I can't say that I like using this Epson Artisan 710.  It's not as easy to use as a similar HP model.  But the photographic output from this six-ink system is superb, and other quibbles I have could probably be overcome with patience in using the custom settings.  If you're already an Epson product fan, there's a lot you'll like in this Epson printer/scanner.  If you're not an Epson fan, though, I suggest you look at the competing HP products with touch screens, an easier-to-use print tray, and similar capabilities.

I've never been quite this glum to give a 2 star review. I love using this scanner, when it works. I want PiQx to have a huge, out-of-control success with this product, and send dozens more manufacturers scrambling to get their own versions to market. (You'll find comparable ones offered on the product's page here, but they are mostly classroom/video oriented, and none can aspire to quite what the Xcanex is positioned to do in terms of document handling, format conversion, image quality, etc. -- not at this price.) But I can't - yet - recommend this product to someone who needs consistently dependable results, or truly speedy scans  (there are other process streamlining features that compensate, I must hasten to add - more on that, below), or a not-so-steep learning curve.For business card and flat page scanning, I will say this little scanner is without peer. Practically anything strictly in 2D is going to come out cropped, lighting adjusted, and ready for OCR, conversion to PDF, or any number of graphics formats. Did I say "ready"? Actually, you can save to PDF format or to an OCR converted format, without intermediary steps. (Oh sure, if you OCR convert heavily italicized, stylized, or just plain tiny text, you might end up with un-decipherable gobbledygook, but that's a limitation pretty universal to OCR readers, last I checked.)For scanning books, magazines, and other things that bend their way into hard to read text or bizarre images with traditional or "wand" scanners, PiQx has come up with software that they call "Flatpage". Its purpose: To "unbend" or "un-skew" curved and tilted page images and faithfully recreate the look of a truly flat page, without having to cut pages away from the book spine, for one example.That's a great idea. However, it's not working out so well for me, at this writing. I'm referencing here the original public release of Flatpage, which was made available on the PiQx website on 10/04/2013. Sometimes it works beautifully in automatic or semi-automatic mode. Sometimes it weirdly distorts the page in question. And occasionally, it doesn't seem to do anything at all.Other issues:1) The Xcanex can compensate for the glare off of a glossy page, however it does so by means of tilting the scanner stand (or laptop screen) to a particular angle. Together with other variables involved in adjusting the scanner's height, angle, etc., this can be a hugely frustrating experience. Time will tell if it becomes less so with practice, but that's what early experience with the scanner and it's manual has yielded, for me. In addition, images "snapped" using the glossy setting are often dark or "underexposed" - not an insurmountable problem for anyone who owns a half decent image editing program, but I do believe that the gorgeous images shown on Xcanex's own site are the product of ideal, vs. real world conditions, and may not be representative of your results, yada yada.I would love to post some of my own images here by way of example, and urge Amazon or Xcanex, as applicable, to facilitate same. (Note that "Share your own customer images" is shown beneath the main product image for many, if not most of Amazon's offerings.)2) The Xcanex is a resources hog. Yes, the bar is always being raised on processing power in computers, but the minimum specs given for systems installing this software are a little, um...optimistic? I was unable to do much with this software on my aging desktop - in fact I had anticipated as much, and getting this scanner was the push I needed to force some much-needed upgrades for my 2.4 GHz Quad Core system: I invested in some memory (going from 3 GB to 8), upgraded from a 32 bit to a 64 bit O.S., changed out the old HD for SSD...short of getting a new CPU and motherboard, I'm not sure what else I could have done to accommodate PiQx's hardware recommendations. All I can say is that I can have a dozen programs open on the desktop and be humming along happily - even when one of them is something piggy like CorelDraw - but if I activate the Xcanex, I need to bring the load on system resources WAY down, pronto. The Xcanex spikes CPU utilization to 100% at or around the start of every scan, and it doesn't cope well with having more than 8 or 10 images "alive" in the thumbnail panel.Oh, and you know how PiQx touts that you can scan more images while the last image "snapped" is still processing? Not necessarily. For me, second only to Flatpage, forcing the Xcanex to multitask that way is the leading cause of major image distortion.3) The Xcanex is pretty ergonomic for a laptop (works well in terms of portability and mobile space limitations), but for a desktop...I tried putting it on a side table. You can't hold a book open at the same time you are trying to watch your adjustments on a screen way over to your right or left, oh, and run the keyboard at the same time. What's a bit kludgy with a laptop is just ridiculous over the more spread-out desktop geometry. My solution is to position the Xcanex on its (included) desktop stand between my two monitors and shove the keyboard off to the side when it's time to start scanning. Obviously this might not work for more space-limited desks, but I think that the convenience of the unit is somewhat lost, at least for a desktop environment, if you have to move and replace the whole scanner/pad assembly on a regular basis.4) The software is unintuitive. I've given somewhere between 25 and 35 hours, so far, to testing the scanner in everyday use, consulting the manual as I go. I still don't think I know the half of how to get the best image out of this thing. There are a fair number of variables, menu and icon graphics are not particularly helpful, and the interface seems to be very much written for a windows/"touch" environment. Great if you're using it on a tablet, not so much if your screen isn't touch or - gasp! - you haven't yet acclimated to the idiosyncrasies of Win8 or IDevice environments. (I'm kind of good, there, but it's still fairly kludgy software for me.)At 90+ pages, the manual is useful I suppose as a start-to-finish read, not so much as a "quick start" reference. And really, how many of us devour manuals from cover to cover? I strongly recommend users of this scanner reference the tutorial videos on the Xcanex website.I can't speak to the video features of this product because I really don't video conference.Now after all that complaining, I still have to say that I love the potential that is abundantly evident in the Xcanex. It is no exaggeration to say that I have been waiting for this kind of scanner for *years*. Flatbeds are not particularly kind to books and magazines, sheet fed scanners can't accommodate them at all (short of cutting the pages from the binding), and wand scanners like theWolverine PASS200 Handheld Portable Documents, Books and Photo Scannerare just plain disappointing in practical use. If PiQx can get the financial backing they apparently still seek - check their Facebook page and you'll see that they are indeed looking - I think that the next generation of PiQx scanners, or maybe the one after that, will be A-Ma-Zing. That said, if you don't have an urgent need for this kind of specialized scanner for research or what have you, I'd say wait a few years.However, if you do have that need, or just a serious appetite for the latest and greatest, you'll find plenty of value in PiQx Xcanex. I find I'm using mine daily, and finally starting to make some small progress towards "paperless" in my own home office.Negative 3 stars for charging a fair chunk of change for a cumbersome, unintuitive interface, testy hardware ergonomics, and software that appears to be buggy or just not suited to less than ideal user situations. Five stars for innovation, potential and for the amazing things that the Xcanex CAN do, once you've learned to work around the various "hiccups".

Yaw is adjusted with the swivel.I also own an Ergotron mount in this same price range that uses a spring arm for adjusting the height.  While I also really like that mount (and probably prefer it), it does not have the smooth action of the of this 3M one.  The Ergotron does have better build quality though.Overall, this is really a great mount.  The ball joint, thumb screws and mounting template make nice touches.  I would definitely recommend.

Haven't had it long, so things could change, but... So far it's worked just fine. I bought this to replace an older Pixma printer which was still working OK after four years, but I wanted to go wireless. All the wireless print-only devices I looked at cost quite a bit more than this unit and the copier function, at least, seemed like a useful thing to have so I went for it.The packaging is impressively robust - like a double-hulled battleship. Somewhere along the way something tried to poke through the side of the box but it didn't penetrate the inner layers so no problem there. Instructions are straightforward and well illustrated. (I counted at least four printed documents warning you to treat the printhead gently and how to insert it, as well as an on-screen slideshow on the built in LCD. If you screw that up, it's your own fault.) Make sure you find all the little orange tabbed bits of tape and remove them - check twice, there are a lot of them.The footprint is larger than the printer it's replacing, but that's to be expected given the dimensions of the scanner component. It doesn't weigh much more and, therefore, feels a little less robust but the construction seems more than adequate for something that's not going to be moved around a lot. It's got the same four ink tanks I'm used to, though slightly smaller in size (#221 vs. #6) with the typical oversized pigment black for text. I expect they'll last about the same with, of course, the first set draining out early.Set up was easy. It detected my wireless router and once I entered the access key it was happy. I then installed the drivers and other software to a Windows 7, 64-bit, system (using the WIndows Vista instructions) and it was all straightforward, including finding the printer on the network. The included performance check tool makes it easy to find a good spot in the house for best reception. (I had to keep reminding myself that I could put it anywhere convenient since there was only the power cord to consider.) I then went to an older Windows XP box and did the same setup there. We'll be doing a Mac in the near future as well as one or two other Windows machines.Text is crisp on decent inkjet compatible paper and the two glossy prints I've produced so far are beautiful. In general, it's always a lot cheaper to have prints made at someplace like your corner pharmacy, grocery store, Costco, etc. and the quality will probably be even better, but when you need a couple of prints NOW it's nice to know they'll look really nice.One comment about ink: I made the mistake of trying some non-OEM ink in my existing Pixma printer early this year and it was not a success. It worked OK for a while, but then it gummed up some of the nozzles. Text smeared easily and photos didn't look all that great, especially in the densest shadows. Cleaning a gummed up printhead is doable, but not enough fun to be worth saving a few bucks. I've never had problems with the Canon ink "going stale" even in cartridges that have sat in the machine for a year or more, or months between photo print jobs. Your mileage may vary, and you may find a brand that works great, but I'm sticking with the "Canonical" brand, if you'll pardon the pun.

Sticky Ass Glue claims to outperform a variety of the best glues out there. There are a lot of good glues on the market, and most are designed to work optimally with specific materials. Sticky Ass Glue claims to work with a large variety of materials and surfaces, both porous and non porous. Gluing porous materials together and bonding them to non-porous ones is not usually a challenge. Bonding non-porous materials to each other can be difficult. That's particularly true with many plastics. They often have specific cements and glues that work very well with one type but not at all with others.I tried this on a broken internal plastic part from a toy gun. It was under pressure from a spring (about four times stronger than one in a typical ball point pen) and was made from a smooth plastic. The end without the spring gets forced toward the spring by a trigger. The "L" shape makes the applied force uneven. Other glues did not hold up to the pressure for more than a second once cured. I applied a moderate amount of SAG to the gluing surface of one piece and wet the other. I held them together and let the glue cure for over 24 hours. Unlike previous glues, this one held up for about 10 seconds.I decided to try again, and scraped the surfaces of both sides of the plastic so the surfaces were rougher. I applied the glue a bit more liberally and waited 48 hours. On my previous attempt, there was a small amount of expansion. The glue more than surrounded the joined areas, but did not have a lot of excess. The second time, expansion was a lot greater and I needed to trim away excess cured material that got in the way. This time, the glue held up fine for about a day. I tried a third time, using liberal amounts of glue so the glue expanded to essentially increase the thickness of the piece being repaired. That was about three months ago and it's still holding up.Since that time, I've used the glue in a variety of less tricky situations, and some difficult ones, and had good results consistently.The glue is a bit tacky, but no more so than maple syrup. Like maple syrup, this glue will not hold anything together very well when it's still wet. Unlike maple syrup, ordinary soap will not get it off your hands, so take their advice and use gloves.Although this glue fell short of my expectations initially, it ultimately proved itself with difficult materials. It's not a miracle product, but I'd recommend it for many difficult tasks. An obvious exception is with whatever plastic they made the cap out of. I'd also look for an alternative when aesthetics might be an issue due to the expansion of this glue.  I'd also preclude its use for bonding metals when you need to fill in small to moderate sized holes. For that, I'd recommendJ-B Weld 8265-S Cold Weld. That still leaves plenty of uses, including many where other glues will not be up to the challenge.

Bottom line: The build quality of the HON sets it well apart from the typical chairs carried at office superstores. Lots of adjustment options, but limited lumbar support and a very stiff cushion downgrade the advantages.Full review: I've been using a Leap chair (Steelcase) for years and have found it to be just about perfect for my needs (sit for a long time, computer user, chronic sciatica issues and disc problems). But, it's quite pricy. The HON seemed to have many of the same benefits, so I was looking forward to giving it a try.Assembly: Straightforward except for the fact that the included allen wrench did not fit the bolts securely, requiring me to use my own tools. But other than that small glitch, everything went together easily (took about 15 min) and all the parts and pieces are clearly labeled, including L and R stickers on both the seat bottom and a L and R stamped into the metal portion of the arm so there's no mistaking what goes where. Assembly consists of inserting the casters (a tap with a mallet helps seat them), attaching the arms (3 bolts each) and attaching the back (4 bolts). All the bolts are packaged well and labeled. They also include some spare bolts which is a nice touch.Seat comfort: The seat cushion is firm. Really firm. Really, really firm. Get the picture? Now, that's not necessarily a bad thing, but it does take some time to get used to. If you like the soft, cushy approach, this is definitely not the chair for you.Adjustments: In addition to the usual up/down adjustment, the arms can be moved up and down, side to side, and back and forth. That's a huge plus for keeping your arms at the proper angle when keyboarding. The arm tops are a bit too hard for my taste, but not to the point where I'd call it uncomfortable.Reclining: The chair allows you to recline without tilting the seat pan. Huge plus for comfort!Back support: Limited. While the mesh back is nice and comfortable, there is little lumbar support and it is not adjustable. This is my biggest problem with the chair. It can be solved by adding a portable lumbar cushion, but I think the omission of lumbar adjustments in a chair that has so many other adjustments is a significant shortfall.Fit and finish: Very nice. Not fancy or stylish, but good quality materials that would look good in any office (or home office). The build quality is much better than the chairs commonly available at an office superstore, but clearly a notch below higher-end chairs. This is more suited to the lower wear and tear of a home office than a commercial office. At home this chair would easily last for many years.Operation: Very easy. Only two levers (one for up/down; one for reclining). The arms are also easy to adjust by grasping and pulling. Unlike some of the advanced office chairs, you don't have to read a manual to figure out how to use it.The best rating for this is 3.5 stars since, at this price point, the issue of lumbar support should have been addressed. I'll round it up to 4 stars since the build quality is quite good overall. It should definitely be considered if you're looking for a home office chair with lots of adjustability and solid build quality without spending a huge amount. Keep in mind, however, that the lumbar support is weak and the cushion is firm.

That tab will also cleanly tear off so that after the label is stuck down it looks nice. The sticky totally covers the back of the label, instead of there just being a skinny strip of sticky down the middle. I like the solid color of the labels as they look nice and clean. These labels are made from 80% post consumer paper so that is always a big plus to be able to help the environment.The negative of the labels is that they didn't always stick down properly. Don't write on them until you have them stuck down to what you want them on. If you write on them and then immediately stick them on something and run your finger along the face of the label, the ink will smear.Overall, the labels do what they say but if you are looking to mainly use them on plastic folders you may want to look for another label. From the picture of this Fellowes I-Spire Series Laptop Lift, it looks like it would be made of metal, but it is actually made of plastic. It's a very sturdy plastic, but it's plastic just the same. The LabelManager LM 500TS is laminated label printer designed primarily for use in a small business or departmental environment. Home users who have an ongoing need to print dozens of labels might also consider the LabelManager LM 500TS.The printer has a keyboard for stand-alone use and can be connected to a Mac or PC for use with Dymo's desktop software. Labels are available in widths of 1/4 inch, 3/8 inch, 1/2 inch, 3/4 inch and 1 inch. There are several print color/background combinations in addition to basic black on white. It uses a rechargeable battery and comes with an AC power brick.The basic functionality of the LabelManager LM 500TS is extensively reviewed elsewhere, so I am going to concentrate on some less-used features.The user guide that comes with the printer gives the impression that the printer cannot function when plugged into the AC adapter. This is true if you are using it as a stand-alone printer. If the printer is connected to a computer, however, it works when plugged in to the power supply.The user guide available from Dymo's web site is three pages longer than the one that came with the machine. It lists five power states when the printer is connected to a computer:Label maker is connected and battery pack is chargingLabel maker is connected and battery pack is charging; printing is not possibleLabel maker is connected and battery pack is not chargingLabel maker is connected and battery pack is not charging; printing is not possibleLabel maker is not connected or is turned offLabel maker is connected and there is a problem with the battery packAn icon in the Dymo Label Software shows the status continuously when the printer is connected to your computer.I had no problem importing and using a couple of basic pieces of clip art (biohazard and recycling symbols). This is a two-bit (single color) printer, so simplicity is the key to choosing clip art to import.One of the features of the LabelManager LM 500TS is the ability to print labels from a database. If your data is available as a .csv file, you can open that file from within the Dymo software and design a layout for the fields in your database.  You can then print your labels in batches of up to 500 at a time. This can be a great time saver if you have hundreds or even thousands of items that need to labeled all at once (doing new inventory asset tags, for example).Mac OSX NOTE: this is, as near as I have been able to determine, the only feature in the Dymo Label Software V.8 that does not work in Mac OSX. It took some digging through the Dymo FAQs, but I did find an explicit statement:"Please note, Import Data and Print is only available on Windows computers, it is not supported on Macs"  - Dymo FAQ Answer 2183 3/13/12Given that the Mac software includes the button to do this (the process cannot get past the first step) it's possible that Dymo may be planning to fix this in a future release.I created a small table that I saved as a .csv file. I was able to import the file and then layout and print labels using the Windows version of the software (running in VMWare Fusion on my Mac). The process to do this is broken down step-by-step and fairly straight-forward.There are a couple of areas where there's room for improvement. You cannot just turn it on and print a label; you always have to wait for the start-up process to finish. At the same time, it just turns itself off without warning when not connected to a computer. This can be really annoying. The machine should ask and wait for 30 seconds to a minute before switching itself off. The D-1 labels required for this machine are not cheap. If you're planning to print hundreds or thousands of labels, you should calculate the cost of the tape in any decision to use this system or an alternative.I been using label makers, hand-held and desktop, stand-alone and computer-connected, since the original Dymo embossed label makers of the 1960's and 1970's. The LabelManager LM 500TS is the most versatile and capable label maker I've ever used.

This tape is same color as regular masking tape but it is thicker and more substantial. It is very easy to lay out exactly where you want it because it is so stiff. When you pull it up it comes up easily with out tearing and leaves no residue. It is stiffer than regular painter's tape. Rated for 250 degrees for 30 minutes.

I wasn't going to drop $48,000 on a PEN, but it has free shipping, so why not?Well, all I can say is that when you need to go to the ER at 2am to get a fountain pen extracted from a usually exit-only bodily aperture, there isn't really much of a difference between this pen and a cheap drugstore disposable fountain pen other than the price and intensity on the lower body X-ray print.Get a nice car, instead, go to a store and buy a disposable fountain pen and spend the rest on health insurance because ER visits aren't cheap.

The size of these pouches might lead to a bit of waste from time to time, however one might also note that it gives you a great deal of flexibility with what you're going to be laminating.  The results are excellent though, crystal clear with a solid seal which is exactly what you would want from laminating pouches.One complain from my end though is the method of shipping.  They arrived in a much larger box than was required, along with the ubiquitous bubble wrap.  For a product that's flexible and essentially unbreakable, I found that to be rather excessive.

I'm curious how these will hold up long term, but for the short term, they're great.  I box up yard sale items year round and use these to label the boxes.  I can then remove the labels and reuse the box over and over.  I also use them to label the back of photographs, Mini DV tapes, and identify shoes in boxes. If the paint can is not labeled, it is typically given away or discarded.I can't tell you how many times I found myself taping regular Post-it notes to make them more secure. These finger-nail size, double-sided sticky tabs are great for all sorts of crafts. With two small children in the house, we put these through their paces! My children used them for making their own school albums (sticking pictures to backing paper), making their own stickers, and I used them for scrapbooking. We moved about a year ago, and the boxes we purchased were about the same price as these but were not quite as nice.  These Fellowes boxes are sturdier than those we used, and best of all you don't have to tape them together or shut(although I recommend using packing tape if the box might move a lot during shipping - such as during a long distance move - or if the box contains a number of small or fragile items).  The ability to avoid using tape is beneficial because if a box isn't weakened through the application (and later removal) of tape, then you can use the box again, or pass the box along to friends who need to move and/or ship items. (Note: please realize that some moving companies will provide you with used moving boxes free of charge; however, you get what you pay for - most of the used boxes we packed in fell apart quickly.)I assembled and disassembled one of the Fellowes boxes multiple times to ensure it would not fall apart easily - it held up like a champ; in fact, after five times being reassembled, it looked great and still folded flat at the end of my experiment.  Also, the box has numbered flaps/sides for easy step-by-step assembly AND has drawn pictures on the bottom of the box to show you how to assemble the box.The medium size boxes are the boxes I found most helpful during our move (although we did not use Fellowes boxes when we moved, the boxes we used were approximately the same size as these boxes).  People have a tendency to pack boxes tightly, so the bigger boxes can become far too heavy - thereby running the risk of either ripping the box or making the box nearly impossible to lift (resulting in back/neck strain). Stick with medium boxes like these for most of your items.  The largest boxes should be saved for clothes, linens, pillows and lightweight but unwieldy kitchen gadgets (e.g., box graters, rolling pins, lighter pots and pans, electric skillets, hot air popcorn poppers).  Small boxes should be used for heavy items such as books and liquids (e.g., detergents and canned food).These are solid, well designed boxes sold at what I believe is the going rate for new moving boxes.  Naturally, you can reuse the boxes to store your yearly tax records, children's old clothes and to collect donated clothing for charity.  Recommended!

I love these! I needed a label for a ziploc of clothes for my kid's preschool, DONE!I needed a label for a book that I was lending a friend, DONE!I needed to label a storage box to store at the top of the closet, DONE!These are just small enough to stick here and there, they are big enough to be seen from a closet shelf. I use this size label not only for addressees, but also to print my own return address labels. Being a pen pal, I've seen plenty of professionally-printed clear address labels. On those, the ink sits on top of glossy, clear "paper" and scuffs right off during shipping. Those address labels are almost always illegible by the time they get to me. And what's the point of an address label if the address chips right off?These labels are different, though, because they're textured and have more of a matte finish. While they aren't completely "invisible" and can still be seen when put on an envelope, they give a nice, professional look that white labels don't necessarily give. It also is surprising that an InkJet printer has the ability to do this type of printing and not smear off. (Note: These aren't colorfast, however. If they get wet, the ink can smear off.)As a handy feature for removal, the backing paper can be bent, exposing just one narrow edge on the right side of each label.The only real problem I have is that my printer isn't always reliable in "seizing" this type of paper, sometimes ending up in a wasted sheet. That's more of a potential issue with certain printers, though.

First, I'll say, this is an excellent sharpener for standard graphite pencils.  This unit comes apart with a simple twist of a knob and a half backward twist of the handle for easy cleaning.This machine worked great for prismas and pastel pencils for about the first three days, sharpening everything to a fine point without breakage... now it won't even sharpen a regular pencil.  I took it apart, cleaned it to 'like new' and still no result... either the blades dulled that quickly or I'm doomed to never find the perfect pencil sharpener for art pencils.The only sharpener I've had consistent use of for art pencils, especially pastel,  is the $7 X-Acto Bulldog (at your local *mart)... a couple months now, sharpening art pencils nearly every day, and it still works great... not as good as the first day, but still very good..... so if I have to buy them by the case and use one a month, that's what I'll do :)My trashcan is full of discarded pencil sharpeners, a Carl, two multipoints, several others... what a waste, and my $7 one is still going strong.

All in all, it was a fun twist but not likely something I would buy again or use at the office (unless I really wanted to mess with people in meetings I suppose)

Ok, so I'm glad to know I'm not the onloy guy who couldn't figure this out.  I am very good at following directions, but this one didn't come with any. September 11.....a bad day for all of us. But on 9/11/2013 I got a Black & Decker Flash Pro XL Thermal Laminator 12.5-Inch (LAM125FH) from Vine. And with that, began a new nightmare of losing precious memories with a laminator that was damaged from shipping or poor construction. I will never know since it went into the trash and I began an equally memorable task of trying to get duplicates of some of my "treasures" lost to that laminating nightmare that destroyed all that it touched....Unlike that prior model, I have had the opposite results with this machine. First and most importantly, I TESTED the operation with a few items that I consider disposable. I want to say at the very beginning, if you have ANY items you want laminated, spend WHATEVER IT TAKES to purchase a quality machine. Also, spend whatever amount of time it takes to learn every single thing there is to know about how to operate it. The consequence of not doing both will end in heartbreak and a lot of tears. With this beautiful machine, it makes life simple. Get prepared and begin by choosing hot or cool, wait until the blue lights stop flashing and glow solid and beeps. Choose the correct size pouch, line everything up, and go. The reward this time was perfection. NO lost treasures and no more fear of losing those valuable memories, some of which I had for over 50 years. One little added thing I do is I place a box behind the machine so my laminated items have a "tray" to land on to prevent it from curling.The cost of this machine may seem high. But the cost of losing, rather than preserving a precious picture or document, or even Military items you want to preserve is much higher.  You get up to 10 mil thickness on pouches, have 5 temp settings for hot and cold.It makes itself friendly for just about ANYTHING you want to laminate. I find myself now completely at home using this. NO more panic, no more fear, no more jams or lost items. It simply was meant for someone like myself, a person who never used a laminator before, to someone like my wife who is familiar with and uses this for business on a daily basis. I believer this would be ideal even for light to medium commercial use. I also believe you would have to TRY to sabotage the process of laminating to get this to fail. A very far cry from my prior experience with the Black & Decker Flash Pro XL Thermal Laminator I had the misfortune of using last time.Rare for me, this is a full 5 star product and like our Fellows Shredder, well deserved. I expect it to last me years and will update the rating if it ever changes in any way. I HONESTLY recommend this to anyone who may be afraid to try using a laminator. This makes it fun, safe, and rewarding.

It's been a while since I had last attempted to print my own business cards, and the memories of those times did not make me overly optimistic about the viability of the whole do-it-yourself approach to business cards. These always looked jagged on the edges, printed on a poor quality paper with the print quality that screamed cheap home printer. However, Avery cards turned to be quite something else. The Clean Edge turned out to be just that - almost completely smooth edges on par with the professionally printed cards. The paper too is thick and of high quality.The business card templates that are downloadable from the Avery website, however, did not impress me all that much. Most of them are rather plane looking, and the selection is very meager. The templates that can be used online were not very intuitive in terms of how they need to be used, and I never got too far with them. The website also provides a downloadable card design program that supposedly works with MS Word. The program is rather large (134 MB), and comes with no instructions on how to use it. The program seems to have installed correctly on my computer, but I was unable to access any of its features from MS Word.Overall, these are remarkably well done blank printable business cards, and if used with a laser printer will provide almost professional-quality results. However, if you are more particular about how you want to design your business cards, you might want to try some other solution.

They have a sticker on the packages saying the colors are brighter and they won't crack.  I tried those first and they are beautiful.  I bought some more, but they didn't have the sticker on them.  Those must be what everyone here is reviewing.  The old ones are indeed waxy with okay colors.  I hope they don't peel like everyone says.  But those improved ones are wonderful - brilliant colors and nice feel, not waxy at all.  Trust me, there is a difference.  I haven't washed the new improved ones yet, but they do look like they are durable and will withstand the wash.  Wish there was a way to tell if the package we are getting from Amazon is new or old.  I think the stock number is the same.UPDATE:  It has been an entire year since I've done some thirty or so transfers using various brands.  Those new and improved Avery transfers are the best.  One year later, through repeated washings, the new and improved ones still look bright and beautiful.  The others are old and faded.  Look carefully on the package.  If they are new and improved Avery, that's the one you want.

Made by Hon, this chair is excellent quality, and is designed so that it remains comfortable throughout the day. Excellent back support.It arrives in a box, needing assembly, but contains the tools needed and takes only 15-20 minutes to put together. Between the breathable mesh back, and the fabric seat, it remains cooler than a leather piece can get (if your office is climate controlled, neither is a problem, but if there's any question, this is a plus). The seat is adjustable, as are the arms (though I was surprised that the arms don't adjust forward and back [only up and down]).Overall, you won't be disappointed.

The Neutroni notebook is so very lovely.  This isn't a notebook to buy for schoolchildren.  It's too nice for that.  Rather, It's one that can be used as a guest book at a vacation home or for journaling.  The binding is sewn, the pages lie open, there's a ribbon bookmark attached.  An elastic band holds the cover closed when carried.The paper is thick, off-white creamy, and smooth in texture.  I used marker and ballpoint pen.  Marker ink does bleed through enough so that one wouldn't want to write on both sides of a page with one.  Ballpoint pens can cause indentations in the paper but not much.In a nice notebook like this, there are no perforated sheets.  I pulled one page out just to see what would happen.  Did it cause the other sewn pages to fall out?  No.  Not at all.  I can't even tell a page is missing.The back cover sports a pocket big enough to hold a variety of notes and documents. It's cleverly disguised.  If I didn't look, I wouldn't have seen it.The only thing I think needs improving is the elastic band, which hangs loosely, I'd even say sags, behind the notebook when it's off the front cover.  This would be much prettier if that elastic was tighter and hugged the back cover.This is a notebook for people who take their notebooks seriously.  Very nice.This product was provided for review by Neuutroni.

Like the title states, I used many of these labels to label plastic containers like the ones in the picture and cardboard boxes as well.  They stick pretty well, and they are definitely removable, but like most post-it-note-like things the edges are harder to keep down after the first time you use them.  They lose their stickiness. The Fellowes L80-95 is a great laminator for personal home use, which means for those who occasionally need to laminate something and don't want to have to go to the local office supply store to have it done.  It's great that it laminates up to 9.5" inches wide, which makes it great for documents, signs, etc.  It will also laminate smaller sizes if you need to make name tags, laminate a recipe card, etc.PROS:*Warm up takes only 2 to 3 mins, and laminating a letter-sized page takes about a minute.*Has a release handle that will save a lamination if you get it fed crooked and need to reposition.*Portable.  Take it anywhere, school, church, etc. wherever you need some short run laminating.CONS:*Only laminates up to 3-mil thick pouches. 5-mil would have been nice in this price range. Would have given it 5 stars.*Seems a little pricey based on comparable models, but this laminator out performs others in its class.

I have an earlier generation Brother HL4570CDW color which has been working flawlessly for printing color documents.  This new Brother HLL8250CDW model works just as well with some additional features. I used the wireless connection which was quite straight-forward to set up and configure with the setup CD-ROM.What I like about this product :- ease of setup with three different connection methods (USB, wired connection, and wireless network connection)- fast printing speed (upto 32 ppm vs 30 ppm for the  HL4570CDW model)- nice color printing quality- automated duplex printing- printing with mobile devices through the brother iPrint&Scan; AppThe product uses two types of Ink Cartridge, the regular type with a 2500 page yield and high capacity type with 4000 yield based on the product specs. The high yield cartridge also has a better cost / page than the regular cartridge.what could be better for this product- the unit is pretty heavy (weights about 48 lb) and large in size (measures about 16"W x 19"D x 12"H)The price point for the Brother HLL8250CDW  printer is pretty reasonable. For those who do a lot of color document printing, I would prefer using  this printer over the color ink-jet printers as it is more economical from a printing cost standpoint.-

these notes feel like post-it flags - they don't feel like paper.the big plus is that these really are see-through. the document even photocopied the text underneath the sticky note, though that portion was slightly lighter than the rest of the document.the minus is that because these are not paper and feel more like plastic, what you write can get smudged easily if you don't use the proper pen or don't let the ink dry.i can't judge if these are better sticky notes than the opaque paper ones since they can serve different purposes, but they're neat and don't require moving around the sticky note, thus remaining stickier than opaque ones. these are basically giant colorful post-it flags. at the time of review, amazon did not have them for sale, nor was i able to discover how much they cost.

Summary: Slim, Solid keyboard tray with decent quality and very easy install.  Competitive on features in a crowded field, but prices vary a lot.My wife is using a recommissioned hollow door on top of filing cabinets for a desk, so a sliding keyboard tray was a must.  We also wanted something that would stow in a shallow space so the arms of her chair wouldn't interfere when the chair is pushed in.  When fully stowed, the keyboard tray is almost invisible and completely under the desk.  When out, you can raise it to your working level.  Track tracel is 17-3/4", slightly more than the 17" 3M knob adjust track, but just under the 18" travel of the Keynetix.  The Kensington has 19" travel.One thing to note is that it is very easy to lift up, but when pushing it back down to stow, you MUST push it next to the hinge as opposed to the front edge of the tray. The only significant question you need to ask yourself is: Have I ever wanted to remove labels from my file folders? If the answer is 'yes,' then this is the product for you. So let's say that you have a folder in a file drawer labeled 'March 10, 2010' for items that require your attention that day. The day passes and you now have a file folder on which the tab is already filled out. You can bend the folder around the other way, then put something on that tab and use the folder again. Or you can place a sticker over the writing. After a while, there will be too many stickers, all of them permanent and difficult to remove without tearing the folder or making a mess.So if this is the way you use file folders, then these Post-It labels will work perfectly for you. They can be printed in a laser or ink-jet printer - there are 25 sheets of 30 labels apiece - using the downloadable MS Word template. I tried the template and the labels worked very nicely without any software adjustment (Mac running 10.6.2, Word 2008, and HP printers). The labels are a dull white and are easy to write on with Sharpie or other implements. Once you're finished with the written use for the folder, you can peel the label off and place a new label on the folder. That works smoothly and leaves the folder in perfect shape - as advertised.The only downside is the recommendation that you not run the sheets through your printer more than once, perhaps because the bending will eventually result in labels popping off and getting stuck in your printer innards. I tried running a sheet through five times and didn't experience any difficulties of that nature. You'll have to be the judge as to what you're willing to try in your own printer. But frankly, given that these are not intended to be permanent labels, a quick handwritten marking on the label as to its purpose is likely to be sufficient.

Firstly, this is the type of printer you need if you print 11x17 or 13x19 often. The WF-7510 has handled both of these tasks beautifully.  Even over my admittedly crappy (currently) wifi network, this printed connected quickly and transfers data back and forth at a more than acceptable rate.  Setup was easy, just finding my wireless router and inputting the password via the small menu screen.  I set up drivers on my main computer but my laptop was able to connect and print to it without downloading the software from Epson (I'm sure Windows update handled the drivers in there, as they supported the special features of the printer).  I've scanned several documents and the scan quality is quite good, and scanning straight to PDF produces clean files at manageable sizes for e-mailing.  I haven't had to go in and play with the scanning options too much to get perfectly acceptable output.I have printed a few proofs for different design projects and the output is great, even on regular paper. And when it's not in use, closing up the feeder and the output tray makes it look like a nice, neat little package.If you're looking for an inkjet printer that truly does it all, and up to some pretty large sizes, this is a great choice.

I have owned this shredder for over six years, and it has endured some heavy use. It is the second home-shredder I've owned, and it is much the better of the two. It is heavy enough that it doesn't tip over, but not so heavy it can't be hauled from room to room by someone moderately strong. The front compartment holding the shredded paper is easily removed--in an identical fashion to our dehumidifier's bucket. You pull on it and the bucket comes out with a forward motion. The sound the shredder makes when in action is loud, as one would expect, but not so loud that you need protective ear plugs, such as for when you are near a kitchen blender, blow dryer, leaf blower or lawn mower.The main thing to be careful about is to not get impatient and overload the shredder blades. Yes, you can use the backup function to try and back out paper you have overloaded it with, but it is a pain. Secondly, be sure and feed paper in straight. If you feed it in crooked, that, too, is a prescription for a jam.When I am shredding, I lay down either a bed sheet or a tarp and set the shredder in the middle of it. This helps me corral the scraps of shredded paper flying around when I empty the bucket into a trash bag. Another option is to shred in your garage or basement, if you have such spaces, and use aShop-Vacto clean up afterwards. If you do it inside your house, plan on having to use a regular vacuum to clean up after each use, because a mess is almost unavoidable no matter how careful you are since this shredder is turning private papers into confetti. That's great for the shredder's intended purpose, but it does have a tendency to give whatever room you are using a strong resemblance to Times Square on New Year's Eve.

Having a package of several colors is very handy in my work as an editor and proofreader for a couple of newsletters - no hunting for another color to emphasize something.  Finally, having retractable Sharpies is a big improvement over having to take off and replace a cap on a pen each time I use it.Finally, and not to detract from the quality of the Sharpies themselves, as a proofreader I can't help mentioning that there are several typos and grammatical errors in the text on the outer packaging.  Shame.

My nine year old daughter enjoys this product. She loves to play "teacher" in her room at night before bed, and this teacher's wall organizer is perfect as part of that play for her. She can list the activities her "class" will engage in for a day, and use dry erase markers so she can start over again the next day. Also, on a Saturday our whole family can use the organizer to schedule our day of activities and chores. It's a handy product, it's inexpensive, and it's versatile. Recommended.

One of the challenges of the Vine program sometimes is evaluating extremely rudimentary products. While some of us may posses testing and measuring equipment that enables them to accurately measure throughput, bandwidth and other hard statistics, I am left giving you my simple direct impressions as a consumer.And with cables, it is ever so.The Belkin MIXIT Micro USB Cable is similar to many others I have seen, but has a few differences that give it that nice Belkin touch. The cable is a bit thinner and more flexible than the many other cables I have used, and is a lovely light blue instead of the ubiquitous black. I remember when early Cat 3 network cables were available "in any color you like, as long as it's black", and then the rainbow revolution began, and tracing patch points became a whole lot easier.Believe it or not, this is a more useful feature than you may first believe; when pawing through my drawer of Cable Hell, it is impossible to miss among the sea of black snakes.Higher priced, perhaps, but if you like Belkin stuff you'll love this one.
This is great for taping around window air conditioners to keep the air out.  We always have a roll on hand for that and other small home projects.  Good stuff and sticks well!

First off, this printer does a LOT but that doesn't mean it's hard to install or configure. If you follow the instructions, it takes about 15 minutes total and you've got the printer set up, hooked up to your computer, and printing like a charm. I quickly hooked this up to my PC desktop using the provided disc, but I was a little worried about hooking it up to my wife's Macbook Air. No problem their either. We just downloaded the drivers from Epson and connected over wifi and were printing off her laptop just as easily.And that's one of my favorite features of this printer - the wifi option allows you to put the printer wherever is convenient for you, rather than needing to keep it next to the computer so that it can stay connected. As long as you have a wifi network you can hook as many computers as you want up to it and print with no problems within minutes. Now both my wife and I can work on separate computers in separate rooms and print via the same printer.Additionally, it prints extremely fast and does double-sided prints (which our previous printer was lacking). The scan functionality works equally easily and allows for quick scanning and storing of documents. We haven't used the fax feature and don't plan to as we don't have a land line.The touch screen monitor on the printer is very advanced and easy to use and helps with the original setup and with changing settings at any point. We've been using this about a month and haven't had a single problem. Highly recommended!

A compact set of 160 file folder labels by Avery comes in four color lines. What I found most practical is the the pad they are bound on. Instead of loose sheets that slip all over these stay put until ready to use. They are for handwriting or stamping information not for ink jet printing. I have even used then for labeling some freezer packages and small jars of strawberry jam this week.What I would like to see in future improvements is to add two more colors instead of the blue, red, green and yellow stripes. My file system has more than four color coded section. Maybe purple and orange?Another suggestion that would make these labels outstanding is to improve the packaging. Rather than a throwaway cardboard cover I would appreciate a plastic envelop or sleeve which to store the pad. But these are minor suggestions for a product that does  a better job for me than the sheet type of folder label.

The vibrant purple is beautiful. The cylinder opens and will magnetically attach to a surface where you will have two half moons.  This would be great in an office or a classroom.  As a former teacher I would have attached it to my magnetic board to hold those dry erase markers that seemed be anywhere but where I wanted them when needed.  For those who dress up the fridge you can use this there or attach it to a metal file cabinet.  Of course you also can place it on a desk, it is quite attractive.  Great gift with some pens or markers.
These cartridges were just like any I'd buy at a supply chain.  They were fresh and worked perfectly in my machine, and they are long lasting.  I would definitely buy again.

I have fixed thoughts on this binder.  On the positive side, I like the rings, they are not the usual rough edged jaws that are normally on binders, they are very smooth when closed.  This makes turning the pages very easy and snag free.  On the down side, there was a roughly 1/2-inch crack on the front inside hinge.  It goes about 1/2 way through, which makes me question the durability of this binder.  When closed, the sides are not even, the back sticks further than the front.  Not quite sure why that is.  My last complaint is that the cover is not smooth, it has a grainy texture, like low-end page protectors.I would probably by a cheaper option than this binder due to the issues I outlined.

This thing is a gimmick. It does shred paper, but only if you do it *just* right. It's not nearly as useful as the description sounds, and frankly, doesn't even work as it should most of the time. If you've got so much to shred that you can't feed a bit of paper at a time to the shredder, I'd suggest investing in a very good, heavy duty standard shredder and spending the extra 30 seconds.Pros:- It does have capacity for 60 pages. It's a neat concept, and it will hold garbage paper.- See through bin. Good feature so I know when it's filling up.Cons:- Poor shredding performance. From constant sticks to jams and everything in between, this performed worse than the most discount models I've tried elsewhere.- The auto feature just doesn't work. It won't pull in the paper, it doesn't get it all, and it's just a disaster.- All the shreds pile into the middle of the collector, so you must shake it to disperse them and get it to work again.- Anything beyond one sheet at a time, neatly stacked - and it jams. The auto-feed feature doesn't work with multiple pages, staples, or anything of the sort.
Nothing spectacular but served the purpose.  It was as described.  I put them in a drawer to keep tall things organized.

This Quartet Dry-Erase Board is a great! It's big and well made, easy to use by either hanging on the wall or using an easel. It's magnetic, so you can also use it to hang notes as well as write them.

WilsonJones heavy weight sheet protectors are designed for frequently referenced documents.  They are acid free, archival safe and print won't stick.  That is nice feature because over time print has tendency to stick to some sheet protectors.  Well worth getting for those scrap book or document projects.

I love the gel pen.  I like the way it writs and glides over the paper without scratching.  Green is a color I like and have using for over 30yrs.  No open carry in  FL so I have to do with my green pen.

For the files you use rarely, open-sided folders or the more traditional, all-cardboard expansion folders are fine.  However, there are a few files which are frequently accessed.  The luxury of being able to pull them out easily and of their staying intact, rather than needing frequent replacement, is well worth the premium price of these "Easy-Grip" expansion folders.The front and back edges have a tacky material which makes the folders easier to grab, but isn't so tacky that they get stuck to each other in the drawer, and the edges are reinforced with sturdy material.(The use of the word "redrope" is somewhat thoughtless, as a "red rope" folder is, to most people, an enclosed folder tied with a red rope, and a purchaser who expects that would be disappointed).

This is a reasonable shredder for the price. It won't handle 12 sheets well-it seriously bogs down, but 5-10 are no problem. Note that it's a cross-cut shredder, not a confetti shredder so if you're not happy with something that leaves about two inch long strips look elsewhere.Unfortunately, the auto on/off feature has failed with one month of light to moderate use. I chose to exchange it under warranty, which was pretty painless. So far the replacement unit works.May 2014 Update: I received a replacement unit in May of 2012. In May of 2014 the auto on-off failed again, but since I'm beyond the original warranty period I'm afraid I'm SOL.As a result I've revised my rating from 3 stars down to 2.

I love this little thing both my husband and I have back pain issues from time to time and this really helps with that...with our posture at the Pc. You dont have to bend and slump over when you can bring the keyboard to you. It is also fairly easy to install. You should make sure it is compatible with you desk and keyboard size. I highly recommend this!

All the reviews of this printer are 95% accurate.  The printer does everything I want it to do for my home.  I like this particular model because it has the large ink tanks that are available from Cannon as well as aftermarket producers.  This allows the ink to be fairly low cost compared to other ink jet printers.  Here is my review below....1) Image Quality.  This was not one of my primary concerns, but I have no issues with the image quality.  5 of 5 stars2) Set Up.  Set up was fine, but a bit lengthy.  However, once its set up on one computer by USB cable (not included) other devices will see the network printer once you choose to add another printer.  I even found an app for my Kindle Fire that allows me to print from it.  That app is called 'PrinterShare Mobile Print'.  5 of 5 stars3) Merchant:  The merchant was Harold's Prairie and was fulfilled by Amazon.  They sent me the wrong color from what I ordered.  0 of 5 stars.4) Paper Handling.  Its a very small paper tray, but I don't really care, I don't print that much.  Probably wouldn't be good for the office.  Since I use it for the home 5 of 5 stars.5) WiFi Networking.  This is one of the Primary reasons for me to get this printer.  I want a central printer where my family members can print to.  I don't want them rummaging in my office waiting for the printer to print.  I've located it in a lower cabinet in the kitchen near the bar.  That way nobody has to go into someone else's room to get what they printed from another location. 10 of 5 stars!If you get this printer, and have an android phone and/or a Kindle Fire HD, I highly recommend this app:Dynamix USA LLC PrinterShare MobileAll in all this was a good decision from me.  However, I am still upset at Amazon for shipping the wrong color.  Thats the only reason why I gave this printer 4 stars and gave 1 star on the merchant feedback form.  That's the 3rd time Amazon has shipped an incorrect item.  But because the printer is located in a cabinet, I will live with it rather then endure the hassle of working with Amazon Customer service to swap them out ... Still have a bad feeling about it though.  It will probably be the last time I buy a computer component from Amazon.

The thing is handy, especially for wrapping.  But If you are a lousy wrapper like me - you always use way more tape than is necessary.  With this gadget and it's small pre-cut tape strips - it emptied out really fast. Fine for free, but not worth the extra $$$ to but versus a regular roll of tape.  Of course, if you wrap like a pro - that's another story.

These are great for privacy and soo............. easy to use. I love not having to lick them shut, especially since since some of those types of envelopes don't always stay glued shut, and nice to know if someone gets a letter they think may have been opened they will be able to tell that by the flap. It's also very nice to know when your including a check it is not visable to the naked eye, even if that's all that is in the envelope. Now that I tried these I will use nothing else. You'll love them too & well worth the little bit extra they cost.

I have the Letter variation of this expanding file folder.  Each letter is printed between on the file and you just drop whatever you need to file between the paper slots.  If you've got very basic filing needs, this is perfect.  If you are particular about your filing, you may need to get creative with labeling unless you don't mind some overlap.For instance, if you're filing multiple things, such as utility bills, important documents, tax papers, and medical bills, you'd either have to put "LabCorp" and "lease addendums" together, or create one spot for Medical (maybe under M) and one spot for property documents. I'm a bit anal retentive sometimes, so this was an issue for me - just figuring out where to put what so that I didn't have to search multiple pockets, but didn't have too many things in one file.I wish the closure were different.  Since there isn't much in my file at the moment (largely because I'm still figuring out wher to put everything without making me batty), the Velcro strip isn't much of an issue, but I could see that as it fills, it may become less of a closure at all, for one, and for two, it may not survive many openings and closings as I add paid bills or other important papers several times a month.  If you save all your filing for once a month, this may not bother you, either.  I am considering using my snap press to convert the Velcro strip to a simple snap, but will update later (with pictures) if I do.Happy filing!

These are some great slide tabs for hanging folders.  They seem to be very reasonably priced and they do what they are supposed to do.  They are great for filing and seem to work with different folders as we have a couple of different types in our filing system.  So I would recommend if you are needing extras or replacement tabs.
These are great for the price.  None have given me a problem yet.  I recommend them over the more expensive ones.

Ever since the passing of the 35mm camera with the coming of the digital cameras on smartphones, tablets, etc those of us stuck with boxes of slides and negatives have had to make a trip to an available camera company (if one can be found) to transfer our old images to jpeg status to use in communicating with not only family, but with submitting images to articles we are writing, newsletters for small businesses or holiday greetings. Now with this superb scanner/digitizer within a few seconds and with the press of a single button Presto! - out comes a storable jpeg, immediately viewable on the 2.4" LCD on the device, to transfer to a memory stick or send directly to your computer.It really is so very simple to use that there isn't even a learning curve. Set up the machine, insert a slide or a roll of 35mm negatives, and the built in software converts your images to 14 megapixel digital images which actually can convert up to 22 megapixels - not quite the desired clarity for professional use, but certainly adequate for keeping track of images in the computer for organization and reference. Or if you prefer, you can save the scans to a memory card. There is a video out for connection to television - MAC and PC compatible.The really impressive additional aspect of this device is that it is stand alone - no additional computer or software required. For everyone who is entering the Internet age and is stuck with loads of old slides and negatives that have become all but obsolete, here is the solution. Highly recommended. Grady Harp, March 14

I have used several different Canon photo papers during the years that I have had my Canon Pixima MP510, always looking for what seemed to be the best value considering both price and quality of the prints.  I will be looking no longer.  The first thing I noticed when the paper arrived was how heavy the packages of 20 sheets were  compared with the other papers I have used.  The weight difference was confirmed when I looked at a package of Canon Photo Paper Plus, the paper I have been using.  According to the information on the package the weight of the Photo Plus paper is 69 pounds whereas the weight on this paper, the Canon Pro Platinum paper, is 80 pounds.Not being sure what weight difference contributed to the quality of a print, I did a Google search fir information, learning that:  "Thicker papers hold up well when there is heavy ink coverage. For full color photos from your desktop, thicker inkjet photo papers are best."My Canon printer handled the heavier paper without difficulty and I would expect other Canon inkjet printers to do the same.Also, "heavier, thicker papers feel more substantial and can lend visual weight to a project".The main test, of course, is how the prints look, and on that score, I could not be more satisfied.  I am also pleasantly surprised at how fast the ink seems to dry on this paper, giving the print a finished look almost immediately.

My kids used these for their school binders and think they are wonderful.  I've used them for my files and love them too. They are easy to apply and can be staggered how you would like them to be, not just how the pre-packaged index pages come.  A good buy.

I just wrote a review on theBrother Printer HL5470DW Wireless Monochrome Printer. I have been using Brother printers for 8 years. Toner is expensive. It's easy to want to save whatever you can when buying it. I have tried compatible brands. Yes, you can save a bundle by doing so. Nevertheless, in all these years, every time I have tried to use even a highly-rated compatible brand, I have been disappointed. I always find a significant difference in the print quality.I am pretty much committed now to using Genuine Brother toner. The Brother TN-650 Toner Cartridge is a very long life cartridge. I think it is worth it. However, I find that if I shop around, which can take a bit of time, I can find a promotion or some other way to cut the price considerably. It pays to shop around. Amazon.com is also a great place to find bargains.Since I am sold on Brother Printers. I think I should be sold on Genuine Brother Toner too!

I took a BUNCH of photos for this review...they are uploaded above.  (There are pix of the packaging, the accessories, the printer, the set up, the software, the iPhone app and various screens, and the finished documents.)  CLICK ON VIEW AND SHARE RELATED IMAGESWhen I first got this to review, I was thinking, "Oh, golly, another printer???"  I have three already (that I have deemed worthy enough to keep) and I didn't need another one.  I figured this meant I could give a pretty darned honest review.  If anything, I'm really hard to please.First, this thing is big.  I know, it has to be, to have the scanner and all, but it is tall and relatively cumbersome to move.It was difficult to remove from the box.  I had to flip it upside down and carefully lift the box off of the printer.  Don't let it tip over.Once out, there is a TON of tape on this thing.  Just when you think you've gotten all of the protective film, tape, and cardboard squares off, there is another one hiding.  This is a good thing, because it has that very shiny, reflective finish, and you don't want to have scratches upon arrival.  (A drawback to the glossy finish are the innumerable fingerprints and smudges that are apt to happen--you can see them in the photos and I was trying to keep it nice and pretty for you.)Insert your CD with the software/drivers into your laptop...let it autorun.As directed, plug it in and go...put the ink cartridges in (easy!) and have printer paper on hand for that test print.I have set up so many printers, and yes, you can do it wirelessly--but it's ALWAYS easier to do with the USB cable.  Without exception.  So, I tried the wireless connection first (just for you all, folks!) but when it hung up (as it always does--here and at friends' houses, too), I resorted to the included USB cable.  Piece of cake.Except.When the software says that it can't find the printer--wait another 30 seconds.  It will find it.Just don't touch anything and let it finish.Once it's set up, follow the directions to run the test print.During the set up process, I took my iPhone and went to the App Store.  I searched for "Canon print software" and downloaded the Canon iEPP program.I ran the test print sheet.I printed a photo from my iPhone (see pictures).I scanned a document.The quality of the prints are really NICE.  The speed is what impressed me--the sheets were printed very quickly (quicker than my Epson or either of my HP's) and this thing prints QUIETLY.  Very nice.I printed a 20 page document without issue.  Colors of the photos are nice, crisp, and bright.  The print is clear.  The pages ran through quickly and didn't jam.  And it was beautifully quiet.The price of this printer is amazing for what it gives you.  It's NOT a FAX (bummer, Canon!) but aside from that (relatively big) drawback, but the other aspects are really great.
I would recommend getting this to wrap all your coins.  This makes it easier to bring them to the bank and deposit it.

I've got one dispenser on the back of my laptop screen, and one on the fridge.  The biggest problem with the notes on my laptop is that I forget they're there--out of sight, out of mind.They're handy, two of the dispensers are brightly colored and easy to spot (if they're not hidden, of course,) and the dispenser hasn't done any damage to my laptop.You get 3 packs of 20 notes and three folded plastic dispensers.  I've removed and replaced a dispenser a few times without tearing it, so if you stick it to a clean surface you should be able to refill these things a few times.Refills are available here.

I'm using this for a work project, and I think it will be perfect. I love the addition of the file folder section, which you can access through a separate zipper or through the main section with a Velcro latch. There's an interior zippered pocket and another pocket that closes with Velcro.My only gripe is that it's so bulky, which is totally understandable given the file section and pockets. The Smead Self-Adhesive Poly Pockets do precisely what advertised...they are perfect for storing those documents and items you need to protect in a see-through package that will keep them safe.
