I have used HP Glossy Paper for Years, but with a new Canon printer, I decided to try the Canon Glossy Photo Paper in 8x10 format and then 4x6. I was not as pleased with the drying time of the 8x10 Canon paper, although colors were great. However, the 4x6 Canon paper was well worth the money, the colors were bright, and the drying time was about an hour.When I say "drying time," I'm addressing the time that the print remains too tacky to put into an album or frame. Although HP is much faster drying (the 8x10 and 8.5x11 dries in 45 minutes compared to Canon's 24 hours), Canon is certainly acceptable in 4x6 format. And I'll give it 5 stars because the cost is reasonable. I haven't figured out the cost per print yet, but when you read that 70% of HP's profits came from ink, you don't really want to know. (Figures for Canon couldn't be found since Canon makes cameras and other things that HP no longer is into.)

I didn't find much difference between these "new" sticky notes than the regular sticky notes,  other than these are somewhat more transparent, but not enough to easily read what's behind them.  I don't see any advantage in buying these over the regular ones.

We have a small dry-erase board at my work that we use on daily basis to write down things that need to be ordered/purchased. The big problem with this is that either markers get lost or they dry out and are almost illegible. So I got these markers to use for that and they work great. The pack of six means we won't run out for a while and we can just throw them away when they dry out. The caps have magnets on them so they can hang out on the board and not get lost, as well as an eraser, which is far better than using your finger.As others have pointed out, these are fairly fine-tip markers, so they won't be of much use on large boards, or for things that need to be read at a distance. But for small boards, especially ones shared by different people (co-workers, families, etc), these are perfect; and the mix of colors can be handy too, so each person gets their own color.

This adhesive dot roller is so easy to use and mess-free.  It is great for craft projects and as a tape/glue substitute.  It comes in a compact applicator that can easily fit in your back pocket for easy access.

These Smead classification folders are great for projects, financial files and so much more. They are made from 100% recycled content and are very durable and expandable. I can stuff so many papers into these, keeping everything neat and organized.With fasteners attached to the front and back panels as well as the divider panel, each classification folder has up to six separate filing surfaces so you can quickly and easily categorize types of documents. They expand to hold up to 2 inches of paperwork. They are available in standard green as well as assorted colors for easy color-coding. They are great for organizing. Highly recommended.
Products such as these can be very convenient to purchase online. This is one of those products.

These pens are so awesome. The color is great. They do not bleed. I would recommend these pens for keeping notes when you need an eye catching color to keep you on topic and focused. This item does what it advertises, so I do not have any huge complaints about it.  It is also packed with features that make it more versatile then other label printers.  For starters, it features a QWERTY keyboard that makes typing on it more natural as compared to other printers that just have the letter keys in order from A to Z.  In addition because it is wide, it allows for two handed typing as opposed to the hunt and peck method that comes with more narrow printers. In addition there are tons of options in different fonts, font size and font style (Bold, italic, outline, shadow, etc), as well as printing borders, mirror images, and two lines.  There is also the option to purchase different print cartridges you can purchase that allow for different color combinations (i.e. Gold on Black, Black on Clear, and even iron on labels as well).  Even with this small list of feature there are many other features that I don't have the time or space to mention here and to be honest, I believe I haven't even scratched the surface on the many things this printer can do.The only small complaint I have is that is a somewhat awkward trying to type special characters such as ", +, -, and _ because they are all mapped to one button on the keyboard and you actually have to cycle through many pages to find the character you are looking for.  Another minor complaint is that it does not come with an AC adapter, however it does come with two batteries to get you started, but the jury is still out on how long batteries will last.  Other than that however this is a good label printer and while I haven't found and real practical use for it at home yet, it comes in handy at work when labeling our gaming machines to make it easier to find out which wire at the Network switch goes to which machine.This is an very well designed label printer and I would recommend anyone looking to purchase one to take a look at this one.

They always work, give good quality printing, dries fast and not dry up when not used for lengthy periods. I tried the cheaper bargain inks and many failed, were not detected etc. Go with the HP ink. You will save more in the long term and not get frustrated.

We had been using an earlier Canon Pixma rear-fed all-in-one printer for quite a while when I had a chance to try this newer version out.  So I sent our old printer off to college with our daughter and I installed this new one in our home office.The installation was easy and intuitive.  The unit is quiet, and works extremely well.  We use our printer almost exclusively for photocopying and printing.  I have never tried to FAX anything from it, and we have a flatbed scanner so haven't used the printer to do that.One thing I like about this printer is also one of the things I don't like - it's where the paper feeder is located.  Our old printer was rear-fed, so there was a panel that flipped out in the back and the paper stood upright waiting to be fed into the printer.  The downside of this arrangement is that I couldn't put the printer as close to the wall as I'd like.  On this unit the paper a panel drops down from the front of the printer and paper lies in a tray there from which it is fed into the front of the printer.  This allows me to move the printer closer to the back of the desk and closer to the wall.  The downside is that this does not really save you much room, because if you want to keep paper in the paper tray the front panel stays open and the paper sticks out.  This actually gives the printer an effectively larger footprint than our old one had.The other thing that is a design flaw is that when the printer spits out a page it will fly out and onto the floor.  Well, that is unless you extend the paper catcher.  This paper catcher swings out of the end of the paper tray.  Not only that, but you have to rotate it out toward you and then you have to flip up a second hinged piece to complete the paper catcher extension.  We don't like to leave this extension out, since it extends close to or beyond the edge of the computer desk, and it's actually kind of flimsy.In my opinion, this paper catcher unit feels like a last minute engineering answer to the discovery that the paper will shoot out onto the floor.As for operation of the printer - it's nice.  It does a good job, and we are happy with that.  It also works well as a photocopier.It loses a star for the paper catcher issue and because we can't leave paper in it and close the front panel when it's not in use.4 stars, and second best overall to the back-loading unit we sent to college.
What can you say about a pencil sharpener? It sharpens. The receptaclefor shavings is fairly adequate, but it could be a bit easier to but back on.

Maybe I'm just dense, but it took me quite a while to figure out how to work the pencil portion of this device.  There are no instructions included and it's not immediately obvious.  I ended up taking it apart and by trial and error figured out to extend the pencil lead you have to keep pressing down the "handle" bit (the clip you can use to clip it to a shirt pocket) repeatedly all the way.  Would have been nice to have that made clearer.Otherwise, this is pretty much the same "multi-pen" unit you've probably seen for decades.  You press down the red button and it puts out a red ball point to write.  Do it with the blue and amazingly, blue comes out.  If you do green though, well boy let me tell you...it puts out green.  So yeah, nothing revolutionary, though I will say unless they're being tricky with the plastic for the ink reservoirs, there's more ink than I've seen in one of these before.  Usually it's only just a tiny little bit, but t his looks to be about a normal pen sized for each.  Definitely a plus there.  I wouldn't have been able to give a tiny amount of ink a good review.The pencil is a nice addition I hadn't seen before.  It's handy for switching between doing something for work, like writing notes, and going to do a Sudoku puzzle or a crossword later.  Looks to be 2 or 3 little bits of lead in there, also a reasonable quantity.  You should be able to refill with normal mechanical pencil lead, I'd imagine, but it does take the .7mm which is larger than my preferred .5mm.  Still, not awful.  The cap at the top covers the usual sized eraser.So is it worth it, well yes and no.  It's definitely a convenience to be able to have any of the colors in a single pen.  The pencil part is unquestionably a nice addition.  The down side, well it's still the same format you're  used to, no button to just release an ink, you have to half-push down another color to retract the first one, then extend that color.  A minor annoyance, but shows no improvement in the general design of these things.  Also, the pen is slightly wider than I usually like to have them and the ink not as fine a point as I'm used to; you can also get 4 pens and a mechanical pencil separately for less than the cost of this.

This paper cutter is like the kind you might see at Kinko's or at your local school but instead of the huge cleaver blade that can chop off your finger, this one has an enclosed blade that only cuts when you put pressure on the plastic guard.The blade then comes out of the guard and cuts the paper, safely away from your fingers or whatever body part.The blade cuts very well and you can replace the blades as needed.It does hold about 15 sheets of paper and can cut cardboard about that thickness with no problem.Only downside is that you must apply downward pressure during cutting to engage the blade so this could get tiring if you are cutting a lot of paper.

This is a very good concept.  The idea is that you take notes on this special notepad, take a picture of them with your phone or tablet, and import the resulting Shot Note into Evernote or Dropbox.  It works, but there are a couple of issues:First, the paper in the pad allows some inks to bleed through.  Fountain pen ink is a particular problem, but I found that some gel inks bleed trough, too.  In addition, the pads are pretty expensive.  This 5X7 inch, 40-page pad is currently about $5.75 here on Amazon.  Ouch.It's important to understand that this system relies on an app.  It's free, but it seems rather slow and clunky.  Further, the note images can be hard to read, depending, I think, on what kind of ink you used and how much text you squeezed on to the page.There are, in my view, better, cheaper alternatives.  I use a free app called Scan to PDF.  It doesn't require any special paper or ink type, and the scans become PDF files that can be combined, loaded into Evernote or Dropbox, etc.My bottom line:  This is a good idea, but it's not very well implemented here.  There are better, less costly ways to do the same thing.

It took a few attempts for me to figure this out and it took two attempts for the printer to hook up with the router.  It took about 30 minutes to set-up.  The good news is that if you can set it up to the router, you do not have to download any software.Printing, copying and scanningOnce I captured the printer on my laptop, printing was easy.  Copying was also easy.  The problem is wireless scanning, can't be done!  This you need to use a cable.  The print quality was good but didn't "knock my socks off."Overall, the main reason to choose this printer is for space.  It has all the functions that I require in a printer, including doc feeder but is very compact.

I'm a BIG fan of mechanical pencils. I started using them wayyyyy back in high school (*cough*1989*cough*) to take notes and never stopped using them. I like how light they are, I like how you can either write very finely or with bold strokes, I like how they ERASE, I like how smooth they write, and I like not having to deal with the whole wood pencil barrel thing, which always made my hands feel a little gritty. The only thing I *don't* like is when you get to the bottom of a piece of the lead and you push down to write and the lead just goes back inside the pencil. No matter how many times that has happened, it still startles me.ANYWAY, I have used all sorts of mechanical pencils. Some are good, some are great, some are crap.These pencils are nice! They write VERY smoothly, the lead is very strong (I tend to break mechanical pencil leads when writing TOO emphatically), and the barrels are VERY comfortable to hold. They are also nice to look at. I like how bright they are and I love the clear colored barrels. I know exactly where the pencil is in my bag and in the jar on my desk. I hate when a mechanical pencil tries to look like a real pencil. That was a novelty for, like, two minutes and now I want something fancy and different.My two favorite features about these pencils are:- the erasers, which are lovely and soft and rubbery and do an amazing job of picking up the pencil without being the least bit crumbly (nothing is worse than when an eraser splits in half or crumbles all over when erasing).and- the tip of the barrel, where the lead comes out. It's actually like a metal point, which actually looks like the tip of a pen, and supports the lead so it's not as likely to break. And it's RETRACTABLE- when you hold down the eraser of the pencil and push down on the pencil, the entire nib retracts so it won't poke through through your bag or your pocket and impale you when you least expect it. I've tried a lot of wide-format printers over the last year trying to find one that I was happy with. Canon and Epson make high-end wide-format photo printers which are expensive, but I need one appropriate for general use in an office setting, which means printing lots of graphics and the occasional photo. Three I've tested in the last few months are the Epson Artisan 1430, Canon IP8720, and HP Officejet 7110.SETUPI intended to use the printer via a wireless connection. All three are easy to set up via WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup); just press a button on your router, then press a button on the printer and the connection is automatic. The HP printer setup guide stated that I would need to connect the printer via USB cable first, but this was incorrect. All three preformed flawlessly via wireless.INK SYSTEMThe HP is the winner here in terms of ease-of-use. It uses the fewest ink tanks (four, vs. six for both the Canon and Epson), and to install the cartridges you simply click them in and click them out, sort of like using a ballpoint pen. There were no tabs to pull or caps to remove, as there are with the Epson and Canon cartridges.OUTPUT QUALITYBoth the Canon and Epson had excellent photo-quality output. Even when using the "standard" quality setting I was able to get beautiful, vibrant prints on photo paper. If you compare the output side-by-side, the Canon may have a very slight edge in quality, but I really needed to take time and examine the prints closely to make this determination. The HP however wasn't up to the level of the Canon or Epson, probably in large part because it uses four ink cartridges vs. six for the other two. The HP's output looked dull and a bit washed out, even on the "best" quality setting.PRINTING ON MATTE PAPERSince I'm using this in an office I do most printing on matte photo paper. Here is where the Canon was the big looser. In printing graphics and images that covered large areas of a page, the paper that came out of the Canon was wavy like bacon, even after waiting for the ink to fully dry, and even when printing on thick (60 lb.) matte photo paper. I don't know if the Canon printer puts down more ink than the other printers thereby soaking the page, or if the ink is more watery in consistency, but the finished product was unacceptable. The HP was the best in this department with only slight wrinkling in areas of heavy graphics. The Epson was somewhere between the HP and Canon, with some wrinkling, but still very acceptable on 32 lb. matte photo paper.PAPER HANDLINGBoth the Canon and Epson have rear-loading paper slots, while the HP uses a slide-out tray on the front of the printer underneath the output area. Consequently, the HP has a smaller footprint when loaded with paper. The rear-loading method should theoretically allow for better handling of thicker paper, but I had no problem using 60 lb. matte photo paper in the HP.SOFTWARESoftware installation was about the same for all three printers. (I always forgo using the included CD and instead download the latest software directly from the manufacturer's website.) When printing, the Canon and Epson both have a good number of custom controls in terms of color adjustments and custom paper sizes that were more than adequate for my needs. The HP had by far the worst software, offering very few options for color control and custom paper sizes. The HP software would also pop up a message for "free offers" every time I changed an ink cartridge; these were nothing more than advertisements.The Canon did have one annoying trait in its software. There is a setting to "avoid paper abrasion"; this basically increases the distance between the print head and the paper to avoid the print head coming in contact with the paper and causing scrape marks. I had to use this setting because of the paper wrinkling as described above. However, when you print a page with this setting enabled, the Canon software throws up a warning message EVERY TIME a page is about to print, and you need to click "OK" to dismiss the message before the page starts printing. This made it impossible to print multiple pages and walk away from the computer, because you needed to click "OK" before the next page would print. The Epson printer also has the paper-abrasion setting, but it does not throw up a warning message and simply prints what you ask it to.CONCLUSIONAll three printers have their strengths and weaknesses. For me the Epson Artisan 1430 was the easy winner. The output quality is fantastic, it didn't saturate the page with ink like the Canon, and the settings you have in the software are more than adequate.If I was printing only graphics where vibrant photo output didn't matter, I would choose the HP. It has the smallest footprint and is certainly the most uncomplicated of the three printers. It is also the least expensive of the three by a good margin.If I was printing mainly photos on heavy gloss photo paper, the Canon would be an enticing choice. It had a very slight edge in output quality over the Epson. However, the Epson has great output quality and has performed flawlessly in the several months I've had it, and if I had to buy another general-use wide-format printer today it would be the Epson.

I received the Fellowes Starlet 90 Home Binder as part of the Amazon Vine Reviewer Program, along with supplies to test drive it.  NOTE: these supplies -Fellowes 5/16in Black Binding Combs (25 Pack),Fellowes Binding Covers Expressions Grain, Oversize, Navy, 50 Pack (52127), andFellowes Transparent Presentation Binding Cover, PVC Material, 8.75 x 11.25 Inches, Clear, 25 per Pack (52309)were sent with the Amazon Vine packaging of this item, but are NOT INCLUDED with the item and must be purchased separately. Covers were 'mid-weight' for this light-duty use machine.Having never tried a binder, I was eager to give this one a go. I quickly got stuck on how to load the binding comb and the directions were no help. After several frustrating minutes looking at the diagrams and wishing the pictures were more clear,  I went online and found a Fellowes binder  video on YouTube (for a different model from Fellowes), which gave me a tip regarding how the comb should be placed with the teeth up and facing the user.  That tip did the trick, and allowed me to figure out how to load and bind after about 30 minutes of scratching my head.There are essentially three steps to using this machine:  punch holes  for the pages and the covers, set-up the comb binding in the machine, and then bind your project.  But before any of this can occur you have to buy supplies, which do not ship with this unit.You need to purchase binding combs in the appropriate size for your projects (larger comb size means more pages that can be bound together - up to 90 for the " comb), and covers if desired. Once you have these accessories, which are actually `necessities', you can begin the process.The good news...after all the frustration I encountered trying to use this unit for the first time, I liked the end product - a professional looking binding job.  It is sold as a light-duty binder with a 2 year warranty.  It's not for those who have large or multiple projects.  If you are looking for one of those I'd consider this one:Fellowes Quasar 500 Comb Binding Machine (52168)or theFellowes Galaxy e-Wire Binding System, Gray (5217801)instead.The bad news...the lack of directions on binding comb placement and how to put on the paper to be bound on the combs, needs much improvement. Novice users like me will find this part very frustrating with the existing instructions.  This unit also needs to be shipped with a sample pack of binding combs and covers. You can't even try it out without them!Rating: 3 out of 5 stars. The poor directions and the overly optimistic recommendations for number of sheets of paper to punch at one time (7 is recommended and I think 5 works best), indicating that you can both punch holes and bind at the same time (you can't without four hands...), and for the lack of side guides to assist in keeping the paper to be punched in place, all were negatives for me regarding this product.Bottom line: it's not terrible, but it's not great either.I would recommend this binder for students, light office use and home crafters with  projects such as calendars and scrapbooks on their agenda. If your needs are for frequent (daily), thick or multiple projects, I'd consider other binders. Perhaps an electric one?Check out the Fellowes extensive line-up of products and see which one meets your needs.  The quality is not the issue, but your level of experience with this type of project and the jobs you need to get done may be.

Having purchased an HP 4500 officejet a while back I also picked up some ink for it. 901 color and 2 - 901 black  cartridges(family does a lot of B&W; printing)  I am not impressed at all with the 901 black.  It is substandard at best and produces very  mixed results.Usually we print stuff on FAST (economy) and while the cartridge is rated for 200 pages, we actually got around 250-300 on the first one which puts it at around 125-150 for Normal.  (Usually fast/economy uses half the ink as it only does a single pass instead of two or three)  The strange part is.. the second cartridge we got was terrible performance.  I estimate by around 150 Fast/Economy the cartridge was starting to show it was almost out of ink already which would put it at around 75-100 pages normal!?I was a bit shocked because there was such a deviation.  I did some research and found out that HP rates their Cartridges using an ISO standard Text document. They test on a J4580 printer which is an INK SAVER printer. If you do not own a J4580 then obviously you will get different results.Because it is rated on a Text document keep in mind, print out a page that is loaded with black bars(like a bar graph) it will devour your ink; yet print out a page that has only a small amount of text you could go for 300+ pages easily.  I rarely complain about ink cartridges but I must say HP really should put some more ink into the standard 901 black; considering a 901XL has over 3x the rating (200 vs 700). Plus they should rate them using a "Standard" printer not an Ink Saver printer.  VERY MISLEADING !!OVERALLAvoid the 901 black!!  While they perform just fine and do have black ink in it that works, the cartridges performance is determined by how much black you print per page not by # of pages.  I would recommend instead spending the extra money and getting the 901XL black which is rated for 700 pages.  Once I got one of those I found I was able to print an entire ream of paper (500 pages) and the cartridge was still 50% full (all on economy/fast)  So despite paying twice the price I already DOUBLED my output compared to a 901 standardIn short.. avoid!!  get the 901XL as it will pay for itself.

Quartet Enduraglide Dry Erase Markers are very nice dry erase markers for many reasons. The main quality that sets these markers apart and that you notice right away is the three- chamber ink distribution system and the see- through ink barrel. It's an appealing concept and it lets you see how much ink supply is left so there are no classroom surprises. Then, there are the bright, vivid colors that flow from the chisel tips. Among the four shades in each package, I prefer red because I love the brightness but the other colors are equally vivid. And the nice part is that even with this level of color, the ink still wipes clean quickly with one swipe of an eraser.Quartet Enduraglide Dry Erase Markers are intended for dry erase whiteboards, but they are still useful in other ways. For example, I sometimes use mine on regular paper. What I like about using Quartet Enduraglide Dry Erase Markers on paper is that the ink dries almost instantaneously. There is no chance for smearing because it dries almost the instant it touches the paper. The colors are not as rich when used on paper compared to using on a whiteboard, but for a general use marker, it gets the job done as well as any other.One other quality that I like with the Quartet Enduraglide Dry Erase Markers is that the cap snaps in place on the opposite end of the marker. This may not seem like a big deal to some, but in all the years I have used dry erase markers, I have been very frustrated by the tendency of the cap to fall off the opposite end. I like to take the cap off and place it on the opposite end of the marker, as a means for storage while I write with the marker. The problem with doing this is that the cap almost never stays in place. It falls off effortlessly and often rolls underneath a desk or other large object, making it sometimes difficult to find. But Quartet Enduraglide Dry Erase Markers are different. The cap on this dry erase marker actually snaps into place on the opposite end of the market. This means it cannot fall off on its own, with normal use.Overall, Quartet Enduraglide Dry Erase Markers are very good markers I am happy I took the time to try out and get to know. The scent is bearable, the color is good, and the ink dries quickly. Add to that the fact that the cap stays firmly in place on the opposite end of the marker and you have a very good set of dry erase markers for everyday use.

Henkel EZ Start Carton Sealing Tape with Dispenser is a different type of packing tape with a design that makes it easier to use than other packing tape. The manufacturer makes this tape with a no frills, no frustration design that makes it easy to seal boxes and other like items.Henkel EZ Start Carton Sealing Tape with Dispenser is certainly different from other packing tape in several important ways. Among the differences, the one you will notice right away is the way the tape releases itself from the roll. It dispenses with almost no effort and no sound. Other packing tapes are more resistant and they come off the roll with a loud, almost painful ripping sound. There is no such problem with Henkel EZ Start Carton Sealing Tape with Dispenser. It comes off the roll with almost no effort at all.Another important difference with this tape is the tearing of the tape. The dispenser does have a nice, handy cutting bar, but the truth is, you don't necessarily need the tearing bar. The reason is due to the ease of tearing this tape. It is very easy to grab an edge, between the fingers, and tear off a piece of tape. Other tapes are tougher and are manufactured in such a way that a metal bar or scissors are necessary to cut the tape, but there is no such need with Henkel EZ Start Carton Sealing Tape.The above qualities certainly set this product apart from the rest, but this tape isn't without its flaws and the greatest among them is getting the tape started. As you grab an edge with your fingernail, the tape slowly lifts up, but if you lift it too quickly, it will start to tear vertically and this is due to the ease of tearing described above. When this happens, you then have to grab the other edge and lift it up, slowly, until the two sides meet. Getting it started takes effort and patience and because of this problem, consumers should always store this tape by having it stretched out over the cutting bar. If the tape is permitted to fall back in place, touching the roll, it will have to be started again, and this could lead to the same problem just described.One other potential problem with this tape is its overall strength. It has no problems when used to seal boxes, but because the tape is so easy to tear, it doesn't have the diverse abilities of other packing tape. With other, stronger tape, the tape is strong enough and the adhesive sticky enough that the tape can be used for a multitude of purposes. This tape can only be used for its intended purpose and little else.Henkel EZ Start Carton Sealing Tape with Dispenser is, overall, a good product and it does succeed at its main purpose, which is using it for packing and sealing boxes. Its performance is satisfactory when used in this manner, but its overall use is limited and there are other, similar tapes that work just as well and for a lower price.

Let me start by saying that I am NOT a professional photographer.  I am, however, a serious amateur, and take photos of  flowers, trees, etc., and architectural details (trims, doors, gargoyles, etc.) that I like to print and frame for use in my own home and as gifts for friends.  I also print both color and black-and-white art for the handcrafted greeting cards I like to make.  I've been using online photo services for printing my photos, and a reasonably decent inkjet "all-in-one" for the rest, but decided to try this Canon PIXMA PRO-100 as an alternative.So, given that, let's get started --UNLOADING and SETTING UP --First, you need to understand that this thing is SERIOUSLY big and heavy.  No, really.  It weighs nearly 50 lbs, and takes up some sizable real estate: 27" x 15" x 8".  This is not the kind of printer you can fit into a bookcase; it needs its own stand or area on a desk or table.  Unpacking isn't too bad -- but be prepare for the weight, and make sure you have a space to set it up.  You also need to leave at least 10" space behind the printer, and 17 " clearance in front to accommodate the paper feed trays.Once you get through all the packing material (there's lots), hardware setup is fairly straightforward: power cord, print head, ink cartridges -- it's pretty clear from the instructions what you need to do. Software installation went fairly smoothly -- I have a MacBook Pro running OSX 10.6.8 -- and opted for the simplest installation (Easy Install).  Once the software is installed, you run a test to make sure the print head is aligned properly (I assumed it was -- looked good to me!).Setting up the wireless interface is a bit trickier for those of us who don't do this sort of thing very often.  It took me a couple of tries to get it going, but I managed to get it eventually. Suffice it to say I had to consult the on-screen user manual several times to figure it out.PERFORMANCE --The printer comes with a few sheets of Canon Photo Paper Pro Luster 8 1/2 X 11.  I purchased additional paper in order to test print quality:Canon Photo Paper Pro Platinum, 8 x 10 Inches, 20 Sheets (2768B019)andCanon Photo Paper Plus Glossy II, 5 x 7 Inches, 20 Sheets (2311B024).  I also used some smooth white 110# card stock, and some burlap-textured white card stock from my own supply.I printed the same photo on the photo papers, and used two different images on the card stock.  In every case, the colors are simply amazing.  This is especially true on the glossy photo paper.  Bright, crisp, precise.  I used both Airprint as well as my wi-fi network, and both worked just fine.For the test on card stock, I used a color image of water color roses (lots of pinks and greens) on the burlap-textured paper, and a detailed line drawing for the smooth heavy cardstock.  Again, the colors of the watercolor print were superb.  This is dye ink, so I was expecting good color, but I really was blown away.  For the detailed line drawing, again it was crisp and clear on the smooth card stock.SUMMARY --This printer provides unusually good print quality.  It has some potential drawbacks, depending on your circumstances: it is heavy and large and needs quite a lot of space; and the ink cartridges are rather pricey. I have it placed in an out-of-the-way corner so I can use it when needed.  I'm giving it 5 stars because of the excellent quality.  I'll do my best to update this review if I note any issues re: durability, deterioration, etc. over time.  But for now (after 1 week of use), it's really impressive.

This is a black and white printer not color. It does not have wireless, no LCD screen, or a paper tray indicator level but what it is and does so well is print at really fast speeds at laser quality. It prints up to 35 sheets per minute in black and white so with a multi-sheet print that is less than 2 seconds per page.One point worth mentioning is that if you have a wireless router and have it connected with an Ethernet to your wireless network you can print to it with your wireless devices. It goes through the wireless router out into the network and is received by this printer via Ethernet.Setup is a breeze; plug it in, install the CD, connect the cable, and zingo it is working. It connects either through a USB cable or an Ethernet cable. The price to print per page has always been a lot cheaper than using an ink jet however one of my Epson printers is a color inkjet and the print per page cost on that one is about the cheapest of them all. Technology keeps on moving forward.There is much to do about Lexmark getting bold in blocking the use of aftermarket replacement cartridges. I have used some replacement cartridges in my Brother laser without any problems. Of course the OEM cartridges are more expensive, but the cartridges on this Lexmark once you get over the sticker shock of the large capacity ones isn't that bad. I think Lexmark is also considering the warranty problems they run into because using aftermarket cartridges, or refill bottles requires a litle finessing in order to get it right. For example some powder types are not compatible so you need to use a compressor to blow out all of the original powder before replacing with the aftermarket type.Amazon does not like when you supply prices in a listing and I don't blame them so I won't list the full sale price of the cartridge. The latest prices are available through a search, or you can do the math from the following results. The 500AH cartridge is good for 5,000 pages and works out to 3.9 cents per page. The 501 cartridge with the return program in that you return your existing cartridge does 1500 pages at 4.3 cents per page. And the 501H with the return program as well does 5,000 pages at 2.9 cents per page.The HUGE advantage laser has over inkjet is that the cartridge never dries out because it is already dry as in powder. I have a friend who bought an early on NEC laser printer for $1500 and being as frugal as he is hardly ever prints anything. Eight years later he was still using the same cartridge. I can't tell you how many times I got frustrated because my Lexmark Inkjets would have a cartridge dry up on me. Very few pages were printed but the cartridge of wet ink would dry out rendering it useless. I had a new cartridge still in the box unopened and a year later that one was dry also. The really frustrating thing is that the way it was engineered, every time there was a power outage, when the electricity came back on, it would turn on and park the cartridge out in the middle ready to use instead of in the park position which helps to avoid the cartridge from drying out.So not only is this Lexmark laser printer a laser using powder only which lasts forever, the overall print per page cost is great as well. Lasers since they are powder that is melted onto the sheet instead of wet ink, the laser for example when printing envelopes don't have the potential to smear when they get wet the way an inkjet does; at least most inkjets are that way.Overall a nice unit for the money.

The Swingline Optima 45 is an electric stapler suitable for a school or office environment.  It has an "auto" mode which allows it to staple your pages upon insertion.  If you want the ability to more precisely place your staples, you can flip a switch and the Swingline goes into "manual" mode and requires you to press the top of the stapler to actuate.  In either case, the staple is delivered quickly and with a lot of power.  I easily stapled through the claimed 45 pages of paper but when I tried 52 pages, the staple didn't go all the way through.  I was pleased with this performance since Swingline only claims 45 pages.I'm impressed with how quiet the Swingline is.  The sound is not jarring like a typical handheld stapler and disappears in the background of the office.  The sound volume does increase somewhat when stapling through thicker bunches of paper, but it is still a lot quieter than I expected.Using a kill-a-watt I measured the Swingline at 0 Watts when idle.  This is important because it means it won't be driving up your electricity bill in between uses.The stapler has an adjustable guide so you can position the staples to enter closer to or further from the edge of the paper.  The guide gives you consistency between uses.  The Swingline also has a lit guide that shows you exactly where the staple punctures will occur.Because of the large amount of paper this stapler can handle, you'll have to keep this out of reach of very small children.If I could change anything, I'd make this unit smaller.  Because it is an electric stapler, it seems like it could be about half the depth.  Overall, it's done a great job and I'm happy with it.

Epson makes a large number of inkjet printers designed for use either in a home office or in a small office. The WP-4020 is the least expensive in the line for the small office. The printer comes with sufficient ink (black, cyan, magenta, and yellow cartridges) to handle 1000 pages black and 900 pages color, but extra-large carts are available to bring those numbers up to 2400 and 1200 respectively. This unit does one thing: print. There's no scanning, copying, or faxing. Of course, there are a number of ways that it can print, and right out of the box you've got both a paper tray and a multi-purpose paper feeder in the back. Between the two, the unit can hold 330 pages. Envelopes can be accommodated. WiFi is incorporated into the product as well.The 4020 has no direct interface, so the initial setup to get through your wireless password protection must be done with a hard interconnect between a computer, preferably on the network, and the printer. You'll need an ethernet or USB connection for that to take place. Once the printer is properly configured, all other computers on the network will see it without difficulty. I installed the printer software under Mac OS 10.8.2 on a MacBook Pro, then made the connection with a USB cable, and quickly had the printer up and running. I was then able to print from my iPhone 5 using AirPrint, from my desktop Mac Pro without downloading any software at all, and so forth.Printing is quick and I did not have to run through any of the alignment routines. The printer is not particularly quiet, but there is a Quiet Mode (which helped a bit but slows things down a bit as well) if you are using this in the home office. The next step up is to the WP-4530, which has the same print capabilities while adding copying, scanning, and faxing. For two sided printing on the 4020, the driver on the Mac does not allow for that from the Layout page. You must instead go to the Two-Sided printing page while in the print driver. Similarly, the choice as to which paper source is utilized is also made in a different part of the printer driver selection routine than that used for other printer manufacturers. Look for it and you'll find it eventually, but a bit more clarity in the printer driver routines would be nice. Similarly, I would have liked some explanation as to the controls on the top panel, not all of which are described in the QuickStart pamphlet or the HTML based user guide.Roughly the same price will get you the home office WF-3520, which has copy/scan/fax but has a smaller ink capacity as well as a lesser paper capacity. There may be differences between the models in terms of construction quality so as to allow for heavier use on the small office line. However, comparing the three Epsons that we have (the Workforce 840 - last year's home office line - and the WP-4540, which is the top-of-the-line small office printer) doesn't reveal any significant differences in construction, including sturdiness of trays and output areas, materials used in gears, or look-and-feel. All that said, Epson states that this particular model has a 20,000 page duty cycle and is designed to print up to 1600 pages/month.Print quality is up to par with other ink jets in this price category. Photographs are of acceptable quality on glossy paper stock, but this is primarily a business printer which happens to do a nice job with color. The better the paper, the nicer the output will look, so don't skimp and use cheap copy machine paper if you intend to share your color output with clients and associates.The real choice at this price point is the trade off between the 3520 and the 4020. Do you want to have more paper in the printer and longer-lasting ink cartridges? Or would you prefer a single printer that can also copy, scan, and fax? Or you can spend about 1/3 more and have both with the 4530.

This printer is so neat!  It was so easy to set up (even I could do it, and I'm no techie).  We put it in a room that previously did not have a printer and where my computer is not right by it; it's actually across the room so being wireless is awesome. You first need to install the four ink cartridges, the black being larger than the three colored. You also install the duplexer (more on that later) and the paper tray. When you first turn it on you need to set the language.  Then it took about 15 minutes to calibrate the printer; all you need to do is wait for the touch screen display to come on and show you it's ready.  Setting the printer up wirelessly was a breeze; it found our router and then I needed to put in the secret code.  It has an icon to show you the printer is now connected wirelessly (you can also use USB).  We have all Windows computers, but it also is supposed to work on a Mac.The LCD touch screen is so cute; it's 2" x 2 1/2" and is very easy to read.  It shows the date and time at the top, and at the bottom icons and words for copy, fax, scan, and photo.  When you make a copy you can either click on black or color.  After a few minutes of non-use the LCD screen goes black and the power button blinks.  To print again the LCD screen comes on again automatically.The duplexer is so cool; it prints on two sides automatically.  When the first sheet comes out of the printer it sits there a few seconds and you get the message on the touch screen that the ink is drying and then it reinserts the paper and prints on the other side.  Love that feature, especially since I'm not sitting right by the printer so don't have to get up and reinsert the paper.  A little word of warning, when I first printed out a two sized page I did not realize that the printer automatically reinserted the page to do the second page, so while it was sitting there with the ink drying I tried pulling it out; yikes, paper jam!  Had a time getting all the pieces of the paper out; had to remove the duplexer on the back to remove some of the paper.  So, don't make my mistake; don't touch the paper until it's through printing on both sides!Since installing the printer last night I installed a greeting card program and printed out cards, got auto insurance quotes online and printed them out, printed out IRS forms, copied forms and scanned a picture that the printer sent to my computer (it will also email it, how cool is that). You can also insert media cards to print out photos, plus it also has a picture bridge if you have a compatible camera.  I can't really think of anything HP left out. I am so totally enthralled with this all-in-one printer!  I told my husband when we were installing it that at my first job we didn't even have a copy machine (yeah, ok, so that was about 40 years ago; lol).  Having it all in one machine and wireless at that is so totally awesome!  If you are looking for an all-in-one printer look no further, you have found it!!!!!!!!!P.S.  I was so excited about all this printer can do that I forgot to mention how fast it is!  When I set it on draft the paper flies out of the paper tray faster than a speeding bullet (or would if it didn't have a paper tray)!  ;-)  Also, we have not tried out the fax because we do not have a land line.

I decided this past spring that my house needed painting. Now that really doesn't seem to have much to do with a Laminator, of course. But bear with me. When I weighed the pros and cons of painting myself vs. hiring a contractor, I decided to do it myself and I purchased a Grayco semi-professional paint sprayer. The job turned out great. But remembering all the steps to set the sprayer up and, more importantly, to clean it when I was done painting was a chore. The sprayer came with an instructional DVD that ran through the steps, and I watched it, taking notes, each time I needed to paint or clean the unit. I took my handwritten notes out to the sprayer and, covered with paint, with water dripping, sprayer parts in various places and my handwritten notes slowly being transformed to the exact same color of my house, I finally got the job done.Now I consider this sprayer an investment and intend to use it quite a bit more. But the thought of having to watch the DVD each time I paint, taking down notes that will get waterlogged or covered with paint seemed kind of silly. I won't paint often enough to become adept at it. I needed a way to take my notes for my sprayer outside, among the paint and the water and not get them all gunky.I have other important documents that I could justify a laminator for, so I decided to get one. My first project: watching that Grayco DVD, one more time, taking and transcribing notes onto a two page setup and cleanup document that reminds me how to setup and then clean the paint sprayer. I printed out the two pages and opened up the Fellowes Saturn 95 Office Laminator.Where the Grayco sprayer had an instructional DVD that contained tons of setup and operational instructions, the laminator gave practically no advice at all. There was a booklet that had one page of instructions in English, but they were pretty skimpy. The laminator itself has an on and off switch, but there is one direction for ON that is for documents that are 3 mils thick and one for documents that are 5 mils thick. Excuse me! How thick are two pages of paper? No idea, no advice, no nothing. I took a guess and switched the machine to 3 mils and waited about 6 minutes for it to heat up. I placed my document into the laminating pouch - a supply of ten was included in the box with the laminator - and when a chime rang, telling me the unit was up to laminating temperature, I got ready to start.But wait! The instruction sheet illustrates feeding the pouch with the documents into a slot in the laminator, but there is no opening on the machine. Hmmmmmm. Oh, wait, there IS a hidden door that isn't shown or described in the instructions that pops down, exposing the insert slot. OK... I start to insert the pouch, containing my document, into the laminator. I expect that it will be grabbed at some point by the laminator, but as I insert the pouch an inch or so, it's not being taken up by the laminator. Am I doing this right? OK, I keep inserting the pouch a bit more, maybe two or three inches inserted into the machine and pause, then notice that the laminator is pulling - very slowly - the pouch into the machine. Slowly, the document, encased in a now clear laminated plastic cover, emerges slowly from the back end of the machine. It is warm, but not hot to the touch. The laminated document looks professional, sealed against water and probably exterior acrylic house paint and ready to stand up against abuse. For my first laminating job, not bad.Fellowes makes laminating pouches of several other sizes, too. The supply that came with the laminator was sufficient to easily laminate 8.5 X 11.25 standard US paper, but I'll probably purchase some smaller sizes, too.Aside from the spartan instructions that come with the laminator, this is a nice little unit for occasional home or small office use. You'll have fun figuring out how to use it the first time, too! It is small, but produces very professional looking laminated documents.

Kanye West has once again created a musical masterpiece with his sophomore release LATE REGISTRATION.  While LATE REGISTRATION may not be able to edge out the greatness of THE COLLEGE DROPOUT, in its own right, it is much more ambitious and more creative than THE COLLEGE DROPOUT. Here, you see that Kanye experiments with different colors and unique, sometimes even chilling arrangements to back his rhymes up.  Besides that, overall, West chose many good collaboraters including Paul Wall, Jamie Foxx, Brandy, Nas, Consequence, GLC, Adam Levine, Common, and etc...Here is a rundown of the songs:1. Wake Up Mr. West [interlude]2. Heard Em Say feat. Adam Levine- production is superb here with a catchy piano riff, nice emotional piano chords, fuzzy bass line, and the superb falsetto of Levine. Nice opening to this album.  4/53. Touch The Sky feat. Lupe Fiasco- another production showcase with an incredible sample (brass-filled), and a catchy hook.  One of the best tracks on the album. 4/54. Goldigger feat. Jamie Foxx- genius use of a Ray Charles sample with Foxx's superb vocals and a creative rap by Kanye.  Nice drum programming.  One of my personal favorites. 4.5/55. Skit #16. Drive Slow feat. Paul Wall & GLC- nice mellow arrangment with the occasional horn riffs. My attention was first caught by the patent number, US 6,732,494, printed inside the flap.  I have been doing a lot of patent searching lately, so I immediately looked up the patent.  You can also do this very easily. Go to Google Patents and enter the patent number.About the envelope: I have used similar envelopes with self-sealing adhesive in the past. I live in a very humid climate.  We have had nearly sixty inches of rain in the last twelve months.  The old lick and seal envelopes seal themselves and become unusable in a very short period of time.All of the press and seal envelopes that I have tried previously require that you peel off a strip before the adhesive is exposed. With theReveal-N-Seal Envelope, the adhesive is brought into position by folding up a pre-folded flap.  This works very well.  The adhesive is stronger than the paper of the envelope. As a result, attempts to reopen the envelope tear the paper.  Altogether this is a well engineered product that I can give five stars to.Patent Analysis:  US 6,732,494 is well written, with one exception, which I will explain.  There are claims in the patent for the envelope, a method of manufacturing the envelope and a machine for manufacturing the envelope. The claims define the intellectual property.  In order for a product to infringe on a patent, it has to have every element listed in the claim of the patent.  Here is Claim 1 for the envelope."1. An envelope having:a front side and back side;a closing flap connected to the front side;a fold-back flap which can be folded from a stored state into a closed state, which in the stored state is folded against the envelope back side, and which in the closed state is bonded to the closing flap; andan adhesive closure including a contact adhesive coating,wherein in the stored state the contact adhesive coating is applied to a surface area of the envelope having separating characteristics and defining a separating area,wherein the contact adhesive coating, a surface of the contact adhesive area and the separating area are constructed so as to cooperate in such a way that the contact adhesive coating applied to the separating area is firmly bonded with its top onto the surface of the contact adhesive area of the envelope pressed onto the same,wherein the contact adhesive coating becomes separated in the closed state from the separating area, and the previous underside of the contact adhesive coating area now forms the surface of the contact adhesive coating having contact adhesive properties, andwherein on an edge of the envelope adjacent to an outer edge of the fold-back flap the contact adhesive has gripping recesses or a prebreak defining a gripping zone."My observation is that the Reveal-N-Seal Envelope does not have the gripping recesses in the adhesive area, shown as 27 in Fig. 3 of the specification. These are required in the claim, "contact adhesive has gripping recesses or a prebreak defining a gripping zone." I also do not see a "prebreak defining gripping zone." I am not sure that the arrows on the flap satisfy this requirement.Thus, I believe that the Reveal-N-Seal Envelope. which is without the gripping recesses, may not be protected by US 6,732,494.  However, claim 2, the method of producing the envelope does not require gripping recesses.  Anyone who followed the recipe of claim 2, would infringe on the patent.  I am not a patent attorney, so this is only my observation, not a legal opinion.

Printers these days are pretty cheap and ubiquitous.  With just about any printer and any computer you can make some fantastic looking labels, just so long as you don't mind cutting up the 8.5" x 11" paper into little strips and gluing and taping them onto things.  That's where a Label Printer comes in.  The Epson LabelWorks LW-300 simplifies the label-making process while offering the portability of a handheld device.  While you won't have nearly as many creative options, it's a worthwhile tradeoff for efficiency and ease.While you won't be making any showstopping labels (i.e. ones with color pictures of your family), the Epson LW-300 is capable of a variety of fonts, up to two lines per label, borders and a wide variety of pixelated art.  Also, there are many color combinations to choose from.  My favorite ticker tape is the gold on black.  It's great for adding a little personalization to gifts etc.  The more mundane colors are good for professional use or everyday around the house.  A nice, eclectic set of fonts round out the presentation.  Not having the ability to print 3 lines on a label was my biggest disappointment, since it would make return address labels a cinch.The main reason to get the LabelWorks 300 is the ease of use.  The unit powers on instantly and is a breeze to use.  The keypad is easy enough to work with considering the size limitations and most functions can be accessed with only a couple button pushes.  The display could be a little bigger, but it is large enough to display a few words.  Swapping out different ticker tapes is really quick and easy.  I would have liked to see an adjustment for the margins, but otherwise every option I could think of wanting was available.Overall, I'm very happy with the Epson Label Printer.  It is easy to use.  The manual is brief, but explains everything clearly.  A handy reference for most of the functions is on the back (a sticker for french is included as well).  There were a few areas for improvement, but this gadget is a great value and will work great for just about anything simple.

If you've every had a binder with plastic pockets on the front, back and spine, you know that sometimes these sealed areas will start to split away and the plastic will flap loose. After this, you lose the ability to customize the binder with front, back and spine inserts. I haven't had this binder long enough to know if it'll go the distance that others have not, but the edge point do seem to be more strongly sealed than the average binder (this is visually indicated by the broader, deeper connections along either side of the spine). If you are the type of person who needs to customize a binder on multiple occasions and find yourself taking inserts in and out a lot, then the investment in a binder like this may be warranted.I noted that, because of the deep embedding of the plastic to secure the spine and plastic for inserts, the edges of this binder are much more flexible than average binders. I'm not sure if this is a good or a bad thing, though I do wonder if, in the long run, these thinner plastic connections may cause the front or back pieces to tear away with repeated flexing. This seems to be a great potential weakness for a binder which should be long-lasting.Other than the stronger holding pockets, there appears to be little that separates this binder from the pack. The basic material seems no heavier or sturdier than average. The rings are advertised as "never gap", but I don't think this tends to be an issue in anything but the cheapest of binders in my experience anyway. Certainly, good alignment of the rings is important, but, in my experience, they only start to gap after a lot of use and this only has a one-year guarantee.The bottom line is that, as binders go, this one seems fine and it does seem that if you're changing inserts in and out a lot, it may be a strong option. it is a little expensive though for a single binder so you'd have to weight the value of that particular strong point against a more economical option.

I'm largely comparing this to theEpson WorkForce WF-3520 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer, Copier, Scanner, 2-Sided Duplex, ADF, Fax. Prints from Tablet/Smartphone. AirPrint Compatible (C11CC33201)- my workhorse printer around the house for printing, faxing, scanning, etc. This Canon model doesn't have all the same features, but it does do other things better than the Epson.Setup was simple - the quickstart manual included in the box walked me through the steps along with the large LCD screen that had specific instructions. It did take around 10 minutes, most of which was time waiting for the printer to calibrate itself and prepare to be used. The printer was well packaged and wrapped up, and comes with ink cartridges of each variety needed, power cable, driver disc, 3 pieces of photo glossy paper (more on this soon), and some special paper for alignment.Pros:- The setup was super simple. Even better, the cartridges light up when they're installed correctly. This was so frustrating on an old HP printer I had, and is a simple, elegant solution.- The photo prints are extremely impressive, especially on the photo paper. I compared a print I made with this printer with one from Sam's Club I had done the other day on their fancy photo machines. I preferred the printer. Of course, at $.13 each, Sam's does win for value. Photos print quickly, with a 4x6 taking maybe 20 seconds.- Nice big LCD that makes choices obvious. It is not a touchscreen, as I've seen it described elsewhere, but it does have intuitive programming so I found it easy to use.- Document printing is quick and easy, as would be expected. I printed several documents, including duplexed items, and they came out in high quality and ready to go.- The automatic scan settings and simple software made scanning a breeze. It can all be done from the printer directly, and it will send the output to the installed computer. The Epson is more work for scanning but has pretty powerful software (and an ADF). The old HP we had was garbage and basically never worked.- Wi-Fi setup was simple. It just worked the first time. No messing around, no missing printers.- It's rather squat, so if you're limited on headroom, that could be a benefit.Cons:- The big one. It's loud. Extremely loud. Plus, randomly it churns through some stuff to make loud noises. I don't understand what causes it, but it happens. Worse, it does loud things when you want to use it sometimes, too. Maybe it's cleaning, maybe it's aligning, maybe it's trying to communicate. I dunno, but word of advice, don't put it in the baby's room.- The paper tray is rather small. Compared to other models, I think I'd be refilling it more often than I like.- The bottom paper tray is for standard paper, the top for photos. I'd rather see it reversed, especially as I find getting into the bottom tray more difficult than the top one - and I'll use standard paper a lot more than photo printing.Overall, it's a good printer if you really want the photo printing functions. If you're looking for a workstation printer, I'd recommend the Epson WF-3520. It has some additional features including an ADF, good software that functions well (as does this Canon), and fax functionality. It's also much quieter.

This is a good product that works well despite a slow warm up time and a limited instruction manual.  I laminated a fairly thin one page scorecard from a 1977 baseball game and an award certificate from 1987 that was a bit thicker. Both came out great.The longest wait came while the laminator warmed up. The instructions say warm up time takes 5-6 minutes. This seems about right.The laminator comes with 10 letter size 3 Mil pouches. The pouches are open at one end. After placing the item you want laminated in the pouch you just feed the pouch closed side first  into the laminator. Once you feel the laminator taking the item you can let go as it is pulled through the laminator. When the two items I laminated were done they were not even hot (though the instructions warn you could get burned.)  It took each item no more than a minute to go through the laminator.I have never used a laminator before and found the instructions lacking. A few paragraphs talking about about how to use the laminator, the difference between hot and cold lamination and why a person should chose one over the other and what happens when you have something that is small that you want laminated would have made a big difference.I actually called Fellows and asked why someone would choose hot lamination over cold lamination and what to do with some card sized objects I wanted laminated.  Basically you use cold lamination for objects that would be affected by the heat and you need to buy special pouches for this. Also, different sized sheets are sold based on the size of the objects that need to be laminated.There are three pages in the instruction manual that tell you about the laminator.One page of the manual shows the laminator controls and has a quick start guide has no text. (The laminator controls are named on the next page and I found myself flipping back and forth to figure out what control the instructions were talking about.)  I think this was done because the manual is also written in French and Spanish and rather than reproduce this page each time it was decide to use one page with no writing.Pages four and five  have no diagrams but have text explaining how to use the laminator. The text does not always make sense.  For instance at one point the instructions talk about a "Wait" symbol that will flash when the laminator is warming up or cooling down. I have been over this manual ten times nowhere is a "Wait" symbol shown. I finally figured a green button that is called a "pouch selection button" in the laminator control section is in fact the "Wait" symbol.Ultimately this is a good product. I am happy with the two items I have laminated and will be looking forward to buying some smaller sheets to laminate some other items. The instructions are lacking but this is a pretty simple product to use once you figure it out. While you do have to wait a bit for the laminator to warm up, the items you are laminating go through the laminator quickly.

This review is from: Smead Expanding File, Custom Printed Stock, Open Top, Jan-Dec Index, 12x10 Inch (70488) (Office Product)Vine Customer Review of Free Product (What's this?)I gave this product 1 star for a specific reason:Don't tell me something is "leather-like", and then send me a product that is made 100% of paper products. The only thing "leather-like" about this product is that they printed a pattern on a piece of paper and then glued it to both sides of the folio. I won't reward a misleading product description in any way.Further, they made a design mistake on how they apply the "skin" they think makes it look "leather-like". There IS a reinforcing material at the bottom corners of the file. However, the "skin" was glued on last, over the top of the corner reinforcement. It won't be very long at all before the glued down paper starts to separate at the corner, either from humidity or general wear. When that happens it will spread, and eventually the file will look pretty bad.I also think that the file should have been made just a touch wider. It is OK if all you want to do is dump receipts and pieces of paper into it. However, should you want to further organize your dividers by putting file folders into it, that is an issue. While you can get a file folder to slide into it, it is not at all convenient to do so, and it has to squeeze into the wider part of the section, where the accordion side is at its widest. If you want to put a few file folders in it, you'll be out of luck. Even making this 1/8th inch wider would have eliminated that problem. If you've ever put receipts into a file like this, and then tried digging around blind in the bottom trying to find and grasp them, you'll appreciate how much easier it is to have them in a regular file folder that you can slide into one of these and then just pull it back out with the full contents.They make the claim that each pocket expands to 7/8ths inch. Maybe in their dreams. Yes, if you virtually pull the product apart to fully expand one pocket, sticking your hand all the way in to assist in flattening out the bottom, you could get it to extend to 7/8ths of an inch. It wouldn't stay there, nor could you conceivably expand EVERY pocket to that width.I've had a similar accordion file from Globe Weiss for years which has a higher quality glossy exterior, IS wide enough to easily slide a file folder into, and has a fold over top which closes with velcro ... to keep you from accidentally spilling the contents of your file should you accidentally knock the thing off your desk. I would purchase that accordion file product over and over again and never consider this one in a direct comparison, and both are essentially the same price.

This holiday season, the Zebra StylusPen would make an inexpensive present for a friend, relative or coworker who owns a smartphone or tablet with a touchscreen.Joseph B. Hoyos

Note: HP ePrint requires not only an Internet connection to the printer but also an Account Registration with HP Web Services.  (hp.com/go/mobile-printing-solutions)Good for a network of 5-10 users. This printer has a 500-sheet tray and printing volume of 500-2800 pages per month with an upper limit of upto 50,000 pages per month. I am hopeful to know that the printer supposedly prints just over 9,000 pages per black  XL cartridge and over 6,000 per XL color cartridge! I am fortunate and pleased to be offered this printer through Vine; my intended use is to give it rigorous testing alongside my sister and her kids who will use this through school assignments and the normal running of a teenage household with various mobile, desk, laptop and household demands. I'll report back as it goes through its paces and especially if it fails to measure up either in terms of cost or performance. Paper jams may get interesting and I will report back on this too.Print speeds in either black or color are listed by HP as:upto 55ppm in draftupto 36ppm in normal resolution.There are 4 needed replacement print cartidges:HP 970 Black Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge (~3000 pages);HP 971 Cyan Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge;HP 971 Magenta Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge;HP 971 Yellow Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge: composite yield (~2500 pages);HP 970XL Black Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge (advertised as 9200 page yield and $100 on Amazon Prime);HP 971XL Cyan Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge;HP 971XL Magenta Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge;HP 971XL Yellow Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge: composite yield (~6600 pages).If I calculate the per page cost of a black XL cartridge at $100 with Amazon Prime, and I assume the advertised 9,000 page yield for black, my pp cost is .011, just over 1 cent per page. That's a nice price cost point whether you are a business or a family just trying to get the kids papers printed. I bought and recommend a spare set of cartridges before the notoriously small "set up" cartridges run dry. Prime is cheaper than either buying print cartridges direct from HP or from a drugstore late one night and paying the full $120 + tax price tag for just Black!What's in the Box:HP Officejet Pro X451dn Printer;Setup Officejet Pro X Ink Cartridge Black, Magenta, Yellow, Cyanpower cord, phone cordInstallation guideSoftware CD-ROMs for: Windows and Mac printer drivers, and User's Guide.Setup posterNO CABLEOne-Year: Exchange Warranty and Technical Phone/Chat/email support.But I'll admit. If you are a fan of soft feel retractable pens, you will probably like these ones. They work fine.But have you tried their older cousin, the classic BiC Cristal Stics (and I mean *classic,* like 1959 classic)? They are cheap-looking, ultra-simple pens, so they may not have graced your hand if you (like me) thought that a pen needs to be "soft feel" or "rubber gripped" to be comfortable. But then you'd be (like I was) missing the genius of these pens.The classic BiC's were designed exceptionally, like bizarrely well. And I don't mean in a quaint, historical way. In a modern way -- no, in a *timeless* way -- the classic BiC's adhere magnificently to principles of space, form, structure, density, and gravity. Because of their hexagonal shape, they require minimal plastic while also retaining a surprising strength (try snapping one), and the hexagonal grip points give the pens impressive writing stability. A tiny hole drilled in the barrel's body keeps the air pressure the same both inside and outside the pen. Gravity feeds the thick ink down a tube to a free-spinning ball bearing that was manufactured within a fraction of a micron of accuracy. The result is that when the pen is pressed against paper, the ink slides out cleanly and, well,... perfectly. It's not only one of the most inexpensive pens (less than $1.50 for a pack of 10), it's also probably the most efficient pen, with a single pen able to write over 100,000 words (or about 2 novels). Hopefully this helps you understand why, when describing the classic BiC's, I am comfortable using the word "masterpiece."And hopefully this helps you understand why, in comparison, clunky and over-designed "soft feel" pens seem somewhat repulsive.Sorry if I come off as a pen snob.

I was very excited to find this product because I was already creating my own tags for baked good and care package items by finding free templates online and printing them to heavy paper and card stock. Avery does provide ample templates online, including some with graphics already included.  However, all the templates are in Microsoft Word, which I don't find to be very user friendly for this type of thing.  When you are just making standard address labels it is perfectly sufficient, but when you're making branded products like a tag it's not very easy to drag and drop graphics and do different treatments.  In addition, some of the files, when opened on my computer were all messed up - text and images were hanging off the label and all over the place.  Basically, you have to expect to spend sometime creating these if you want them to look professional and a beginning understanding of Microsoft word is needed.Edited to add: I finally found the online interface thanks to some helpful commenters.  I found it MUCH more user friendly than the word downloads, but I was pretty disapointed with the templates available.  Everything seemed a bit outdated and clipart friendly which seemed like a shame to me since I have found great free printables elsewhere on the net (they just don't work with this template).  I expected a bit more since these are billed as products for small business owners.I think they'd be much better off if they created their own software program or had an online interface for customizing labels, rather than trying to use a program that really wasn't meant for involved design.  At the very least, it would be nice if they offered files that could be opened in a program like Photoshop.I also think some of the graphics and styles available don't look as polished as what you can already find at craft stores or patterns available on blogs and sites like Martha Stewart.Overall, I think this product is a great idea, I think it is just a shame that the interface to create the labels isn't more user friendly. This little laminator is a useful and fun addition to my home office. It is easy to use and gives great results.It comes with several sample pouches, so I used some of them to try out the machine. This Saturn laminator is my first-ever personal use home laminator, and I couldn't be happier with the end product this little number creates!Fellowes has made this unit easy all around. It's easy to carry, with a built-in lip underneath the rear of the feed that acts as a little handle. It's easy to use - all you have to do is plug it in, push the power button, and give it just a few minutes to heat up, once you've selected the proper setting for the pouch you'll be using. And it's easy to create professional-looking products: once your item has fed through the machine (which it does beautifully and smoothly; just be sure to leave the rear of the machine clear so your hot laminated items don't bump up against anything and wrinkle or curl), you're left with a product that looks like you had it done at a big-name facility; Kinko's and OfficeMax can't do it any better with their in-store services!I'm especially a fan of the 5 mil pouches, as opposed to the 3 mil pouches. Being a teacher, I have access to a large laminator machine at my school - the kind with the large rolls of thin plastic laminating film. The 3 mil pouches feel as if they're about the weight of the cheapie-cheapie laminating film that's available at my school, and that 3 mil just doesn't seem to be quite as durable (obviously) as the 5 mil pouches are. Considering that a 100 pack of the 5 mil pouches here at Amazon are just pennies in price difference, versus the 100 pack of 3 mil pouches, for me, it's just a given that I'm going to be happier with the end result if my item is enclosed in one of those 5 mil pouches.Aside from the fact that you can use this Fellowes Saturn laminator for hot lamination, is the fact that you can also put it to use for cold lamination. I think that's a great feature to make an option, even if you don't tend to use that feature as often as you do the hot lamination. More options means it's better able to suit your needs. There are other laminators available here (and in your local stores), but I think Fellowes just gets it all right here, and at a price that's better than the bulk of the other offerings out there.Nifty little machine to have on-hand, great end results, great pricing! Definitely a worthwhile addition to your home office/home crafting space!
