Since one's satisfaction can vary based on a pen's intended purpose--jotting notes and memos, sketching, inking art projects, lettering invitations, addressing letters, scrapbooking, etc.--I'll focus on four angles: comfort, ink quality (and colour), longevity, and nib (and line) sizing.COMFORTThe form factor of these pens is incredibly similar to theMitsubishi Uni-ball Signoline of pens except the Signos are a bit shorter, thicker, and heavier (balanced weight). I prefer gripless pens or those with grips close to the base because they afford me greater line control while writing without discomfort. For me, this distance is substantial, but no more so than on the Signo or Pilot G2. The girth of these pens are roughly the size of your standard Bic Crystal stick pen or Sharpie pen, and the grip is more for show than actual comfort--it has no give so could easily become uncomfortable for the heavy-handed or hamfisted writer.The pen is feather light, which could be beneficial for those who write or draw for extended periods, but this pen requires some adjustment because there's no real balance to the weight distribution. (Pilot Hi-Tec-C and Pentel Slicci, which weigh roughly the same as these, have balanced weight distribution, so it's not impossible.) The first few times using it the line got away from me because I forgot I didn't have an anchoring weight, so to speak. That said, I was able to write for several hours without cramping or fatigue. While it's not the most comfortable pen I've ever used, it's definitely far from the least.INK QUALITY (AND COLOUR)One of the first things I do when I receive a new set of pens is take inventory--this case is no different. I didn't receive what's listed in the description at the time of this writing (i.e. 8 basic, 12 neon, 16 pastel, 30 glitter, and 34 metallic). What I received was: 9 basic, 16 pastel, 15 neon, 28 glitter, and 32 metallic.Also, the description might lead one to believe there are 100 different colours (or close to), but that's not the case. There are a variety of colours, yes, but it seems there's no real rhyme or reason and that the colours one receives might be luck of the draw. I say that because some of the colours were so close in hue that I had to wonder why a completely different colour family wasn't offered in place.To give an example, of the glitter pens, I received 4 shades of blue all of which were almost indistinguishable from one another.  I would have preferred a shade of red, an extra black or two, or even a few more earth tones. Luck-of-the-draw colouring probably isn't a major concern if all you want are just some pretty coloured pens, but more so if you are hoping for a specific set of colours (i.e. red glitter, pink metallic, etc.).Here's a breakdown of what I received; the number in parenthesis is the number of pens:BASIC (4 colours): Black (3), Blue (2), Green (2), Red (2);PASTEL (8 colours): Yellow (2), Pink Shade 1 (2), Pink Shade 2 (2), Blue (2), Green (2), Purple (2);NEON (5 colours): Yellow (3), Green (3), Orange (3), Purple (3), Pink (3);GLITTER (13 colours): Black (1), Brushed Nickel (2), Purple Shade 1 (2), Purple Shade 2 (2), Blue Shade 1 (2), Blue Shade 2 (2), Blue Shade 3 (2), Blue Shade 4 (2), Green (2), Yellow (2), Orange Shade 1 (2), Orange Shade 2 (3), Pink (2), Brown (2)METALLIC (14 colours): Gold Shade 1 (2), Gold Shade 2 (2), Gold Shade 3 (2), Red (2), Bronze Shade 1 (2), Bronze Shade 2 (2), Bronze Shade 3 (4), Silver Shade 1 (2), Silver Shade 2 (2), Purple Shade 1 (2), Purple Shade 2 (2), Purple Shade 3 (2), Teal (2), Green Shade 1 (2), Green Shade 2 (2)I've tested each of the colours on both light and dark papers and here are my results based on type:Before I get down to the nitty-gritty, I just want to add a note about yellow pens: all these yellow pens, excepting the glitter, are rather useless--too pale to be discernible on light paper and too translucent to show on dark paper. So if you're planning to write a bunch of cool notes in neon or pastel yellow you might need to revise the plan.BASIC: As one might expect, this is for use on light paper only;PASTEL: It's possible to see these colours on both light and dark paper, though you'll need to go over a line multiple times (~2-3), allowing the ink to dry between passes, on the dark paper in order for it to legibly stand out.NEON: Forget about using any of the neon colours on dark paper; they do, however, pop on light/white paper.GLITTER: On white paper the colours are vibrant (even yellow), but it does suffer from a glitter pooling problem which makes it seem as though there's a whitish mist plaguing the colours; the dark paper is where things become problematic--yes, it's visible, however the pigment is so translucent that most of the colour is lost and it just appears to be a sparkly silver with the slightest wisp of colour (if you care to look that closely).METALLIC: Like the glitter pens these show up nicely on light paper, but they also suffer from the same problems--even more so on the dark paper because there is little to no discerning of colour, just faint gold/silver shine.These pens primarily work best on light papers (if you want something that will play nicely with both light and dark paper, consider theSakura Gelly RollorPentel Sunburst, the latter having the closest line size to these).For the most part, these pens have good ink quality. In fact, I'm surprised (in a good way) at the richness of the basic black pen--it does lighten a tad when dry, but it's still quite bold. The line goes down evenly, though it may take writing a few words to get the ink flowing consistently. Sometimes, however, the nib becomes scratchy as if hitching on the paper (regardless of paper quality).The ink--especially the basic, glitter, and metallic colours--has a tendency to bleed (yes, actual bleed through to the next sheet) and writing is definitely visible on the backside of standard notebook/office paper. Also, the ink requires several seconds to properly dry (glitter and metallic longer) which could be a non-starter for lefties hoping to use these for general writing. Once dry, however, the ink is water resistant (not waterproof), so there will be feathering but the line will remain clear and legible, and the ink is alcohol resistant so I'd feel confident using these on checks, legal, or other important documents.INK LONGEVITYAlthough in general gel pens will burn through ink rapidly (with the exception of a few notables such as Pilot, Uni-ball, and Pentel), the short lifespan of these pens had me doing a double-take.Writing top to bottom, side to side on 8.5"x11" college rule paper, one will only get about 6-8 pages (3-4 sheets) on a single barrel of ink. That's not much if you write or draw or colour a lot, but it might be plenty for the casual doodler. In fact, I could easily see using up an entire pen taking notes in a single university class session. But on the bright side, it doesn't start to sputter or skip the closer to empty it becomes (though it will give out with about 1/8" of ink left in the barrel, or just enough to make you think it's not actually empty).NIB (AND LINE) SIZINGThese pens have varying nib sizes from 0.7mm (basic) to 1.0mm (glitter)--the remaining are 0.8mm--and for the most part the line sizes are what one might expect (i.e. a medium line erring on the side of bold/thick, but people with tiny handwriting or who want to create fine detail would find the line entirely too thick). The nibs themselves are metal and sturdy--at least strong enough to withstand a heavy-handed writer.Of final note is the container in which the pens come--it took a minute to realize that the lid is what's used to create the tiered effect. It's functional, the rows do turn (though slightly inconvenient), and I like that they can be carried around easily by handle when the lid is secured.For what these are (economy gel pens), they're good pens. Will they replace some of the better gel pens available (i.e. Sakura Gelly Roll, Pentel Sunburst, Uni-ball Signo, etc.)? No. If you're picky about your writing instruments and have been spoiled by some of the other brands, you'll definitely note the differences. Are these pens an absolute waste or horrible investment? No. The smoothness and line quality, not to mention ink consistency, make these pens part of the upper echelon of bulk economy gel pens. Not a single dud in my pack. That said, these pens can only do so much. I'd recommend them to a hobbyist or for doodling/note-taking, but not so much for substantial art projects (i.e. large-scale art journaling, scrapbooking, paper crafts, etc.) where a certain quality level is expected.

Print quality is good but this printer is sloooooow.  MyEpson Artisan 800 Wireless Photo All-in-One Printer (Black)(C11CA29201)is easily 10x as fast on photo prints. Our Canon all-in-one printer died so I was looking for a replacement when the Epson WP-4530 was offered.  We don't have a land line and typically don't fax, however we use the remaining features.  I was most curious about the scanning abilities and if I could achieve photo editing quality.Set-up takes a little time between unpacking, removing blue tape and small protective inserts used to protect the crated printer, and preparing for use.  Once completely unpacked, the Epson WP-4530 is plugged in, some basic settings are keyed in, and the four provided ink cartridges are installed.  The Epson WP-4530 begins an ink priming process which can last for up to 12 minutes.  Then the process is finished by loading paper into the cassette, connecting the phone cord, and installing software onto a computer.  The process is pretty simple, but expect 30-45 minutes before the printer is ready.For more functionality, the printer can be registered and an account created at the epsonconnect.com/user website.  Epson connect allows printing by email, restricts email print users, sends email alerts, shows print logs, changes basic settings, and suspends the email print service.  Not only does the email body print, but most common attachments can be printed as well along with a coversheet.Printing from the Epson WP-4530 is amazingly simple.  If desired, the printer can remain wired after setup.  However for us, the network cable gets in the way and is unsightly.  The optimal location we chose for the printer makes going 100% wireless the best option.  We have no problems printing from our computers, tablet, or smart phones while connected to the network.The Epson WP-4530 can copy with auto duplexing for two sided documents while giving the option of a one or two sided print.  This process works well, and is relatively quick.  Print quality is good, but not perfect. I copied a printed color document with standard settings.  The black text came out well, but the logo colors were noticeably light.  I tried again after changing the print quality to best and the copy was an improvement, but the logo colors were still lighter.  My third attempt I bumped up the density a couple steps.  The colors came out great, but the black letters were noticeably heavier.  Even though I didn't get a good match, all versions were sharp and readable.The main paper tray holds 330 paper sheets and the rear adjustable manual feed can either hold more or be used for 4x6 or larger photo paper.  The copying/printing process is a bit noisy, but typical for an all-in-one.Next to printing, creating high quality photographic scans is important to me.  In the past, I've needed a separate scanner from the printer due to all-in-one scanner limitations.  The Epson WP-4530 features a basic scanner by default, where scans are completed with the press of a button and no settings to alter.  This method works well for scanning documents.  However, scanning a damaged photo to restore in Adobe Photoshop requires more control and greatly improved settings.Epson's product page on their website has a scanner tool download, which provides greater control.  The scanner tool includes settings for home, office, and professional users, each providing the same basic options.  However, each user setting presents the most common options for that particular user with home being the most simplistic.  Using the professional user I can produce an enlarged photo scan with extremely high dpi in a lossless photo file type.We cannot connect the fax to a telephone line for testing as we only use mobile phones.  When I have to send a fax, I scan the document and use a website like myfax or faxzero.  Epson provides a Fax utility which is available for download from the Epson WP-4530's web page which can be used to send faxes from a computer through the printer.  It would be a nice built in feature to fax over the web, but as far as I can tell this isn't currently an option.  Fortunately we don't fax often.As an all-in-one printer, the Epson WorkForce Pro WP-4530 does a great job, and is a definite improvement over the Canon it replaced.  With the 50% lower printing costs, Wi-Fi networking, duplexing, and high quality scans, we'll get plenty of use from this inkjet printer.  If exact copies are not a requirement, this all-in-one is a worthy purchase.PROS:Wireless printing and scanning330 sheet paper capacityPrint wirelessly and by emailAdvanced scanning software availableCONS:Copies print acceptably but not exact

The labels themselves are very attractive and have nice texture.  I like the shape since it is different than the shapes you normally see in DIY labels. I find it hard to believe that Avery would not include a template for any Adobe software, minus a star for not having better templates.

First, about the labels themselves: they work very well with ink jet printers, as designed, and fed through reliably with my Canon inkjet. The ink never smudged, and the labels came out perfectly clear. They are easy to peal off, and yet never peeled off when they weren't supposed to, even when I sent sheets through the printer with many of the labels already taken out. So, these are great labels, and I can't come up with a single complaint.Second, about the software: I have a Mac, so I didn't try the desktop software. However, on their website they have literally thousands of templates that will work with Microsoft office, and even Apple Pages. Much of it is a bit cheezy, but they have some very plain templates, and you can always edit out the pictures. This makes the labels extremely easy to use, as the templates avoid trial-and-error on placement and margins.All in all, a very nice label solution. One word of caution, however, and this is no fault of Avery and will happen with ANY inkjet product: the ink in inkjets is water soluble. That means if you use these for mail, you really should put transparent packing tape over the label. Probably not worth bothering to do this if you're making return labels, but mail does occasional get wet (neither rain nor sleet nor snow...) and a single drop of water can bleed an address printed on an inkjet.

Everything the manufacturer says is true, as the reviews here on Amazon already attest:  the Post-It Pockets are strong, and adhere well to clean surfaces, leaving no lasting residue when you remove them.I think the accordion pleat or welts suggested by other reviewers, while increasing the capacity of the pockets, might tend to make them droopy and cause stretching out, or even cause the adhesive to fail, if a welted pocket is packed too heavily.  For some things, an "in" box is probably still the best bet.These also could be a neat application for long term storage boxes, when useful to have a spot for documentation on the outside of the box.  As one example, I have the larger Post-It pocket on a box of knitting yarn, and I can keep the patterns for my next projects, paper yarn ball bands, receipts, etc. in the pocket.  Similarly, I could see using one of the smaller pockets on a large square food container I'm always filling with pancake mix, so as not to mix it up with the flour, etc., and also to hold a few recipes for using that mix. When re-purposing a container, it would be very easy to change out a cut out product box panel (easy visual ID!) as opposed to having to create a new label every time.But I just can't see investing in a bunch of pockets for an entire pantry, considering the cost.One possible alternative: while less sturdy, higher-grade page protectors - you know, those clear 3 hole punched top-loading pockets for binders? - could easily be set up with 3M poster strips or something similar affixed to them, to create a handy, if somewhat more disposable pocket for surfaces or storage boxes. (Keep in mind, though, that page protectors don't have the rigidity of the Post-It Pockets -- but then you may not require that kind of strength or relative permanence for your purposes.) A few minutes extra work, yes, but those page protectors are pennies per sheet, and even factoring in the cost of strong non-mar adhesive, it would be many times cheaper than the excellent, but fairly pricey Post-It Pockets.

I wanted to like this, but I just do not think that the Web feature really justifies doubling the price of the prior Photosmart Premium Fax All-in-One Printer, Scanner, Copier and Fax. (Model C309a)HP Photosmart Premium Fax All-in-One Inkjet Printer (CC335A#ABA).  Since the C309a is the model I am replacing this review is really a comparison of this new model over the old one.  The old one is still readily available for about half the price of this - which is a really big difference.  Also, the C309a - at half the price - has one feature missing here - an automatic document feeder.  Why is that important?  It is important if you want to be able to easily scan multi-page PDF documents.  I can put a stack of papers on the C309a and they automatically run through the feeder (never once had a jam) and a multi-page PDF appears on my desktop.  This new model is missing that.  The lack of the document feeder also renders the fax absolutely useless.  To send a fax you have to stand there and "scan" each page of the fax on the glass.  It is hardly honest to call this a fax machine.The specs between the two printers are exactly the same, except the C309a has the automatic document feeder and this one has the web interface.  Also, the old model holds 125 pages of regular paper, but this one is down to 100 - a move totally in the wrong direction.  Why can't they just design a printer tray (for a non-commercial printer) that holds a ream of paper (500 pages)?  Also, this one is missing the special holder for printing CDs, but I never used that anyway.The new model is smaller (good) and black (instead of a creamy white).  The new model also has better drivers - which were (and still are) a MAJOR drawback of the old model.  You can finally install a basic set of drivers that don't cripple functions, and don't add a bunch of junk software.  This is a MAJOR improvement.Print quality on both is absolutely amazing.  Prints look just like they came from the photomat.  Yes. They are that good. (although, unless you use the little flimsy retainer arm, they will drop on the floor once complete.)I have mine hooked up through wi-fi and that works great.  It is easily seen on all computers on my network that run Win7 and XP.One negative (on this and the old version) is that you still need a computer to be on to do scanning - even to a network drive.  The scanning software runs on a computer, not locally on the printer.  Copying, faxing and printing can be done without a computer.OK.  What about the web interface?  Well, my personal take is that it is a huge gimmic intended to get you to print more and use more ink.  Things take forever to find on the touch interface and it would really be about a thousand times faster just to use a computer.  Of course, if you - for whatever reason - only have your computer in a far-off room, this might proove handy if the printer is in a more high-traffic area of the house.  But is that really a problem?  And would you really put your printer far away from your computer?  Not likely.  I found the touchscreen slow to respond and - although beautiful to look at - I just didn't get the need for the web interface.  The only conclusion I can make is that HP wants you to print more stuff and use more ink.The ink, by the way, goes VERY quickly.  I printed a dozen or so 4x6 photos and a couple of 8x10 and the ink light warning started to go off.  Of course, I really think the light goes off WAY too early.  It does that on almost every printer I have ever used.  I continue printing until I notice a problem with the output.  I am guessing that the low ink warning is set to go off when you have used 40% of the ink.  I was able to print another dozen photos (after the ink warning) before I noticed any ink deficiency.  I could probably print another dozen before it wouldn't let me print anymore.Overall, I really like the printer quality and the interface, but I can't get past the elephant in the room - the old model is half the price and has an automatic document feeder that this is missing.The printer comes with a standard set of ink cartridges (not just starter inks), every cable you could need (including a massive power brick), and sample photo papers.  It is all packaged in an eco-friendly cloth bag.Overall, I can only give this three stars.  If the old model never existed, I would probably give this four or five stars.  The fact that they left off the automatic document feeder is a HUGE drawback for me.  The "Touchsmart Web" is fun to play with, but really amounts to nothing more than a flashy gimmic.  It fixes a problem that doesn't really exist - everything you would do through that interface is easier and faster on a real computer.  Of course, I am also a person who would never just plug a memory stick into a printer and start printing - if you are, this might be a good printer for you.

I wasn't quite sure of what to expect with this type of cutter, having always used the hinged type blade. So plan on being like most techs, and start playing before reading any manual...I don't do scrapbooking, I just wanted this for some things I do with my son for school, and photos and such I printed myself.  And that's where this is both good and not so good.  For papers and such, it held them fine, and the cutting actually went smoother than I had anticipated.  The blade's handle moved freely and easily went through what I was doing.  But when it came to photos, I didn't want to use the tensioner that holds things down, because I didn't want to mar the surface of the photo, so it got really tricky trying to cut without that, since I obviously couldn't just put my hands or fingers on the picture either to hold it.  I finally tried some cellophane type stuff I had, but I still got some marring on photos that were less than 24 hours old.  For photos that were older than that, however, it worked without causing any problems with the photo.  I wish there were some way to just have it grip the edges of what I'm trying to cut.I was half afraid that it would have a tendency to tug things along with it, maybe rip some thinner paper as it cut, but I never had any problems with the cut.  Even on the old hinged blade style cutters, I've had things get pushed some if you did too many papers at once, even less than "recommended".  This one seems to do better so far that way.All in all it does what it should do fairly well, and for most people, will probably fit the bill nicely.

There is a lot to like about Epson's Workforce 3520.  It is reasonably priced and includes pretty much any feature one might want in a multi-function printer.What's In The Box?* WorkForce WF-3520 All-in-One Printer* Four ink cartridges: Black, Cyan, Magenta, Yellow* Power cord* Telephone cord* Instruction manual* Set up CD.* Sample pack of paperSet up of the printer is simple.  Simply connect it to your PC and/or wireless network.  No USB cable is included, so you need one of those if you want to hard wire the printer to a PC or router.  I just used the built-in wireless to add this printer to my home network.  This should take just a few minutes for someone experienced with the technology, or about 20 minutes or so for a novice.The printer is average size for an all-in-one, about 22" wide, 16.5" deep (paper tray closed) and about 9.5" high.  It weighs just under 20 pounds without paper in it.I have not had any issues printing from a PC (Windows 7 32 bit and Windows 7 64 bit, XP, and Mac Mountain Lion.The nicest things about the Workforce 3520:* High capacity paper tray (250 pages).* Print quality: while clearly ink not toner, the results are very crisp and look close to toner for images.  Text print looks just like toner.* Connectivity: Easy to connect to the printer and print from any device (I have used my laptop, iPad, and iPhone.  I have printed using Epson's EpsonConnect as well as Apple AirPrint, and Google's Cloudprint.* Automatic duplex printing.  This model actually handles TRUE duplex printing, copying, and fax.  It has a feeder that will process a page and then turn it over to print/scan/fax the other side as well.  It handles up to 30 pages (I have tested as many as 8).  Many printers claim to handle duplex print, but really amount to having you print on one side then turn the paper around yourself.What I don't like about the printer: Nothing major.  I don't find the secondary paper tray useful, as it is in the rear and I keep the printer on a desk which has a shelf/wall, so I cannot get to the back without moving the printer.  So it is easier for me to remove the paper from the main tray and replace it with whatever "special" paper stock I need rather than pull out the printer.Performance-wise. The printer handles about 15 pages per minute (black) and 9 pages per minute in color.  Obviously these speeds decline when you are printing very dense pages of print.  Duplex print is about 7 and 5 pages per minute, in black and color, respectively.  Colors on photos and photo paper are excellent ad accurate.  Always keep in mind numerous things can cause color variation (your monitor settings, software color calibration, etc.).The warranty on the Workforce is one year, and Epson provides free phone support for the life of the product.There's nothing to dislike about this product.  If you need your fist all-in-one printer/copier/scanner/fax, or its time to upgrade your old one, I would highly recommend the 3520.

Post-it Pockets give you a better way to post papers, letters and other items on walls, refrigerators, or wherever you need a semi-permanent location for placing non-permanent items.  These sturdy folders will hold a multitude of items neatly, and are a clear winner over the refrigerator magnet, clip or cork board solution for holding a small stack of items in a concise space.The pockets are very sturdy and the openings are designed to allow you to add and remove things easily. I was initially concerned that small pieces of paper such as ticket stubs would be awkward to remove from the receipt sized pouch, but the weight, shape and build of the materials used proved to be a pleasant surprise.The pouches themselves attach to cabinets, walls, doors and similar locations with two strips of a padded double sized tape that is designed to be removed cleanly. I found that the pouches stick securely, just as the product claims. I haven't tried to remove it from enough places to assure that it won't damage surfaces, but I haven't had any such problems.  One of the hallmark features of the Post-it line is the ability to easily remove and reposition.  Although this product uses the Post-it name, it does NOT share that feature. These pouches are designed to be left in a more or less permanent location for use with ongoing content, and can be removed cleanly when no longer needed. They are not designed to be removed and then stuck to a different location.  Although the product works well for intended tasks, I suspect some consumers might be misled by the Post-it name.  But it is the expected endurance and long term use of this product that justifies the purchase.

I write and draw for a large portion of my day and I'm a pencil person. As a designer, I don't use pens much. This pencil meets (and exceeds) all of my requirements. It's not too fat (why is there a trend these days to make writing instruments so clunky and thick?), it's just right. There are small silicone bumps around the knurled metal grip making it very comfortable. There is an adjustable window where you can set what softness of lead you are using. The erasers are the standard, easy to find Pentel ones. I prefer 0.7mm leads so for me, Pentel has hit one out of the park on this pencil. If you like writing/drawing with a pencil, this is a perfect choice.

I think this is a great product.  I use these pencils at work because it seems like I cannot find either a pencil or extra leads at the office when I need them.These pencil are comfortable to hold because of the silicone jacket at the bottom of the pencil.  They come in attractive bright colors which make it easy to spot them on the desk. Each pencil has two erasers; once one of the erasers is finished, you simply pop the eraser holder out and turn it upside down to expose a new eraser.  Unlike another reviewer, I had no problem erasing normal writing.  The eraser stayed in its holder, and I did not need to apply so much force that a lead would advance.These are very good pencils.

Well, I just purchased this online and technically have not used any of these yet but had some comments I wanted to share right away.1 CARTRIDGE = ~60-65 PAGES OF 8.5 x 11 SHEETS FILLED:The first ink cartridge that I received with the pen originally filled 64 pages of 8.5 X 11 inch sheets, so that seemed reasonable.  The second cartridge I am using seems well on the way (>54 sheets and still going) of doing the same (hence my recent purchase).  Ideally these will do the same. However if you are going into a meeting expecting the pen to run out, bring the base (or something that can extract the cartridge) so you can change ink on the fly.RED CARTRIDGE MAY NEVER BE USED:I did not like the idea of having to buy a red cartridge, but this is the only way to get refills here. On the pen site you can get just get blue or black cartridge sets, but you also have to pay for shipping.  That's equivalent to the cost of the cartridge.  When I order here, I always get the order cost up (easy to do when you have a Wish list in the thousands), so shipping is free, hence my opting to buy a package that includes a cartridge with red ink.  It kind of irks me that I have to buy something I don't need, to be most cost effective.  Rarely do people use red ink, and since you have to use the same pen, it is really not very sensible to expect people to use this color cartridge. Please correct me if I am wrong here.  Maybe the pen should be fitted with a two cartridges for people that want that option. I don't.

At nearly a dime a label, these Avery labels may be a bit pricey, especially if that amounts to the profits from an eBay or Amazon transaction stemming from the sale of a book or CD.  But for those "special" occasions--sending a CD to a family member, personal friend or musician--it's easy to justify the small added expense.The advantages of the Avery 45280 labels:1.  The "From" portion is no more than 1/3 of the label; the all-important "To" portion is 2/3 of the space, allowing enough room even for some of those wordy international addresses.2.  The label peels off from the backing with the least amount of fuss--simply push backwards on the top edge (the part with the Avery logo and the number 45280), and the sticky label pops right up, ripe for the taking.3.  The label itself is thick yet pliable and "ink-friendly."  You won't have to experiment with several ball-points or roller-balls before finding one that works.  The surface is made to absorb ink readily from any source.4.  The pad supplies a sufficiently firm backing to allow for controlled writing (unlike those "backless" labels that force you to write on the uneven surface of the package itself).5.  The remaining big question: Can the description of the label as "permanent" be taken seriously?  I doubt that Avery would apply the hyperbolic epithet irresponsibly.  Old habits die hard, and I most likely will continue to use transparent wrapping tape to cover labels stuck to packages containing valuable items.  But I have enough confidence in this label, based on its feel and texture as well as Avery's claim, to apply it to the majority of envelopes and packages without the use of transparent tape for that "extra" assurance.I can find only one minor disadvantage: it's not an "all-purpose" label.  It'll do for padded envelopes containing CDs as well as books and photos.  But for larger items (a folio-sized book, for example, or a big box) you'll probably want a larger label to assure it's not missed by an overly hasty, tired postal worker.  I doubt that I'll use more than several pads a year, but it's definitely a product that has found a permanent place in my desk drawer.

This is a great AIO printer for photographic printing.SIZE:Wow...this AIO printer is huge and it weights more than 20 lbs. The duplexer hanging off the back adds about 4 inches to the depth. I have to move things around in my room to accommodate it.SETUP:The touch screen is easy to use and it's pretty responsive.The wireless setup was the best I've seen. Turn it on, it detects the network. Enter your SSID right on the panel, and your done. Big thumb up on this.PRINTING:The printer is fast without compromising the printing quality. Photos were astounding! It uses 6 ink cartridges which probably accounts for the vivid colors. You would be hard-pressed to tell the difference between an Epson print and a print from a photo developer.Better yet, I did borderless 8.5 x 11 and there was no smearing at the edges, amazing!.Additional added value is the disc printing. Just printing my own discs ten sessions have paid for this printer :-)INK:While some people do not like the multiple ink cartridges, I like that way as some colors always get used more frequently than others.I'm hoping the dye based inks are less likely to clog the printer head due to their smaller particle size. Time will tell if my concern is legitimate.SCANNER:An important feature to me is being able to scan documents. I usually archive paper documents into digital form. The scanning operation is very easy with Epson's software and it has a number of settings. I can either do a quick scan with some default settings or tweak the software settings for a very specific type of scan quality.I am happy for the faster speed for high resolution scanning.DUPLEX:It's a two step process: Print top page first, then print the bottom page. So, be patient with the duplex printing.COPIER:The AIO has a very impressive copying capability, it copies undetectably like the original. Be honest, I couldn't distinguish between a print and a copy of the print. One word...amazing.MISC:It has a separate tray for photo paper (4x6), so I can keep the printer loaded with both plain paper and photo paper. Quite a convenient thought.FYI: this AIO printer does not have fax capability.And just like all other inkjet printers, it Will not print if any one of the ink cartridges is empty.ISSUE:1. The paper tray is made of light-weight plastic and it feels flimsy. So, be easy with it when loading papers.2. There is no paper feeder for scanning/copying. I have to scan/copy each paper individually. For people tend to have big scanning jobs, this is a big issue.3. It's kind of loud when it feeds paper and prepares to print. The actual printing operation itself is much quieter though.SUMMARY:All in all, this is a great choice to be used mainly for photographic printing and occasional text printing. People will be disappointed with the diffused text printout on regular paper (not photo paper) from this printer. That's a typical symptom for dye-based inkjet printers.For general purpose and occasional photo printing, you want to look for particle-based ink system like Epson's most 4 ink particle-based printers. Particle-based inkjet printers produce laser sharp text on regular paper and GOOD (not excellent as artisan) quality photos on photo papers.

Nowadays, almost all the all-in-one printers have very similar functions: printing, scanning, copying, faxing (not a main feature anymore, so some have this function and some don't), wireless connection, two-side printing, LCD control panel. Also, all-in-one printers at this price range can print out good photos, but never be able to match the quality from those high-end models.So, what factors to be used for finding a relatively good one from this over-crowded market? Every person has different needs. Personally, I use following criteria:First is reliability. Some printers last longer before printer heads get clogged. Only time can tell if this Epson XP-600 has a longer printer head life. One of my last printers last only for 3 months, while my last Canon printer last for 4+ years while being used on daily basis.Second is the cost of ink cartridge. The Epson XP-600 comes with 5 separate ink cartridges, with the black cartridge in double size. This is better than some models with all colors packaged into a single cartridge.Third is the printing speed. Some printers are so slow in printing. Some even take 1 minute just to warm up from stand-by before starting printing! The printing speed of XP-600 is on the average for printers in this price level.Forth is two-side printing. Don't be surprised that some all-in-one printers are still one side printing only. This XP-600 is duplex-printing capable.All in all, I don't see any special feature that really makes this XP-600 printer/scanner stand out from the crowd. However, in the same token, I don't see any deficiency in this printer also. Just for that, I would say this is a good little printer for home use.

We'd been using a little shredder we got nearly free at a Black Friday event some years ago.  It was a maximum 6-sheet one with no credit card or CD/DVD shredding capabilities.  Always meant to upgrade, so when I got the chance I jumped at it.  Not disappointed at all.The first thing you need to know is it's big and hefty.  It stands probably around 3' tall and while a big chunk of the size is the bin, this is not exactly light weight shredding.  It seems best suited for a small office or possibly a home office than just a personal one to shred things and protect yourself from identity theft.  Still, I don't personally have any problem with the size.  The foot print on the floor isn't that much bigger than our old one; it's just a lot taller.  Just be aware the box it comes in is BIG so depending on where the delivery guy needs to leave the package that might be a problem  Unwrapping it was "frustration free" as Amazon could make it, with just a cut with the scissors and then pulling it out of the box by the convenient handles on each side; again, slightly heavy so some may possibly need help or someone else to do it, but most adults should mange just fine.This thing can shred.  It's not just some cheap strip on, this one cross cuts, and it does it fast, and with a couple dozen sheets at a time.  We were feeding unopened credit card offers into the thing and it didn't miss a beat, though long term we probably won't since that is kind of thicker so it'll be a little harder on it.  The credit card and DVD/CD work great and give a little bit of extra security.  One tip an old boss gave me, when you dump the bin mix it up and only dump 1/2 at time; that way it's nearly impossible for someone to put everything together.  Also, they suggest you use shredder lubricant once a month, but say cooking oil will work as well.  Just get a bottle with a narrow spout to only put a little in there.  Canned stuff like WD-40 are supposed to be avoided as a fire risk, though I'd guess that's probably more the lawyers being overly cautious than a real risk.Speaking of lawyers, the shredder has icons on it not to put in the usual stuff, staples, aerosol spray, metal (tools), but they also feel the need to include neck ties and girls pigtails (1st time I've seen that one) and what appears to be imploring you not to feed a child through it; I'm going to assume the last one means don't let children operate it.  Had a teacher sometime back who decades before had stuck his hand in a lawnmower, to the expected result, and he'd just said it was his fault, despite the mower not having a label to tell him not to.  Times have changed I guess.Operation is perfectly and was simple to learn.  If you can figure out pressing a big on button and then feeding paper into the hole marked for paper, you've got 90% of the operation down.  The only real warnings you have to watch out for are overheating, but you'd have to do quite a bit to heat it up, and the bin being out.  Even taking out the bin is as simple as basically just pulling it out.  There aren't any tricks, special hooks, etc. that might complicate things.  It's entirely straight forward and aside from maintenance/troubleshooting you really don't need the small manual that comes with it.  The wheels are there if you need to push it around, but lifting it isn't a big deal so I usually do that.This is the third Amazon branded item of various types I've tried out and I can say without any reservations that each and every one of them were as good or better quality than some of the more "name brand" items and generally cheaper.  This shredder is no exception.  Trust me, if it dies tomorrow I'll come back and adjust my review to say how awful it is, but I really doubt I'll ever need to be doing that.  I am extremely pleased with both the look and operation.  Very cool.

Bottom line:  Good hardware, terrible software. The result is a scanner that's okay for Windows users, roughly on par with the Fujitsu iX500, depending on intended use. For Mac users, it's a disaster, and should be avoided until and unless Epson addresses the software issues.The details:I tested this scanner in three different environments: Windows XP, Windows 7, and Mac OS X 10.9.1 ("Mavericks"). First, the good news: On Windows, the scanner functioned pretty much as advertised. Although installing the software for the first time was a slow process (taking over 20 minutes -- why??), once the install completed, there were no errors or other issues to speak of. The one-touch scan button worked as you would expect right from the start. Scanning directly to Google Drive worked without a fuss, as did creating a searchable PDF. Scanning speed was good, and quality was also good. There was only a small delay for additional processing when creating a searchable PDF.The biggest drawback is the software. For both Windows and Mac, there are actually three separate programs to control the scanner: Epson Scan Settings, Epson Scan, and Document Capture Pro. The Epson Scan Settings app isn't really an application -- it has very limited functions, and can be mostly ignored by the user. The other two applications, however, are full-fledged scanning programs, each with its own settings and functions, many of which overlap. Knowing which app to use and where to configure settings can be a challenge.That's unfortunate, because the default settings are probably not the best for most users. For example, the option to "skip blank pages" is turned off by default. That means you'll get a blank page in your PDF file for the back of any single-sided sheet you scan, until you find and change this setting.But if the software is bad on Windows (and it is), it's even worse on the Mac. On Windows, the applications look and feel like they were written 8 years ago. On the Mac, the software literally looks like something from 1998. And I do mean literally: the style and appearance matches the Mac OS from 1998, complete with rudimentary black-and-white wristwatch icon to indicate when the program is busy. Worse, it's prone to crashing often, and some features aren't offered or don't work with OS X 10.9.From the very beginning, the experience of setting up the scanner on Mac OS X was plagued with crashes and errors. After installing the software, the Epson Software Update application automatically opened to check for updates. Software Update reported that there were no updates to the Epson software available, so I quit the updater and tried to open Epson Scan Settings to set my preferences. The result was an error message: "Cannot find necessary files. Please re-install the software." Next, I tried to open the Epson Scan application. The application simply crashed ("EPSON Scan quit unexpectedly"). Reopening resulted in the same error.Resolving these issues required several rounds of updates using the Epson Software Updater. Each time I ran Epson Software Update, a new update was found that hadn't been listed previously. Even after repeated updates, reinstalls, and troubleshooting, some key functions simply failed to work, or weren't available. The one-touch scanning button, for example, never worked with the Document Capture software. It worksedwith the Epson Scan app, but not Document Capture. The ability to create a searchable PDF simply isn't offered in the Mac version of Epson's software, either.In summary, this scanner is serviceable in a Windows environment, and works largely as advertised by the manufacturer. It's roughly equivalent to the similar model from Fujitsu, with the added advantage of TWAIN drivers for those who need such a thing. It's also slightly less expensive at current prices.In a Mac OS X environment, however, this scanner is a dog. A better alternative for Mac users would be the Fujitsu ScanSnap, which offers a much better software user experience, a smoother installation, and the ability to create text-searchable PDFs when scanning.For both Windows and Mac users, the Epson doesn't offer much reason to purchase it over other, similar scanners. If you don't need the TWAIN driver that the Epson offers, or don't plan to purchase the additional network interface Epson offers as an optional add-on, you won't be missing anything by picking up a Fujitsu ScanSnap instead.
