I have to admit that this printer scared me right out of the box.  It had been such a long time since I had purchased a new printer that my old one still hooked up to the computer through one of those big printer cables that have gone the way of wired mouses.  I had a feeling that the directions on this contraption would probably speak heavily of cables and software using terms that I had yet to learn.  I was so intimidated by the thought of it that I enlisted the help of a neighbor that well understands this stuff much better then myself.  As it turns out, I really feel that with a couple of exceptions where I was a little nervous, I could have easily gotten this thing up and running on my own.  Hard wiring this printer is a snap.  With the exception of the directions insisting on calling the USB cable the power cable or something or other, it really is as simple as following the directions provided.  And that holds true even with the fact that my printer is wired into a very old desktop computer simply acting as a host for the series of laptops we have in the house.  After we set up the wireless connection, (that I swear went as easily as described in the directions) it was just a matter of setting up the laptops to find and recognize the juice now flowing through the house.  In just under and hour I was enjoying wireless printing from my laptop in one room, and hearing it quietly process in another.  Simply wonderful.  Make no mistake about it, this baby has not become a victim of all the downsizing that is going on in the electronics business these days.  It has the look and feel of being a throw back to an era when electronics had enough heft to them that you actually felt you were getting your moneys worth.  Some other reviewers have stated some irritation or surprise at this units size.  But in all honestly, unless you are talking about a situation where space is a premium, it shouldn't be a concern in my opinion.  Actually, I think it looks right handsome all lit up and ready for action.  It's truly a fine all in one machine that has the look and feel of true quality to it. It's actually been some time since I have been so satisfied with something as new and intimidating as this.In conclusion, I must confess that as of the time of this writing, I have not as of yet tried out the FAX part of this model.  I have printed with it and used the scanner, but have no need yet of the FAX.  I had never used a scanner before.  But once again following the directions with a little patience had me becoming comfortable with it in less than 30 minutes.  If my satisfaction with this machine changes any in regards to the fax, I will certainly be back to report it.  There is no question that one can get a printer for a lot less money than buying this piece.  Even an all in one model can be had for cheaper than this Canon model.  However I feel that the quality look and feel of this baby, along with the flawless performance it is producing, well justifies the  higher price.  If I had run into any problems with the set up and operation of this model, I would pass them on in ragards to any and all advice and experience.  But truthfully I did not.  I am very happy with this all in one printer, and I highly recommend buying it right here on Amazon...

The plastic seemed a little thin, the pop up display is super low quality, and I was prepared to be disappointed. I wasn't. I use paper cutters for a variety of tasks.  My previous paper cutter was a 12-inch plastic cutter that had some issues.  It did not cut more than a couple of sheets very well and I had to do some workarounds for larger pieces of paper.  A more substantial 24-inch paper cutter seemed like it would be an improvement.The first thing I noticed about this paper cutter is the size.  A 24-inch paper cutter is a large beast.  Fortunately, I have a large area available just for the cutter.  While the paper cutter platform is 24 inches by 24 inches, the paper cutter is larger than that because the handle extends away from the platform to the front and the hinge for the cutter extends out the back.  The total distance from the back of the hinge to the front of the handle is about 32 inches, give or take.The second thing I noticed is the weight.  Because the platform is wood and the handle is metal, the paper cutter is relatively heavy.  The benefit to the weight is that the paper cutter sits solidly on a table or desktop.  The disadvantage is that the paper cutter can be a bit unwieldy when moving it around.  You probably do not want to move the cutter very often.Beyond the heft and weight, how does this thing cut?  It cuts extremely well.  It slices through multiple sheets of 20# paper, manila folders, envelopes, construction paper, and just about anything else that will fit under the blade.  The blade is quite sharp.  Indeed, this equipment is something to keep away from children, as it would be easy to lose a finger, or even a whole hand of fingers.While I first noticed the size and the weight of this paper cutter, the other thing that struck me is its beauty.  The wood platform is gorgeous.  I would keep this device away from people who do not take care of equipment well, because I can see that it would be easy to damage the beautiful surface of the wood if the cutter were abused.The only negative comment I have about this paper cutter is that the wood pieces supporting the platform are not of the same quality as the platform, the metal cutting bar, and the metal plate for the cutting bar.  I can understand that the wood pieces only serve to support the platform, so X-Acto would not want to spend much money on them.  However, they are functional and unless you look at them closely, they look okay, so my complaint is a minor one.If you have a frequent need to cut paper that is two feet wide, and you have room for a large paper cutter, this could be the cutter for you.  I think this cutter would be perfect for schools, offices, and anyone who needs a sturdier paper cutter than the low cost plastic versions with their flimsy handles.Enjoy!

I am extremely happy with the Powershred 99Ms.  This Goliath of a shredder is extremely easy to set-up and use.  Make sure you have ample space for this shredder.  It's larger than the average computer tower case.  In fact, it towers over my PC tower.This shredder is replacing a 9-year-old Fellowes, which is still working.  I wanted something more powerful. While the shredding sounds are audible, they aren't deafening.  The shredding action is smooth once the shredder senses the size of the item to be shredded.  It takes a second or two to sense the item being shredded before it starts shredding.The pail that collects the shredded paper pulls out easily, so that it can be emptied.  It holds far more than my old shredder and has a clear window so you can glance to see how much space is left.The bits of shredded paper are quite small.  The Powershred almost pulverizes the paper.  Re-assembling the pieces would be next to impossible.  For every day use, the micro-cut shredding is almost overkill.The Powershred also shreds credit cards without a problem. However, it shreds credit cards easily. In the middle of the shredding mechanism is a little outline to let the user know where to place the card to be shredded.One note about this shredder is that it has to be oiled occasionally.  Fellowes recommends oiling it after the pail is full.  I haven't had the shredder long enough to try oiling it, but it seems like it will be an easy process.Overall, this is a great shredder.  It may be a little overkill for most homes, but it's essential for anyone running a small business.

இ Fuzzy Wuzzy's Summary:ѾѾѾѾѾ Highly recommended with warm fuzzies!փ Positives:փ This laminator has a good balance of laminating warm-up time, speed, and performance for the price.փ The 60-second warm-up time and 24"/minute laminating speed are considerably quicker than most of the bargain-priced laminators.փ Even when hot-laminating uneven objects like pressed-and-dried leaves, I do not get wrinkling, warping, buckling, or curling on the laminated output.փ This laminator has two safety features in case you forget to turn it off: (1) it beeps every 10 minutes to remind you that it is still on, (2) its auto-shutoff mechanism automatically turns off the laminator after 60 minutes.փ The laminator includes a corner punch to round the corners of a laminated item for a more professional elegant appearance without stiff corners that can jab you.փ The laminator comes with a 2-year warranty.ჯ Negatives:ჯ The list price is somewhat expensive if you are only going to use this a few times a year.What is in the box package?₪ Model LAM95FH "Flash Series" thermal laminator₪ 30-page English/French/Spanish instruction manual₪ 9"x12" Laminator Cleaning Sheet₪ Sampler pack of Black&Decker;'s "TimeShield" brand of laminating pouches: one 5-mil 9"x11.5" letter-sized pouch, two 3-mil 9"x11.5" letter-size pouches, one 4.5"x6.25" 4x6 photo pouch, one 2.25"x3.75" business card pouch, one 2.5"x4.5" luggage tag pouch, one plastic luggage tag loop strapOver the years, I have used laminators made by both Scotch/3M and Swingline/GBC.  The Scotch-brand laminator is, by far, the most inexpensive, and it is quite usable for home applications as long as you do not need a laminator that quickly warms up and has a quicker laminating speed.  Both the Swingline/GBC laminators and this Black&Decker; model cost more, but they are also higher-wattage laminators that warm up within one to two minutes (compared to the 5-minute warm-up time on the Scotch laminator) and the more-expensive higher-wattage laminators laminate quicker than the 12"/minute laminating speed of the Scotch laminator.  If you have a lot of regular laminating projects, the quick start-up times and fast 24"/minute to 48"/minute laminating speeds may justify the extra cost so you can laminate items two to four times quicker.I have previously used a variety of Black&Decker; power tools and I have been uniformly pleased with their reliability.  Black&Decker; appears to be a newcomer in the laminator market, and this model LAM95FH is their mid-range laminator.  Black&Decker; also makes a slower LAM95 that is 3.6 pounds, 400 watts, with a warm-up time of 120 seconds and a laminating speed of 12"/minute.  This LAM95FH (the "FH" in the model number refers to its "Fast Heat" ability) is 7.3 pounds, 1050 watts, with a speedy warm-up time of 60 seconds and a laminating speed of 24"/minute.  And Black&Decker;'s fastest laminator, the LAM125FH, is 11.7 pounds, 1750 watts, with a warm-up time of 60 seconds and a laminating speed of 48"/minute.  All three of these Black&Decker; laminator models accept a laminating pouch as wide as 9.5", which is a very common maximum pouch size for most laminators.I am thoroughly pleased with how easy and trouble-free this laminator has been during the past two months of usage, and how nice the results are.  This LAM95FH model has settings for using pouches of 3 mil and 5 mil thickness, with either cold lamination or hot lamination.  For the past few months, all of my experiences with this laminator have been with hot lamination using bothBlack and Decker TimeShield Thermal Laminating Pouches, Letter, 3 mil - 100 Pack (LAMLET3-100)andScotch(TM) Thermal Laminating Pouches, 9 Inches x 11.4 Inches, 50 Pouches (TP3854-50).  Both the Black&Decker; and Scotch pouches give equally good results, so you can use them interchangeably.  You should only use laminating pouches in this laminator as it will not work properly with self-adhesive laminating sheets.  This laminator lives up to its "Flash" and "Fast Heat" names.  From the moment that I plug it in and push the [Power] and [3 Mil] buttons, it is ready for hot lamination within one minute, beeping three times to let me know that it is ready for use.I have successfully used this LAM95FH to laminate not only documents, business cards, luggage tags, cooking recipes, photos, and other keepsakes, but during the past two months, I have laminated more than 30 sheets of pressed-and-dried autumn leaves that have been collected over the past few years.  The autumn leaves of maples, oaks, aspen, sumacs, and smoke trees are now preserved and protected with this lamination.Using this laminator with flat objects made of paper is easy, as long as you do not laminate heat-sensitive documents using the thermal mode, but laminating pressed-and-dried autumn leaves requires more careful preparation.  Here is how you can use this laminator to preserve beautiful autumn foliage:1) First, as soon as you collect the leaves during autumn, press and dry them.  I sandwich the leaves inside the pages of large phone books, lining both sides of each phone book "sandwich" with a paper towel.  Let the leaves thoroughly dry in this flattened state for at least several days.  I usually keep the leaves sandwiched undisturbed inside the phone books for a whole week before carefully taking them out.2) To laminate the pressed-and-dried leaves, I set up the laminator on a table or on the kitchen counter.  I stack some books, magazines, or phone books in front of the laminator to create a platform that is 1.8" to 2.0" high and then place an inverted baking/cookie pan on top of that stack.  The baking/cookie pan should be place right up against the laminator, and its surface should be aligned and level with the laminator's slot where the pouch is fed in.3) I place a new laminating pouch onto the cookie pan, with the folded sealed edge pointed toward the laminator's slot.  For both hot and cold laminating, the sealed edge of the pouch should always be fed into the slot first.  Since the pressed-and-dried leaves are very brittle, I carefully place leaves onto the back sheet of the pouch using one hand while holding up the top sheet of the pouch with the other hand, filling up the bottom side from the folded sealed edge first and working my way down.  As I fill up the sheet with leaves, I progressively lower the top sheet onto the leaves; this holds the leaves in their place.  I position the leaves so that there is 1/8" to 1/4" spacing between the leaves and a similar distance away from the edge of the laminating pouch.  Place the leaves so that each leaf is pointed towards the folded sealed edge and each leaf's petiole (leaf stem) enters into the laminator AFTER most of the main leaf has already entered into the laminator's rollers.  The reason for not having the leaf petiole enter the laminator first is that if you have a large leaf with a thicker petiole, when it hits the laminator's rollers first, the rollers may push back on the leaf petiole, nudging and moving the leaf inside the laminating pouch.  But if most of the leaf has already been rolled through the laminator before the rollers go over the petiole, this does not shift the position of the leaf inside the pouch.  If a leaf has a really thick petiole (e.g. a large maple leaf), you should cut some of that thick portion out before placing the leaf on the laminating pouch.4) After the laminating pouch has been filled up with pressed-and-dried leaves, I CAREFULLY slide the pouch along the surface of the cookie pan into the laminator's slot.  I do not lift the laminating pouch up to insert it into the slot or else the leaves inside the pouch will move around or fall out.  Once I have slid the laminating pouch into the laminator's slot, the rollers will start pulling the pouch in after about one-third of the pouch has been carefully pushed into the slot.  As the pouch is going into the laminator, I use my fingertips to lightly press down on the areas of the pouch that are just about to go into the rollers in order to hold the leaves in place and prevent the possibility of any leaves shifting or getting nudged inside the pouch.  I continue pressing onto areas of the pouch until the last one or two inches of the pouch are about to go through the laminator's rollers.  Even though I have not tried laminating pressed-and-dried flowers, you could probably also do that as long as the flowers are not too thick.For both laminating documents and leaves, I find that there are a few things that I can do to minimize the possibility of ending up with wrinkled, buckled, or bent laminations.  This laminator has a handy output feed tray that swings out and keeps the laminated sheet more level as it is rolled out from the laminator.  As the laminated pouch exits the rear of the laminator, it stays relatively flat compared to some other brands of laminators that let the laminated sheet dangle downward as it exits from the rear.  Keeping the entire laminated sheet level after it has exited the rear of the laminator is crucial to prevent the still-hot sheet from warping, wrinkling, or curling as it cools.  Most importantly, as soon as the sheet has completely come out of the rollers, I IMMEDIATELY place it on a flat surface.  I then also place a clean cookie pan on top of the still-very-warm laminated sheet and I place about a one-pound weight (e.g. soup can) on top of the cookie pan to keep the sheet flat as it cools.  I find that the laminated sheet is most prone to bending, wrinkling, warping, buckling, and curling when it is freshly laminated and still very warm.  So, for thermal laminating, it helps to immediately place the warm sheet on a flat surface and keep it flattened with something placed on top of it while it cools.The laminator comes with a 9"x12" 'Laminator Cleaning Sheet' which you are supposed to use after each series of laminations to clean the laminator rollers and remove any excess adhesive that may have bled out from the pouches onto the rollers while laminating.  I have not used the 'Laminator Cleaning Sheet' yet, but I have gone through two boxes of laminating pouches, and not once have I encountered a jam where I had to pull this laminator's "jam release lever" and press and hold the [REV] reverse button to clear a jammed sheet.This laminator has a very handy corner punch feature that rounds the corners of a laminated sheet.  All of the previous laminators that I have used did not have this corner-rounding punch feature, but it gives the laminated sheets a more professional elegant appearance and prevents the stiff laminated corners from jabbing your skin.  All laminators really need to have an integrated corner punch like this!  An integrated cord wrap slot that goes around the rear of the laminator lets me quickly and neatly store the cord when the laminator is not being used.  If you do not need to laminate items every week, I suggest storing the laminator inside the cardboard box that it was originally packaged in.  The box package can be used to securely store the laminator, and it also includes a handy carrying handle on the box.Overall, this is a great high-performance laminator with several thoughtful design features that are not found on other brands of laminators.

When purchasing binders, one needs to consider the use you have intended for them.  There are two things I look at,  the cover and the rings.  As a teacher and a mom, I have a lot of experience with binders.The cover:If I am simply going to put papers in them and store them on the shelf, I like the hard binders.  I use this type for filing recipes and documents I need to access.  Since they are stiff they are easy to shove back onto the shelf.  In the classroom these also work better, as they are less likely to slip off the shelf than the flexible cover binders.However, I find that buying hard binders for my kids leads to problems.  The kids like to stuff these into their backpacks, and the edges where the plastic is sealed quickly start to peel off, and the covers get folded over.  For them, I have found that a flexible binder in general will make it farther though the school year.  They will sometimes crack along the spine, but usually not enough to make the binder unusable, and a little duct tape will fix it.The rings:The second thing to look at is the rings.  The best ones (in my opinion) are the D shaped, as they hold more, with the little dimple on one side that fits into a depression on the other side.  This prevents papers from getting caught as you flip through.  They also hurt less if you snap them onto your fingers!  The other closure (a zig zag) tends to get misaligned over time with hard use, and the sharp edges hurt more if you close them on your fingers.This binder is one good looking binder,  and has an insert for a business card on the inside along with two very shallow pockets and a pen holder.  However, the binder has the less desirable round zig zag rings.  And on the inside back cover mine has bubbles, as if the fabric were not completely adhered to the underlying material.  At this price point, I would expect more attention to detail.  It is also a bit smaller than a typical binder, do not plan to use this with inserts for example, they stick out over the edge.  I was also disturbed by the Prop 65 warning,  especially since I don’t know what it is for, I found the list for Prop 65 online and it is 23 pages long, with some chemicals added and crossed out as time goes on making me wonder how  the criteria for inclusion are determined.  For example, nickel is listed (perhaps that is in the rings?)  or it could easily be a chemical used to soften the plastics,  but I also see stuff like wood dust (seems not too evil) and lead (which I would not want to be handling on a daily basis).  This list seems to have no level of toxicity discrimination so I have no idea what caused this binder to land on the list, is there a little wood dust on it?  Who cares?  Or is lead in the cover (then I care!).

I am very familiar with both regular 4 ink inkjet printers and the more expensive 6 ink inkjet photo printers as I print a lot of photos for family history as well as for a collectibles magazine and have used both types of printers. I have always preferred using a good quality photo printer, however, this new 5 ink inkjet printer gives you better photos without the higher price tag of a photo printer.  For those unfamiliar with the differences between photo and regular printers, I will tell you how the inks make a difference. The best printers for photos are always inkjet printers. Nothing can compare to the deep rich colors you get from inkjet inks. With a regular printer, you get 4 inks- black, cyan, magenta and yellow. With a photo printer, you get 6 inks- black, cyan, magenta, yellow, light cyan and light magenta. These extra 2 light inks give you complete depth of even the slightest color shades that any serious photographer can notice. For a non professional photographer, these slight variations of color shades may not mean as much. This Epson Expression Premium XP-600 Small-In-One Printer gives you 5 inkjet inks- black, cyan, magenta, yellow and photo black. You don't get the slight color depth of shades as you would with the 2 lighter inks, but the new photo black ink really enhances the photos, giving them great depth and sharpness. These Epson Claria Premium Brand Inkjet Inks are quite amazing as they are smudge, scratch and water resistant. The photos you get are as close to professional without having to pay for a more expensive photo printer.As for the printer itself, it is a great compact size, considering you have an inkjet printer, flatbed scanner, copier, 2 sided duplex printing which also prints from an iPad, iPhone, tablet or smartphone and with your 2.5 inch LCD panel, you have the ability to do quite a bit of photo correction above and beyond red eye before printing. You can print directly onto inkjet printable CD's and DVD's, although you have to watch what color inks will show up clearly on the CD's and DVD's. The automatic 2 sided printing is nice. The set up was an easy 5 minute task on my Windows 7, with the exception of setting up my wireless network, which had to be done manually. Once connected to my network, I couldn't believe how easy it is to print from my phones and tablets. It also prints from Apple Air Print and Google Cloud Print. What you get inside the box is the XP 600 Inkjet Printer, your 5 Claria Inkjet Inks, a SetUp and Instruction Manual, the CD-Rom containing the drivers and the power cables. You DO NOT get the USB cable and of course you have to purchase paper. The USB cable can be bought here on Amazon for only a couple dollars, so that's no big deal, as I've never bought a printer that included this cable. Not only is the printer a great small size, it is super quiet when operating.The photos you get from this Epson XP 600 are not only fade resistant from the superior Claria Premium Inkjet Inks, but they claim your prints will last 200 years in album storage, so you know even your grandchildren will enjoy your photos. Another great thing is Epson makes all 5 of the Claria inks in XL sizes, so you save a lot of money over time. Epson scanners are truly the best, as I have used an Epson Perfection Scanner for over a decade now. This scanner may not be Epson's top of the line Perfection model, but it is superior in capturing fine details, as I compared the Perfection scans with this XP 600, and the results were very close. One thing I noticed upon first using the printer, as I had to choose ALL PAPER TYPES before printing, as it was pre-set for only one type of paper I wasn't using, and would not print until I set it to all paper types. Now I can put in any type of paper with this setting and it puts out the right amount of ink for your photo or paper. Another thing I noticed is that this printer will only print when you remember to pull the output tray out after loading your paper.  This Epson Expression Premium XP-600 is a truly fantastic buy for the money. You may not be getting professional photos with 6 inks, but you are getting close to pro photos with the 5 richly colored inkjet inks and highly detailed scans that will give you gorgeous sharply detailed documents and photos and for that, the Epson XP 600 deserves 4 1/2 Stars.

Wireless Fax, Scanner, Printer Easy Install (unless computer challenged) Decent quality, does the job.ConsLike any other "Ink Jet" there is the cost of the cartridges. Yet it was fairly simple from my point of view.Installation was as followed:Unwrap printerPlug into power outletInstall printer using the included CD using the "Network" option only.The install guides you, when prompted you plug in the USB cable (included) and hit next.(You only need to plug in the USB on the first computer you install in order to set up the network on the printer)Follow onscreen instructions by simple READING and fill in the blanks. Make sure to select the Network option only! not the USB. This time around the software will find the printer in the network and will show up on a list. Select the printer and hit next. Just to note save yourself the problems and READ the instructions and DON'T PLUG THE USB until the install prompts you.(If USB is required). I needed a printer when I got a new Windows 7 64-bit computer.  My old HP Deskjet 960c, which worked perfectly on the old XP computer, was not well supported by Win7 -- it declared the HP 960c driver to be incompatible, and it replaced it with a Windows driver.  The Win7 driver allowed only minimal control of the printer, and color photos that had printed well in WinXP now came out muddy.  HP doesn't offer an updated Win7 driver for the 960c.I got the HP D7560 based on Consumer Reports ratings that showed excellent 8x10 photo quality.  The installation in Win7 was lengthy and difficult -- the computer rejected the HP installation disk on the first try -- but eventually I got everything done including the installation of a versatile HP driver.  Photo quality at both 8x10 and 4x6 is excellent -- I couldn't ask for more.  But here are some downsides.1.  Noisy.  My old 960c was so quiet that sometimes you couldn't even tell it was printing.  The D7560 lets you know it is there during printing, and makes fairly loud noise when cleaning itself.2.  Inconvenient.  It has two paper trays, one for photos, but it only holds 4x6 paper.  You have to use the 8x10 plain paper tray for photo paper.  From the product description offered at Amazon and HP.com this limitation was not apparent ("Print photos without changing paper using the additional 20-sheet photo tray").3.  Quirky.  While using Printmaster 15 to print a collage of 4 photos, the printer printed an 8x10 sheet with only 3 of them, leaving a blank space for the fourth.  WinXP and the 960c printed this page correctly.  I'm hoping HP will have an updated driver for the D7560 to correct this problem (are you listening, HP?).4.  Unnecessary bells and whistles.  The printer has memory-card slots and an LCD screen, and it prints on printable CDs.  Very nice for those who need these features, but I do not.I consider these downsides acceptable in view of the excellent photo quality.Update 04-29-11.  the "missing photo" problem mentioned above disappeared when I got a new motherboard installed in my Win7-64 computer.  I can't explain why, I merely note that it happened.  Meanwhile the excellent photo quality continues.

The Zebra stylus pen is a great pen for those who want a pen that can also be used as a stylus with a smartphone, iPod, or tablet computer.  In my line of work I have to sign a lot of documents on paper but also on tablets.  Many times the reps who want me to sign on their tablet do not have a stylus for me to use, and I end up having to try to sign my name with the tip of my finger.  This stylus pen completely eliminates that hassle.The pen arrives on a cardboard card.  There are no instructions with it, but it is pretty intuitive to use.  The pocket clip on the pen is pushed downward to open and retract the gel tip ball point pen.  It writes very smoothly and, just as it advertises, glides across the paper.  I have experienced no ink "blobs" with this pen.  The back end of the pen has a rubber tip for use as a stylus.  It works perfectly with my iPad.There are ink refills available for the pen, although the product card does not tell you how to remove and replace the ink.  As it turns out, you unscrew the chrome tip of the pen (where the ink ball point comes out) and that gives you access to the ink cartridge.  I looked up the Zebra ink replacement on Amazon, and it will cost you $8 for two ink refills.  So the ink is a little expensive compared with other ball point pens.  I haven't looked at an office supply store, though, so it's possible there may be some other type of refill that might also work with this pen.  Aside from the ink it looks pretty generic.In summary, if you need a ball point pen that can also function as a stylus you need look no further than this Zebra stylus pen.  It looks and works great, and writes wonderfully.

If there are 'south-paws' scissors searches for the left-handed users in your home or office, the Westcott Scissor Mouse may end the scissors safaris once and for all.  This ergonomically designed paper cutter in the shape of a computer mouse, will work for all of us.PROS:Any paper project is made easier because this mouse has a built-in ruler to guide your straight edge cuts.  It's equally useful for curvy cutting.It is compact enough to fit in most drawers and its color makes it easy to see.For large cutting jobs, this mouse won't tire your hand as would standard scissors.You can cut paper placed on a table or counter because the cutting edge will not touch it.CONS:Don't expect this mouse to cut anything firmer than heavy-weight paper.Paper must be placed between the plastic guide of the mouse (and not merely placed on top of the paper).  This step is a bit time consuming.The same guard that prevents the work surface from being cut by the blade, stops you from merely rolling the mouse over paper to cut it.  You must start at an outer edge, just like you would when using conventional scissors.  This is a drawback if you want to cut something (a coupon, perhaps) in the middle of the paper.THE FINAL WORD:This mouse is a cut above ordinary scissors.  It will prevent hand fatigue and if you've used Fiskars Softouch scissors because of it, you may find using the Westcott Scissor Mouse even less tiring.For projects, this mouse may be just right for you.Good scissors are not cheap.  Fortunately, this mouse's price point makes it a great value.

The soft cloth bottom is also nice; far superior to rubberish lap desks.Beyond keeping your lap cool and comfy, however, it takes good care of your lap top.  Flip up tabs keep one's computer from sliding down into one's belly region.  Size mismatch aside, the Logitech Lapdesk treats my Toshiba Netbook well; immobilizing it and comfortably resiting it on  my lap.The large size of this unit seems to distribute the heavy weight of the larger laptops across one's lap allowing for a more comfortable experience.  Be aware, however, the N700 is so wide it does not fit between the armrests of many office chairs, thus limiting its usefulness.  Also know the sound quality of the speakers is not terribly good.  They sound tinny.  Even my all business Vostro has sound approaching the N700's.  My Toshiba netbook, however, does benefit from the boost in power and quality this lap desk delivers.This products biggest downside is its draw on the computer battery.  Fortunately, the N700 does not come with DC adapter.  It elegantly draws its power from a USB port on the "host" computer.  One can disable the fan and speakers, though, to save one's computer battery.I have no complaints about this desk.  I have hooked it to 3 different laptops-- running XP, Vista, and Windows 7 starter-- without incident.  My favorite place to use this is in bed or in front of the TV.  Nice job, Logitech.

First before my review, please note that you are not getting what is pictured--you are getting rolls of tape.My two granddaughters are curious about everything in the world.  We are going to go visit the CSI exhibit at one of the casinos next month so I thought this would be a good learning tool for them.Fingerprint identification or dactyloscopy (good word to use to explain orgins and to practice spelling 'hard' words) has experts comparing the ridged impressions on the fingers. Since, like snowflakes (another learning moment) no two fingerprints are alike - fingerprints can be used to identify people for several purposes.  A classification system is used that is probably too complex for them at their grammar school ages, but any opportunity to introduce some math is one not to be missed, right? So there are many potential learning opportunities to combine with the tape that will interest them and help them with spelling, language, math, history, science etc.So I'm off to design a grammar school "lesson" plan to incorporate the tape into our CSI casino exhibit visit.Also, if you don't have a dispenser probably getting one would facilitate getting the tape off the rolls. I have one from a packing tape package. You might be able to find a cheapie for $2 or $3 or ask friends and neighbors that have moved recently they may have one. It really will help keep your fingerprints off the tape!

I am using these kid scissors in a homeschool environment. They are well constructed for children, with handles that fit small hands (tested on ages 2-8) well.  The ends are blunted enough to prevent impalement from an accidental fall while carrying them. The blades are sharp enough to cut paper and string, but already seem to dull quickly after only a few weeks of use.The quality seems moderate. As I said, the blades dull rather quickly, which only poses a problem when cutting thicker material like string or cardboard. Also, there is some give at the hinge, so the blades are not held in super close apposition, which can lead to frustration when cutting papers because the paper can fold in between the blades if the kids don't hold them just right. This was not a problem with all of the scissors, but a few did have this problem out of the box, and the construction seems to be such that others will develop the problem over time. I am not saying that they are cheaply made at all, but just that lots of craft use will wear them out, and that they do not cut like high quality adult scissors.Nevertheless, for the price point and the number of scissors, I consider this a great buy for home use with a number of kids; the number of scissors included make it so that you can throw away used or broken ones without qualms. For classroom use, the antimicrobial protectant will be a nice addition. I anticipate that the only problem for classroom use may be the inconsistent quality across scissors bringing some frustration on those pairs whose blades are not as closely aligned. Nevertheless, teaching the kids to hold the scissors appropriately, even those scissors cut fine.As an additional note, the storage rack advertised on the box is not really any good for storing the scissors (just flexible plastic). We just keep ours in a plastic bin.

The Fellowes "Smooth Move" boxes are a lot like their "Banker Box" product in that you assemble it by pulling open the box and then folding down an interior flap that forms a second layer of the box bottom.  Unlike the Banker Box, there are not additional flaps to provide a third bottom layer or a second side layer.  As the printing on the box says, these are intended for "lightweight, bulky items", so no loading it up with books or LPs (what?)The top flap "assembles" by tucking small cardboard flaps in the handle holes, adding a bit of cushioning and loosely holding the flap in place.  This method won't stand up to much bumping, but it will suffice for casual moving.  Just don't expect it to hold if you turn the box upside down or even sideways.I like that the boxes can be folded flat for later reuse, though it took a few minutes of head-scratching and trial pushes to get it to collapse again.  There are "assembly instructions", in the form of a series of diagrams, printed on the bottom of the box.  Really, all you have to do is separate out the handle flaps and then fold things in the order of the printed numbers on each flap, 1-5.

This printer is basically a souped up version of theEpson WorkForce 635 Color Inkjet All-in-One (C11CA69201)that I reviewed a few months ago.  Performance wise there is little to no difference in the print speed or quality (which is not a bad thing, since the 635 is an excellent printer).  However the 845 offers a few more features to make things a little easier and more convenient.1.)  Two print trays, vs one on the 635.  Having an additional tray on this printer allows for double the paper capacity.  Though its quite simple to add more paper, it is sort of a convenience to not have to do this as often.2.)  Touch screen button panel instead of actual buttons, while this doesn't really add much in terms of usability, the touch screen is definitely more cooler looking then having actual buttons.  One drawback for me is that with the touch screen, you don't get that response from actually pressing buttons.  It does feel weird at first especially if you are used to pressing real buttons.Other than these two features, and a bigger display screen for viewing pictures, the 845 and 645 are virtually the same printer in terms of functionality.  The touch screen may draw many people to this printer instead of the 645, but if you don't care about having touch screen and also dual tray capacity, you very well may suffice just fine with the 645.You can't go wrong with either choice as both are excellent printers.  Choosing between the 645 and 845 is basically the equivalent of choosing to buy a car with or without navigation.

This small laser printer is appropriate for home office use and is similar to many of this type available from other manufacturers. The printer ships with a 1000-page starter printer cartridge. The standard cartridge (Samsung MLT-D103S/XAA Toner 1.5K Standard Yield (ML-2955ND/DW, SCX-4729FD/FW)) yields 1500 pages, and a high-yield cartridge (Samsung MLT-D103L/XAA Toner 2.5K High Yield (ML-2955ND/DW, SCX-4729FD/FW)) yields 2500 pages.The setup was straightforward and could be done without instructions with one exception: it was not immediately obvious how to extend the paper length guide in the paper tray.The only guide for the machine was provided on a CD. The function of some of the control panel buttons/lights was not obvious, so the user would benefit from the inclusion of a small card containing a control panel overview, as well as a machine overview. The printer's paper level indicator was not an obvious feature, for example. A 20-second glance at a printed guide would have saved five minutes using a CD to hunt down answers.The printer does not come with any cables. Fortunately we had an extra ethernet cable lying around so we were able to plug it into our router. All the computers in the house are able to print to it wirelessly without any trouble.The machine is relatively quiet and I have not seen anything to complain about in the quality of the printout.In sum, the printer is much like others. I would use the cost as my prime criterion in determining which of many to choose.-- Debra Hamel

I have no complaints about the noise, and knock on wood, I have experienced no problems with this product.  It is reasonably stylish, but a bit larger than it looks in pictures or that I would like.It sharpens "standard" sized wood pencils.  It is somewhat startling the first time you use it as the auto-feed mechanism seems to grab the pencil out of your hand and starts to "eat" it.  When done, it ejects the pencil.  I found it works best on pencils with beveled edges, but it also works well on round pencils.  The only pencils that I had to help it were some flocked/fuzzy holiday pencils that my daughter had.  In that case, I had to grip the pencil to keep it from turning.Both a pro and a con is the pencil sharpening angle.  It is quite narrow. The first time you use it, you will think it won't stop eating your pencil, but it is actually sharpening it to a very fine, narrow point.  If you take an already-sharpened pencil, you will see that it has some sensor and essentially shaves no more off.  The narrow point is nice in that it lasts a long time between sharpening, but the con is that you will have to write carefully in the beginning (if you press heavy) so that you don't break it.  Can't say it's better or worse, just different than most pencil sharpeners.  I guess I like the narrow angle better, but not that it is so pin sharp.  Overall, it did exceed my expectations.

To start with I'll address the speed issue since that is the focus of my review title. I purchased this for two reasons: First, I wanted a good multifunction printer that could also print excellent photos. Second, I wanted the print speeds that this printer advertises.I do not know how they arrive at their speed specs, but here are my test results:Although black text printing is lightning fast, color printing on high quality settings is not much faster than my 5 yr old epson Stylus. A 4x6 borderless photo printed in 'best photo' quality using glossy photo paper took 2 minutes, 20 seconds!!! I was floored at how long it took. So then I decided to do some direct comparisons with my old Epson Stylus Photo (R320).I chose to print color flyers that I needed to print anyway. They are full color (including backgrounds), and some photo work. I used the regular Photo Quality, on 8 1/2 x 11 premium presentation paper. One flyer took 1 minute 20 seconds on the Workforce. The same flyer my old Epson printer (a Stylus R320) took 2 minutes 23 seconds, on the same setting, but it produced a much better looking flyer. Then I tried using the 'text & image' setting, both printers. It only took 40 seconds on the Workforce and 47 seconds on the old Stylus. The interesting thing was that on the stylus, I could get the same quality on 'text & image' setting as I got on the Workforce 'photo' setting. So basically, when you compare actual printout quality, the Workforce takes 1 min 20 sec compared to the old printer's 47 seconds, because I have to step up the quality setting to get the same results with the Workforce. To be fair, I do hold the flyers side by side when comparing quality. It's obvious in that situation, but someone only seeing the lesser quality flyer would probably not know the difference. But here's an interesting thing... Printing a photo in regular text setting (not text & Image) the quality is better on the Workforce. It did not degrade going from 'text & image' to just 'text'. On my old printer it does degrade.So this brings me to the Quality issue. Yes, I was pleasantly surprised at the photo quality, given that this is not your typical photo printer. Colors are very slightly less saturated than with my old printer. But you have to hold the comparisons literally right next to each other to tell the difference. This difference could easily be compensated for in Photoshop. Also, you pretty much have to use the highest setting (best photo) to get really good quality, and when you do that the speeds are definitely not there. Because of the speed issue alone, I was tempted to go three stars instead of four, but since I was undecided I 'rounded up'.For the rest of the issues, I am completely satisfied. Although I am a network idiot, I was able to set this up wirelessly no problem. I love the two paper trays, since I do print a lot of photos. The only jam I experienced so far was when I printed on photo paper with regular paper under it. the photo paper came thru first, part of the picture was printed on it, then the rest of the picture was printed on the regular paper that came right behind. I haven't tried multiple copies with photo paper but that'll be my next test. I have yet to test other features, but I was pleased to see the OCR program being installed during setup. I guess I didn't realize it had that. I usually don't install a lot of the extra software that comes with printers, as I prefer to use Photoshop for everything, from scanning, to photo manipulation. But this time I did install the extra software and so far am impressed with the Easy Photo Print. Very straight forward and easy to use. Just click on the pictures you want to print (using ctrl key to choose more than one) and then you are taken to a very simple & user friendly photo fixer. Being anal about my pics, I'll still use mostly Photoshop, but I was impressed nonetheless.That's about it for now. Bottom line, I'll keep it and it will serve me well. But I am definitely disappointed in the speed, and the fact that you really need the highest quality print settings to get good photos. But at least you CAN get good photos, and that was one of my initial concerns.4/6/11: Ok, for the first time I printed multiple copies on 48 lb. trifold brochure paper. So far I've run 50 through and No JAMS!!!! Yay!

These boxes are reusable, re-foldable shipping/storage cardboard boxes that come in a package of 8. They are not heavy, and are fairly easy to fold out for use, once you figure out the rather obtuse instruction diagrams which are inconveniently placed on the bottom panel which is hidden inside the box when folded. Not exactly a wise placement for a diagram meant to help one unfold and set up the box.The measurements are rather generous, and I found that the stated 16 x 18 x 18 inches more accurately described the inside than out. While not designed as well as some of the document-sized boxes I have used, these certainly are adequate for many shipping and storage tasks.There are designated spaces on the side for marking contents and room placement. They way that the boxes fold out is much simpler than one assumes at first, and the bottom folding section is covered by an internal fold-down panel which is held in place by the weight of objects placed in the box. Not the strongest of methods, but certainly adequate for most tasks.The fold down flaps on one top panel curl under and fit into the hand slots on two sides of the box, but do not expect them to hold very tightly, as they are just extensions of the same cardboard as the lid flap. They will not stand a great deal of tucking and un-tucking before they wear out and are useless.The boxes are reasonably strong, but not double-walled or very thick cardboard. They are a medium-weight cardboard, and I would not place heavy objects in them, such as mechanical parts, heavy electronics, books, etc. They should be adequate for linens and well-padded dishes, stuffed animals, lighter weight toys, etc. They have virtually no resistance to water, and would be easily damaged by even small amounts, especially if the boxes are under any kind of weight stress. A dry, clean environment is a definite necessity.All those caveats considered, these boxes would be very useful in moving and storing a large variety of items, and the uniform size and shape would be a definite plus over scavenged boxes. Not sure if I would consider them enough of an advantage to merit the cost, but then how valuable are the items you are packing?I would probably be more inclined to go with the more office-based document style boxes with lids, but these boxes with built-in lids certainly have their place.

QUICK SUMMARY:  The XP-610 is a very modest update of theEpson Expression XP-600 Wireless Small-in-One Color Inkjet Printer, Copier, Scanner, 2-Sided Duplex. Prints from Tablet/Smartphone. AirPrint Compatible (C11CC47201).  Read all the reviews for the XP-600 and you'll have a pretty good idea of what to expect from the XP-610.BACKGROUND:  We've had the XP-600 for about a year now, and the XP-610 is almost identical to it.  In fact, it's very hard to tell them apart.  We don't use the XP-600 (or, now, the XP-610) as our primary printer because it lacks the intuitive, touchscreen interface that theEpson C11CD29201 Expression Premium XP-810 Small Wireless Color Photo Printer with Scanner, Copier and Faxhas.Here are a few differences between the XP-600 and XP-610:- The XP-600 is rated to print 12 pages-per-minute (black) and 8 pages-per-minute (color).  The XP-610 prints 1 page faster than both of these.  From a practical standpoint, the difference is immaterial and unnoticeable.- Copy speed is exactly the same- Scanning speed rates the XP-610 as faster than the XP-600, but that difference didn't show-up in real-world use- XP-610 sound level is 38 decibels, the XP-600 is 43 decibels.  From a practical standpoint, it's very hard to tell the difference.- About everything else, like dimensions, weight, functions, connectivity, etc, the XP-610 is the same as the XP-600In short, there is really nothing new that is apparent with the XP-610 over the predecessor, the XP-600.  The primary reason why we don't use the XP-600 (or XP-610) very much is because the touchpad is a little confusing and a little cumbersome to use.  Everyone in my family prefers the touchscreen interface of the XP-810 over the XP-610.  For a budget printer, such as for use in a college dorm setting, this is a fine printer that will do the job.  For a whole-family workhorse, I think the XP-810 is a better choice, plus you get the faxing capability of the XP-810, too, making it a complete all-in-one solution.

I got two of these books at one time, not in any particular order. I have three little ones aged 7, 5 and 3 1/2 so I figured that we could find a place for them somewhere. The Number Stories for the K-2nd grade seemed a little too young for my first grader (age 7) at first. That was a learning curve and we didn't get through it as fast as other parts, but the rest of these types of word problems that fit his level of understanding.There were lots of parts of the book that were just fun (the exercise portion, the Shuttle countdown, etc..) and he seem to enjoy it.I tried a couple pages out on my pre-kinder-gardener and while he did well with the tracing of the numbers in the early pages, many parts were just beyond his reach -- obvious exceptions being the easier ones that he was familiar with, like the countdown and the counting of the cut-out pieces.At first I thought this was probably too easy, but the book did progress and there were some word problems that I thought were at least one level above where my first grader is at. Since this was marketed for k-2, then I guess it's right on target.For about five bucks it's a pretty good workbook. I wouldn't buy it for my pre-k student, that's for sure, but I did think overall it was well suited for my first grader. If I could have offered it at a different time, it would be during the summer break between 1st and 2nd grade, that way we could use it as a summer supplement to keep up his number and math skills.Over all we're quite pleased. If I had any suggestions it would be to have pages that could be wiped clean and used again for the next kid, but for the cost, this is perfect.

Before the Ivation portable scanner ever landed on my doorstep, I was totally enamored with the concept.  I used to use a flatbed scanner and now make use of one in an all-in-one printer.  Mind you, I'm semi-satisfied with the one in my current printer, but the versatility I want and need simply isn't there.  It's fine for things such as copying individual sheets, but as far as scanning book pages or documents in a library it's not.  For one thing, it's not portable and secondly if I try to hold something still I often end up with a blurred mess.  I confess to being a big time scanner, especially in libraries.The value of having a portable scanner for me is obvious.  I have page after page of handwritten articles that I need from libraries.  Unfortunately, many of them are in rare books that are practically under lock and key.  For example, I have been know to practically monopolize a copying machine (under the scrutiny of an overzealous librarian) copying upwards of 250 pages a day.  I have not yet had the opportunity to take this little Ivation on the road, but am looking forward to doing just that.  With the addition of an SD card, I'll be good to go in that department and in the meantime I'm "practicing" my scanning technique.The Ivation is ultra-simple to use.  If you simply want to scan documents around you house, you don't even need the SD card.  Three AAA batteries (included), a steady hand, and you're good to go.  You can easily get rid of that paper clutter and get it into your documents in the format and color you want.  The two formats are JPG and PDF and you can either choose to scan in color or black and white.  The included user manual, which is quite comprehensive, uses charts, visuals, and easy to understand directions.  For example, for those who are tech-challenged those visuals are perfect.Probably the hardest thing is getting the door open to put the batteries in.  One of the things I like the best, or should I say others might like, is that you don't have to install any software or even purchase an SD card to use the Ivation.  It's just one of those plug-and-play types of things that are awesome.  If you are a researcher or someone who sells a lot of ephemera on eBay this has got to be something you'll wonder what you ever did without.  I know that I'm quite enamored with it (I think I said that) and will be making good use of it both at home and in libraries.  Definitely a product many people should take a close look at.SPECS:~  Image sensor:  A4 Color Contact Image Sensor~  Sensor Resolution:  900 DPI~  Scanning Resolution:  300 dpi (default) / 600 dpi / 900 dpi~  Scan Width and Length:  217mm(W)*1200mm(L)  (8.64" x 47.24")~  File Format: JPG or PDF~  External memory:  Support Micro SD card (up to 32GB)~  Focus range:  Contact plus or minus 0.2mm (.0078 inch)~  LCD:  Scanning status display~  USB Port:  USB2.0 high speed~  Power:  3 x AAA alkaline batteries (included)~  Support system:  Mindows XP Sp2, Windows Vista, Windows 7, MAC OS 10.4 or above (direct plug-in, driver installation not required)~  Dimension (L x H x W):  253 x 39 x 25mm (9.96" x 1.53" x .984")Sample provided for review.

I bought theAmazonBasics 8-Sheet Micro-Cut Shredderin early November 2013 to replace anExecutive Machines crosscut 12 sheet shredderI bought years ago from Staples that finally gave up the ghost.  There are several improvements in this machine that would make it worth `upgrading' to even if you current shredder is doing just fine.Comparing the two, my old one could shred CD's and credit cards, and most machines that can at least crosscut are usually able to at least shred credit cards.  This one has a dedicated slot for CD's and can chop them into about 4 separate pieces.  My old shredder would cut the CD in the same slot as paper and into tons of tiny pieces, however I like that it is separate on this machine to keep your paper cutting blades in top shape.  I think the fact that the old one used the same slot for everything wore it down much quicker.Something to love about this machine is the included wheels.  It makes moving the machine around really easy and its one feature that is great if you shred in different rooms on occasion, which I do.  Two of the wheels have locks if you need to stabilize the shredder for any reason which is a great safety feature.  This unit also feature a removable basket with a window to let you know when it's time to empty.  It's really great not to have to remove the top from the machine to empty it because that can often be cumbersome and difficult.This machine does a great job shredding just about anything.  Credit cards and CD's are no problem, paper is easy, just be sure to keep it close to the 8 sheet thickness at one a time.  This shredder is great to pop in junk mail without even opening.  The micro-cut is much more secure than my older crosscut, though I still put parts of the shred in different trash bags just to keep things really secure.  The shredded material is great for packing material and there are so many other great uses.Overall, I really like theAmazonBasics 8-Sheet Micro-Cut Shredder.  If you compare comparable prices for a "micro-cut" shredder you are easily paying 2-3 times the base price of this model.  This product is a really great value and I would recommend it.

To be honest, before I even opened the package I had this review all planned out. I have a mail order business, & I have used Avery labels many times in the past. The quality has always been superb, but they're just priced too high for me & that's what I'd planned to say along with 4 stars (5 for quality, 3 for price).Well, I'm glad I printed a few first. In fact the backing is thinner then the 2 brands of generic labels I normally use.Out of about 15 prints in an admittedly picky HP 4400, there were 3 "paper jams" caused by the HP not being happy with the backing. I use quotes around the phrase paper jam, because they weren't full jams; the printer just stopped & thought it was jammed.I recently returned a batch of a new brand of generic labels for the same problem, but again the generics I normally use don't have this issue. I printed around 30 of my usual generic labels tonight with no problem before switching to the Avery's.On the other hand, the actual labels continue to be best in the business. Solid, thick, great adhesive, as smudge proof as they get & easy to peel.Unfortunately, between the thin backing (which also curls after 1 of the 2 labels has been used) & the high price (about 6 1/2 times the cost of quality generics), I can only go 3 stars.I look forward to comments from regular Avery users regarding the thin backing issue. I use labels for my business, & it would be useful to know if Avery is now using this thin backing on all their labels.

I love this printer/scanner/copier/fax machine!!First off, it was packed very, very carefully. It's sleek and black, and we actually decided to place it on top of a low bookcase in our living room. Nothing ugly or industrial looking about it.Setup was truly a breeze. I have to say, though, that the software setup on my Mac did not go smoothly, but I knew how to get around it. The disk was supposed to go out to the Internet and retrieve the Mac Mountain Lion setup software, drivers, etc., but it would never get to the download page. Instead, I went to the Canon website, searched for the MX522 software downloads for Mac, and just installed each module individually. It went pretty quickly and everything worked just fine. I added the printer and scanner to my Print and Scan system module, and I was able to print and scan anything I wanted--even scanned a multipage document after I inserted it into the document feeder. I just went into one of my usual applications (could be Preview or Photoshop or Graphic Converter) and imported the document using the multipage checkbox in the dialog box for scanning.Printing was easy, and the output looks great!Then I was really impressed by the ease with which I could print from my iPhone or iPad. The printer is AirPrint compatible right out of the box. I just have to select the forward or output function in any app, and one of the choices in Print. I choose Print, and the file starts printing on the Canon within seconds.I've used it for copying. It has a 2-sided option, which is really good for saving paper. You can also print 2-sided by choosing that option via the print dialog box on your computer.I haven't tried faxing yet, but if the function is as good as all the other functions on this device, I'm sure it works perfectly. I certainly never carried one along with my laptop with which I use an externally attached mouse for ease.  I found I could get by most times just using a hard surface. But, that's a minor nit - since it does still work like it's supposed to.Bottom Line:  A great idea from the 3M folks that provides a sturdy, ultra thin and portable mouse pad with a well-designed surface that works as promised.

It took me a few weeks to get the Brother MFC-9320CW to a point where I could actually use it and give it a review. My first problem was electrical. This big boy pulls some juice. I set it up and plugged it into the wall outlet where all my other computer equipment is plugged in through a UPS and when I rebooted my computer... uh oh... computer didn't work (that was scary!). Unplugged the printer and started the computer again and it worked fine. Tried plugging the printer into another outlet but on the same circuit and everything worked but got a very bad hum in the computer speakers both in that room and the next. Finally ran a cord across the room to a plug on a different circuit and all is well. I am using the printer in a home office with 30 year old residential wiring. If you're in the same situtation, you might have to do some rearranging to handle the load. My second issue was the installation. After using the recommended install procedure and software, any time the printer went into its power saving sleep it became disconnected from my compuer and couldn't be reconnected without a reboot. Convenient, huh? I finally had to delete the printer and let Windows autodetect and reinstall it for it to perform properly. As far as print quality and performance, as a casual user I am completely happy. It's very nice to have a machine with output that doesn't smear when it gets wet! I do find the button interface to be less than intuitive. I am accustomed to devices that are "copy ready" as default and this device switches itself to fax mode as the function that is set to when ever idle. As I do not use it for faxing, it's kind of annoying to have to poke several buttons to make a single copy of something. And if I did want to use it for faxing, I'd hate it. You cannot use the fax function on a shared single telephone line with voice calls and an answering machine and set to automatic. You can either get calls and use your answering machine and pick up faxes manually or get faxes automatically and take voice calls but no answering machine unless you have distinctive ring service from the phone utility. I know it is possible to do this, but HP devices seem to be the only ones that can do it. You might also care that this printer is a bit noisy when it's not in sleep mode. The device has a rattly sort of hum that would probably be undetectable in a busy office environment, but in a quiet home, it's fairly noticeable. It's possible to set time before it goes to a fairly short span though, and then it is silent. So, after a few trials 've got a very serviceable printer/scanner/copier and a not so useable fax machine.

This scanner is suprisingly both solid and lightweight.  It is smaller than my giant film/negative scanner (which I love and which also is an Epson), and it doesn't have a carriage lock.  The included cable and power supply are nice heavy gauge and have chokes.Setting it up was fairly easy.  The scanner was not recognized natively in OS X Lion, so I needed to install the driver package. Unlike my earlier Epson software, it also runs very smoothly and quickly without hangs or crashes.  Using it on fully automatic settings, it recognized photos, color documents, and text documents and rendered excellent images of them.There's no sheet feeder, so I would never use this for heavy duty document scanning, but it is an excellent photoscanner.  The scanning software automatically enhances the images unless you set it to manual.  The results were pleasing for quick copies, but I would probably tweak for enlargements.  I would give this four stars based on quality and ease of use alone.  However, I have given it five stars accounting for the value conferred by virtue of the very reasonable price.

Wow! I was very impressed with Canon's attention to detail for the out of box experience. Even so far as the box itself - it had the handhold cutouts and it was a fair sized box big enough to be awkward without them but small enough that other mfgs wouldn't have gone to the expense. Compared to a similar sized Samsung laser printer box, Samsung chose to go with the less user friendly handhold-free box.Opening the box reveals, sitting right on top, clear instructions on how to safely take your investment of money out and how to set it up. It seems funny having to mention that this is an oobe attention to detail thing but lots of expensive bulky boxed items are a bit mysterious along these lines. You dump it out or try to pull it out and sort of hope for the best.All restraining/shipping tape is orange for high visibility rather than plain masking tape. The instruction sheet clearly marks the location of all of it and the doohickey that secures the toner cartridge.The toner cartridge removal is very easy but that seems to be typical for laser printers. You need to remove it and give it a good shake before printing of course.Set up on my home wireless lan was easy as pie. I downloaded the latest drivers from Canon's website for Win7 and had them installed with no problems.The printer is compact for an all-in-one. About the size of most of the 'compact' class machines from what I can tell. If you have a good sized desk you could have this sitting on your desktop. Or on the return if you have one.It looks good. The control panel extends out from the body of the printer at an angle so it is easy to use and looks spiffy too.Sadly, Canon has decided not to provide Linux drivers. That is a real shame to limit the market on a great printer.Now, if you need only to print you can save a substantial amount by getting one of the single function B&W; laser printers like this Samsung:Samsung ML-2165W Wireless Monochrome Printer. Post-it notes are one of the most amazing inventions in the history of office products.  There are now dozens of iterations- big ones, small ones, tiny tabs, clear stickies, you name it.Avery has jumped on the sticky notes bandwagon with a variety of great products.  I'm something of a post-it note fanatic- I have these things stuck all over my books, notebooks and office in general.My excitement peaked when I saw these Avery See-Through stick notes. The colors are somewhat unusual which makes it easier to pick them out from among standard single folders (my other folders are primary colors).The only drawback is that they are attached at the sides very weakly (though they are very strongly connected at the bottom). I'm not sure if the way in which they were connected on the sides was supposed to be that way to make it easier to simply open them up fully if one would like to do so or if this was perhaps a gluing mistake and they were never supposed to be connected at all, but I found it odd that they weren't either completed disconnected at the sides or more strongly attached. I was really impressed with these boxes.  I use "Banker's Boxes" all the time, and just assumed these "Moving Boxes" would be the same type of thing.  I was pleasantly surprised when I found how different these boxes were, and I immediately saw some great benefits depending on what you were using them for.Well, these Moving Boxes are NOT Banker's Boxes, and while I think Banker's Boxes excel at the purpose of STORAGE, I think these boxes truly are dedicated to the singular task of MOVING your possessions.Here is a comparison of the two styles:The Banker's Boxes were 16 inches long, 13 inches wide, and 10 inches high.The Moving Boxes were 17 inches long, 12.25 inches wide, and 12.5 inches high.The Banker's Boxes were not as tall, and were slightly shorter lengthwise.  This meant that they fit more comfortably in my closet where I store things.  The Moving Boxes, on the other hand were a little larger and probably wouldn't fit the way I would want in my closet, and for all storage related purposes I would probably go for the Banker's Boxes.  In addition, the tops of the moving boxes are not flat like the Banker's Boxes -they have a cardboard fold on the top of the box, so there is double cardboard for half of the top, and single cardboard for the other half.  Therefore, two boxes on top of each other (long term) might not be quite as stable -especially since they are taller.In addition, because of this fold, and of the way they lock, Moving Boxes don't open quite as easily or quickly as Banker's Boxes -whose tops come off with the flick of a finger.However, the Moving Boxes really shone in a couple  of areas:1) Easy to make: They were SUPER easy to put together; a lot easier than Banker's Boxes, and you can save time using them (over Banker's Boxes) -especially with people who haven't put together boxes before.  The Moving Boxes were a single piece of cardboard, and by a few quick motions, turned into a full box with a built in top.  The Banker's Boxes take at least twice as long to put together (because you have to make the tops and the bottoms separately), and when you are using them for moving, this can add some time -especially when you are talking 20+ boxes.2) No tape: The other huge advantage for Moving Boxes boxes is that they do not require tape.  "Well", you might say, "Banker's Boxes don't require tape either".  Yes and no.  Banker's Boxes don't require tape for storage, but if you have ever moved an entire apartment with Banker's Boxes, and you've been stacking them high to move them, and any wind picks up, you might see the tops fly off, and end up running down the street to get them.  (I ended up putting tape on all the tops of my Banker's Boxes so that this didn't happen, and this took even more time and materials.)  The Moving Boxes, however, have an innovative design which folds the top down upon itself, locking it tight, (providing even more cushioning for the hand holes), making it very unlikely the top would fly off in the wind.3) Re-use: Are you one of those people who like to take apart boxes after a move, compress them flat, and use them later on? Then you'll love the Moving Boxes.  Unlike the two piece Banker's Boxes, these Moving Boxes are only a single piece -they are much easier to take apart, store, and reuse later.  (Taking apart the tops of the Banker's Boxes and storing them along with the bottoms is a little bit of a pain.)4) Sturdiness: The Moving Boxes are definitely more sturdy.  The cardboard is thicker, and they would definitely not get as beat up as the Banker's Boxes if you are moving them around a lot.  I would trust my delicate possessions more readily to the Moving Boxes than to the Banker's Boxes.So, all in all, if you are looking to MOVE, then these Moving Boxes are fantastic.  If you just want boxes for STORAGE only, I would probably go for banker's boxes.  And if you really want something that does both, you could go either way and be fine.

This nifty, small (4 x 3 3/8) Spanish-English "speaking" dictionary fits handily within coat pockets and purses.  It holds eight "books", including two dictionaries, a thesaurus, and grammar guide. There are, as examples, 13 test lessons in Spanish grammar, five in English, and additionally the item will benefit those who primarily wish to readily conjugate.  The keyboard is quite little but will be acceptable to all but those with the most uncoordinated fingers.  It is to be hoped that a subsequent model will incorporate a much needed back light as the screen is difficult to see in darkened rooms and other areas.  Otherwise, the product's vagaries are those to which most will speedily adapt.  The package contains required AAA batteries (Energizer), a USB cable that will facilitate downloading of user inventories onto the dictionary, and adequate headphones.  Simply by entering a single word, a user will activate an inclusive search engine for conversational Spanish phrases.  There are other valuable components to the item: a back navigation key, an automatic shutoff following a selected three or five minute span of inactivity to extend battery life, even a screen symbol that displays the amount of battery life remaining.  Most will likely not delve into the offered word games, and a standard phrase book/dictionary will be the preference for field use by many, but this mini laptop (the screen folds back to 180 degrees), in spite of its rather substandard speaker quality, will please those users who will take the time to explore its attributes.

Scotch Adhesive Dot Roller is a useful device that makes a practical alternative to glue, ordinary tape, and other types of adhesive. With this roller, you can reach areas that may be out of the reach of other types of adhesive, while avoiding the mess common with liquid adhesives.This adhesive dot roller is simple enough to use. You just use your fingertip to pop open the white, protective flap and lock it in place. Then, with the tip of the device touching the paper, cardboard, or other object, you slide the roller across. It will leave a narrow strip of adhesive behind. The device needs to be held near a ninety- degree angle in order for it to work. Held at a smaller angle- say forty five degrees- will not work. The roller on the tip will not touch the paper and no adhesive will release. You will know when adhesive is released because you will hear a clicking sound. If you don't hear the sound, adjust your angle and try again.Scotch Adhesive Dot Roller has many uses and it provides enough stickiness to hold items in place, yet not so much stickiness that it damages the surfaces of the item being stuck or the object to which it is being stuck. I have found this device most useful for adhering small pictures to a scrapbook and it is also very useful for self- printed address labels. Just a swipe or two down the backside of your address label, picture, or other item is all it takes to prep it for sticking. Removing the item is simple enough and there are no signs of damage, as long as you remove carefully.I find this adhesive device useful and practical and I like that it can be refilled. However, I'm not too crazy about the price and the amount of adhesive it contains. There is a total of forty- nine feet of tape in each roll. If you do a very large amount of taping, a roll isn't going to last for very long. Other, similar devices offer more tape for a lower price. This device is more compact than its closest competitors, but for cost and efficiency, there are some better options available.Still, in spite of the relatively small amount of tape and the price, I like the Scotch Adhesive Dot Roller. It comes in very handy when you need to attach pictures, notes, and other paper or cardboard items to scrapbooks and other places. I will continue to use it for these and other purposes.

Okay, start with a printer that doesn't use a standard USB connector (U means universal, Kodak, what part of that don't you understand?)  Then missing at the unusually high price are an automatic document feeder and fax and the ability to scan larger items like books.  Add a pretty dated design and some seriously cheap plastic parts.  What do you have?  A name that is barely known in the printer business compared to the grandaddies HP, Epson and Canon (remember those names in inkjet printers that are long gone like Xerox?)So what about its so-called major virtue, cheap ink?  First off I would have to balance that against the price of the printer, which is almost 3x what I can get one of the big 3 (four if you count Lexmark).  Will I make up that difference?  I haven't had this long enough to find out.  And then there's that universal warning about worrying about the cost of ink cartridges for your printer ... it's not how much the cartridge costs, but how many pages you will get out of the cartridge.  Again, I haven't had the Kodak long enough to compare.  I will try to update this review once I know.Other than that, Kodak is a known and trusted name and the printer is functional.  If you buy one you will probably find it does about as good a job as any other brand.  Printers are a commodity anymore, they're all good.  I would make just one final observation.  Inkjet printers ALL cost a lot to operate, even for black-only text.  Your best bet is to own two printers ... a laser for 85% of what you will ever print, and an inkjet for the rare times you really need color.  And of course for printing photos, if you really do that.  And if you do, if you really print photos, do NOT buy a cheap inkjet.  Get a quality photo printer and enjoy the art of digital photography.
